When it comes to long-lived assets, like e.g. power generators or electricity infrastructure, which operate for many years or decades, purchase and investment decisions lock in path- dependencies for many years and even decades (unless these assets are prematurely retired e.g. due to economic or regulatory forcing). It is important to make such decisions based on a forward-looking assessment of the enabled average lifetime impact compared to a fair counterfactual scenario (e.g. “not making the purchase at all” or “purchasing a fossil fuel asset instead”). People often underestimate the full cumulative negative GHG emissions lifetime impact of setting up a new gas-fired powerplant that is likely to operate for the next 20-30 years. Likewise, the positive GHG emission avoidance impact enabled by setting up a new wind power plant that is likely to operate for the next 20-30 years is underestimated, too. Consequential lifetime estimates initially require working with assumptions about average performance and preliminary scenarios about how the power mix/grid intensity is expected to develop over this timeframe. After the asset has been installed and is operated by the new owner, actual data about annual yield, uptime, power mix etc allow for updating the initial assumptions by actual data.
There is a trade-off between pragmatism and accuracy. Depending on the use case, the level of precision and certainty required varies, too. A rough 80/20 internal estimate is often good enough to provide directional guidance for business decision making. In this case, demanding the resource investment for a 99% accuracy level would simply be economically unfeasible and overengineered. It would discourage making pragmatically and reasonably informed decisions. For internal business decision making, strong additionality doesn’t need to be proven, double counting is less of an issue. Indeed, it is only when actual carbon credits are issued and paid for by customers that additionality represents an important requirement and overlap (i.e. two customers paying for the same real-world impact claim) should not be allowed.
It is crucial to recognize that lifetime avoidance is enabled by multiple value chain actors in a collective impact effort, where each agent – suppliers, OEMs, planners and installers, owners and operators (and waste managers at end of life) - contributes to the outcome with different levels of quality, which can range from trivial/commodity (e.g. for standard screws, cosmetics, or standard material, which can be easily sourced and serves many industries) to substantial and fundamental (e.g. for highly specialized climate solution-related materials – e.g. SiC semiconductors - or components and services, without which the total system couldn’t function or would perform significantly worse):
1) On the supply side, up until the final handover of the installed turnkey system to the end-customer, lifetime GHG emission avoidance (estimates based on average future performance assumptions) is enabled by the upstream value chain (from raw material sourcing to planning, EPC, assembly, deliverable and installation, training). Similarly to scope 3, where overlap is a feature, not a bug, enabled avoidance (which are based on comparisons of LCAs, including scope 3) builds on another and overlaps rather than - misleadingly - adding up to 100%.
2) On the demand side, after the transfer of ownership, the potential of enabled lifetime GHG emission avoidance becomes actually realized over time (based on empirically measurable performance) by the owner and operator. Here, maintenance activities enable annual impact realization.

The Scope 2 TWG subgroup formula is good for a very specific, limited and laborious use case: estimating scope 2 for a given year with unprecedented (and usually unnecessary) precision. But when presented as a general formula, it can be unintentionally misleading and impractical. If it is easily possible e.g. with a smart meter, accurately measuring and aggregating the *hourly* impact of electricity consumed for a single year might be most accurate for an already existing, operating asset (or purchase agreement), but seems to create unjustified workload for little impact value. In any case, when compared against the GHG intensity of electricity that would have been otherwise consumed, the scope 2 measurement represents an impact measured on the demand side, but this has little to do with broader guidance needed for consequential GHG accounting at the technology or production asset level e.g. to inform investment and business decisions.

There are many important use cases for consequential GHG accounting on the investment and supply side, e.g. when the asset in question is operating or when it is still within the value chain in the process of being delivered or has just been sold (perspective of the selling company), that don’t benefit from aggregating 8700 hourly states. Estimating the enabled impact of clean electricity production/transmission&distribution/saving/trading/consumption (for electrification purposes!) is much broader than what the scope 2 TWG subgroup formula represnets: Trying to estimate the impact of a newly installed solar PV farm or wind power farm in terms of the amount of clean electricity that is likely to *produce* during its operational lifetime (ready for transmission and distribution to the places of consumption) in order to displace a dynamic, declining average power mix (unless more specifici information is available) that would have been consumed otherwise. In this case, forward-looking annual lifetime averages serve their purpose, they are “good enough”, inspite of uncertainty, which needs to be tolerated (e.g. within a reasonable tolerance band or with conservative assumptions).

Upstream GHG emissions (in gCO2e/kWh) are usually not negligible, and especially high (+15-20%) for fossil fuel -based electricity as the GHG emissions from the continuous extraction, processing, transport, including methane leakage!, need to be accounted for. Clean energy generators only incur GHG emissions once during the production process, wheras the operation and maintance is near emission-free. When distributed across average lifetime output, windpower carbon intensity including upstream GHG emissions would be within a range of e.g. ~8-15 gCO2/kWh.
It is important to be consistent and transparent - when adding upstream GHG emissions for renewable energy, it should be added for fossil fuel generators or the power mix, too.
Reported once for the lifetime of the project

Both. Both reports are not mutually exclusive. The forward-looking lifetime estimation is based on typical, average performance assumptions, the annual reporting is based on actual performance and updates the initial assumptions.

We need to be careful about what kind of additionality is really needed and how high the burden of proof is for a given use case, and whether a proof of additionality is needed or effective at all. IF public funding or performance-linked payments, or purchases for carbon credits are involved, the burden of proof for strong/deep additionality is high, of course. This usually requires proving that e.g. for economic feasibility reasons, the project would not have been funded by a commercial investor or company (were it not for an enabling (catalytic) grant or subsidy (additionality of funding/investor impact). More generally, it may require proving that without a specific activity a specific impact could not have been possible (additionality of company/product/service impact). In case of green marketing, there is a need to make sure that impact claims are well substantiated and trustworthy, but the additionality evidence required depends on the strength of the marketing claim being made. Evidence for additionality may not be needed at all when the assessment serves internal decision making purposes. Of course the quality of an impact is higher, but in a competitive market environment, the scalability of climate solution impacts is higher when no economic concessions are needed in the first place (institutional investors are constrained by fiduciary duties and company managers are constrained by director duties). So, all tests should be optional, depending on the need for evidence and the strength of any “additionality claims” being made.

With regard to the regulatory test, the establishment of a strong mandatory regulatory standard does not suddenly nullify avoidance impacts that are enabled by companies in the value chain. If there were, for example, a sales ban of ICE cars in 2035, it would be unreasonable to conclude that from 2034 to 2035 the very real and important GHG avoidance impact of EVs would suddenly disappear or become void. Selling EVs until the last ICE has been retired is a crucial activity that must be continued regardless of supporting legislation. Company activities are crucial to make sure that the impact potential enabled by a new regulation can actually be realized. The quality of regulation matters, too. A weak regulation that legally requires what is already economic market standard has no accelerating effect on the energy transition. A strong regulation forces market share shifts to happen faster than would otherwise be observable. However, overly ambitious regulation that exceeds economic/technological capabilities of companies will again fail to make any difference in transition dynamics.

From an MRV (Measurement, Reporting, and Verification) perspective, the proposed Scope 2 TWG subgroup formula referenced in Section 6.1 of the Consequential Electricity-Sector Emissions Impacts document is structurally appropriate for quantifying emissions impacts from electricity projects, for the following reasons:

Clear causal framing (consequential logic)
The formula is explicitly designed to capture changes in system-wide emissions attributable to an intervention, rather than simple attribution. This aligns with internationally accepted consequential accounting principles used in policy and market-impact assessments, which is essential when evaluating electricity procurement decisions that alter dispatch or investment behavior.

Logical separation of effects
The structure distinguishes between:

Primary effects (direct changes in generation or procurement), and

Secondary/system effects (induced dispatch or capacity changes elsewhere in the grid).
This separation improves transparency and verifiability, allowing MRV practitioners to independently assess each component and avoid double counting.

Consistency with existing GHG Protocol architecture
While expanding beyond traditional attributional Scope 2 accounting, the formula remains conceptually consistent with GHG Protocol guidance by:

Using emissions factors multiplied by electricity quantities (ΔMWh × EF), and

Applying aggregation over a defined reporting period.
This consistency supports auditability and comparability across reporting entities.

Verifier-friendly structure
From a verification standpoint, the equation is:

Modular, allowing assumptions and data sources to be checked per term,

Traceable, as each variable can be linked to metered data, modeled outputs, or documented system parameters, and

Scalable, applicable to single projects or portfolios without structural modification.

Appropriate neutrality on methodological inputs
Importantly, the formula itself does not hard-code methodological choices (e.g., specific marginal emission rates or eligibility thresholds). This is appropriate at the structural level and allows such parameters to be governed separately by methodological rules, which supports flexibility while preserving rigor.

Conclusion:
As an MRV verifier, the structure of the proposed Scope 2 TWG subgroup formula is sound, transparent, and suitable for quantifying consequential emissions impacts from electricity projects. Any remaining concerns relate to parameter selection or data quality, which are methodological issues appropriately addressed outside the formula itself.

Additional context on secondary effects (MRV verifier perspective)

When quantifying emissions impacts from electricity projects under a consequential accounting approach, several categories of secondary effects should be considered, to the extent that they are material and can be credibly quantified. These effects reflect how electricity systems respond to an intervention beyond the directly procured or generated electricity.

1. Dispatch (operational) effects

What they are:
Changes in the short-run operation of the power system, where increased or decreased electricity generation or demand from a project alters which power plants are dispatched.

Examples:

Renewable generation displacing marginal fossil-fuel generators.

Increased electricity demand causing higher output from peaking plants.

How they may be quantified:

Apply marginal emission rates (MERs) or short-run marginal emission factors to incremental changes in electricity generation or consumption (ΔMWh).

Use historical dispatch data or production-cost modeling to identify marginal units.

2. Capacity investment effects

What they are:
Longer-term changes in power plant investment or retirement decisions driven by sustained electricity procurement or demand signals.

Examples:

Accelerated retirement of high-emitting generation.

Delayed or avoided construction of fossil capacity due to long-term clean power contracts.

How they may be quantified:

Use long-run marginal emission rates (LRMERs).

Apply scenario-based power-system expansion models comparing a “with-project” vs. “without-project” case over a defined reporting period.

3. Market and price-mediated effects

What they are:
Changes in electricity prices or market conditions that indirectly influence consumption, generation, or fuel switching.

Examples:

Lower wholesale prices increasing electricity demand elsewhere.

Reduced fossil generation affecting fuel markets and plant utilization.

How they may be quantified:

Econometric analysis or integrated assessment models.

Simplified elasticity-based approaches where full modeling is not feasible.

Key references:

WRI – Power Markets and Emissions Impacts
https://www.wri.org/energy

4. Temporal and locational shifting effects

What they are:
Changes in when and where electricity is generated or consumed, which affect emissions intensity.

Examples:

Load shifting from peak to off-peak hours with different marginal emissions.

Imports or exports across interconnected grids.

How they may be quantified:

Time-resolved marginal emission factors (hourly or sub-hourly).

Regional or nodal grid emissions modeling.

MRV applicability and safeguards

From a verification standpoint, secondary effects should be:

Material to overall emissions impacts,

Transparent and well-documented, and

Conservatively estimated where uncertainty is high.

Where data or modeling constraints exist, it is acceptable to prioritize the most significant secondary effects (typically dispatch and capacity impacts) and disclose exclusions with justification.

Conclusion

Secondary effects such as dispatch changes, capacity investment responses, market-mediated impacts, and temporal or locational shifts are integral to accurately quantifying emissions impacts from electricity projects. These effects can be quantified using marginal emission rates, scenario-based system modeling, and time-resolved data, consistent with best practice in consequential GHG accounting.

From an MRV and assurance standpoint, emissions impacts from electricity projects should be calculated and reported on an annual basis, for the following reasons:

Alignment with established GHG reporting frameworks
Leading standards require emissions to be quantified and disclosed per reporting year, reflecting actual system conditions during that period rather than ex-ante projections over a full project lifetime. Annual reporting ensures consistency with corporate and national GHG inventories.

Improved accuracy and environmental integrity
Grid emissions factors, dispatch patterns, fuel mixes, and market conditions change over time. Annual calculation captures these dynamics, whereas lifetime-at-outset estimates rely heavily on assumptions that may become inaccurate or outdated.

Stronger verifiability and auditability
Annual reporting allows verifiers to assess emissions impacts against observable data (metered generation, grid data, updated emission factors). Lifetime upfront estimates are inherently harder to verify and more sensitive to modeling uncertainty.

Avoidance of over- or under-crediting
Reporting impacts once for the project lifetime risks locking in emissions claims that may not materialize as expected due to curtailment, grid decarbonization, or operational changes. Annual reporting enables corrections over time, reducing misstatement risk.

Consistency with MRV best practice and conservativeness
Periodic reporting supports conservative accounting, transparency, and comparability across projects and years, which are core MRV principles under both voluntary and compliance-oriented systems.

Conclusion

Annual calculation and reporting of emissions impacts provides greater accuracy, transparency, and verifiability than a one-time lifetime estimate, and is therefore preferable for MRV-aligned electricity project accounting.

1. Regulatory test — Required

Why include:
Confirms the project is not mandated by law or regulation. Crediting legally required actions would violate environmental integrity by rewarding business-as-usual outcomes. This test is a foundational safeguard against non-additional claims.

2. Timing test — Required

Why include:
Establishes causality by showing that the project decision occurred after (and was influenced by) the incentive or procurement mechanism. Without this, projects that would have proceeded anyway could be incorrectly credited.

3. Common practice test — Required

Why include:
Prevents crediting technologies or project types that are already widely deployed without incentives. If a project type is common practice, it is unlikely to be driven by the incentive being assessed.

4. Contractual / tenor test — Required

Why include:
Especially relevant for electricity procurement (e.g., PPAs). It tests whether contract duration, firmness, and risk allocation are sufficient to plausibly enable new renewable capacity, rather than merely reallocating existing generation.

Optional tests
5. Financial analysis test — Optional

Why include:
Demonstrates that the project is not financially viable without the incentive. While powerful, it is sensitive to assumptions (prices, discount rates) and can be burdensome to verify, so it should remain optional rather than mandatory.

6. Barrier test — Optional

Why include:
Identifies non-financial barriers (institutional, technical, regulatory, market) that prevent implementation absent the incentive. Useful in emerging markets, but inherently qualitative and harder to standardize.

7. Positive list — Optional

Why include:
Allows streamlined eligibility for predefined technologies or contexts with strong evidence of additionality (e.g., early-stage technologies). Making it optional avoids over-crediting once technologies mature.

8. Performance standard — Optional

Why include:
Uses benchmarks or thresholds (e.g., emissions intensity) to identify projects that outperform typical practice. Effective where robust data exist, but not universally applicable across all grids and technologies.

1. Grid congestion and deliverability test

What it assesses:
Whether the renewable project can physically deliver electricity to the grid or load without persistent congestion that limits displacement of fossil generation.

Why it should be considered:
A project that is frequently curtailed or constrained may have lower real-world emissions impact than assumed. Including this test strengthens environmental integrity by linking additionality to actual system influence.

2. Curtailment risk test

What it assesses:
The likelihood that renewable generation will be systematically curtailed due to grid conditions, market rules, or oversupply.

Why it should be considered:
High-curtailment projects may not deliver incremental clean electricity to the system, weakening the causal link between the project and emissions reductions.

3. Policy interaction / overlap test

What it assesses:
Whether the project’s emissions impacts are already accounted for under binding policies (e.g., renewable portfolio standards, capacity auctions, ETS caps).

Why it should be considered:
Avoids double claiming of emissions reductions and ensures the project drives outcomes beyond what existing policies would deliver.

4. Durability / persistence test

What it assesses:
Whether the project’s emissions impact is durable over time, including operational lifetime, contract stability, and risk of early termination.

Why it should be considered:
Short-lived or easily reversible impacts undermine long-term decarbonization claims. This test complements contractual/tenor analysis by focusing on actual persistence, not just contract length.

5. Exclusivity / claim-rights test

What it assesses:
Whether the project’s environmental attributes (e.g., RECs, GOs, carbon claims) are exclusively claimed by a single party.

Why it should be considered:
Prevents multiple entities from asserting additionality or emissions benefits from the same MWh, reinforcing credibility and market confidence.

6. Incrementality / scale test

What it assesses:
Whether the project represents a material increase in capacity or generation relative to baseline trends, rather than a marginal or token addition.

Why it should be considered:
Very small or symbolic projects may pass formal tests yet deliver negligible system impact. This test supports relevance and proportionality.

7. System marginality alignment test

What it assesses:
Whether the project is aligned with periods or locations of high marginal emissions, increasing the likelihood of meaningful displacement.

Why it should be considered:
Projects that generate primarily during low-emissions periods may be less consequential. This test links additionality to actual emissions leverage.

Regional differences should be considered when designing and applying additionality tests for renewable energy projects, because electricity markets, policy environments, and investment conditions vary substantially across regions. Applying a uniform set of tests without regional adjustment can either undermine environmental integrity or unnecessarily exclude genuinely additional projects.

Key reasons regional differentiation is necessary:

Variation in regulatory frameworks
Renewable energy mandates, subsidies, and grid access rules differ widely by country and region. A project that is clearly non-additional in a highly regulated market may still be additional in a region with weak or absent policy support. Regulatory and common-practice tests must therefore be assessed in a regional context.

Differences in market maturity and penetration
Renewable technologies may be common practice in one region but nascent in another. Regional deployment levels directly affect the relevance and stringency of common practice, performance standard, and first-of-its-kind tests.

Divergent investment and financing conditions
Capital costs, cost of capital, currency risk, and access to finance vary significantly across regions. As a result, the financial analysis and barrier tests may be critical in emerging markets but less informative in mature markets.

Grid characteristics and system constraints
Grid emissions intensity, dispatch behavior, and capacity adequacy differ by region. These differences affect both the credibility of additionality claims and the suitability of contractual/tenor or performance-based tests.

Alignment with international best practice
Leading frameworks explicitly recognize the need for context-sensitive application of additionality tests, allowing different combinations of tests to be applied depending on regional circumstances, provided transparency and consistency are maintained.

Conclusion

Considering regional differences allows additionality frameworks to remain robust, fair, and environmentally credible, while avoiding one-size-fits-all rules that fail to reflect real-world electricity system and investment conditions.

The level of rigor in additionality tests should vary depending on the type of claim an organization intends to make, because different claims imply different degrees of causality, confidence, and risk of misinterpretation.

Key reasons differentiated rigor is appropriate:

Different claims imply different causal expectations

Association claims (e.g., “this organization supports renewable electricity”) do not assert that the action directly caused new generation and therefore warrant lower additionality rigor.

Causal claims (e.g., “this procurement enabled new renewable capacity and reduced grid emissions”) explicitly assert impact and therefore require strong, multi-test additionality evidence.

Alignment with environmental integrity principles
Stronger claims require stronger proof. Applying the same rigor to all claim types risks either:

Overstating impacts for weakly supported claims, or

Creating unnecessary barriers for modest, non-causal claims.

Consistency with existing standards and guidance
Leading frameworks distinguish between claims of use, support, or causation, and implicitly or explicitly tie claim strength to the robustness of additionality demonstration.

Improved clarity and reduced greenwashing risk
Graduated rigor helps ensure that claims are accurate, proportionate, and not misleading, which is critical for credibility with regulators, investors, and the public.

Verifier practicality and proportionality
From an MRV standpoint, tailoring rigor to claim type balances assurance effort with materiality, focusing verification resources where the risk of misstatement is highest.

Conclusion

Applying different levels of additionality rigor based on claim type is necessary for credible, transparent, and proportionate emissions and renewable energy claims, particularly when distinguishing between associative and causal assertions.

Beyond traditional operating margin (OM) and build margin (BM) emission factors, several additional emission rates and metrics can be appropriate for assessing the emissions impacts of projects, depending on project type, scale, and the nature of the claim being made.

1. Short-run marginal emission rates (SRMERs)
These reflect emissions from generators responding to incremental, short-term changes in electricity supply or demand. They are appropriate for projects affecting real-time operations, such as variable renewables, demand response, and storage dispatch.

2. Long-run marginal emission rates (LRMERs)
LRMERs capture emissions impacts associated with changes in long-term capacity investment decisions, including avoided or delayed fossil generation. They are suitable for large projects, long-term PPAs, or interventions plausibly affecting future build decisions.

3. Time-resolved emission rates (e.g., hourly or seasonal)
These account for variations in grid emissions by time of day or season, improving accuracy for projects whose generation or consumption profile is time-dependent, such as solar, wind, storage, or load shifting.

4. Locational marginal emission rates
These reflect emissions impacts that vary by geographic location, accounting for congestion, imports/exports, and regional dispatch. They are appropriate for distributed generation or projects in constrained grid areas.

5. Fuel-specific avoided emissions rates
Where evidence indicates displacement of a specific fuel type (e.g., coal or gas), fuel-specific emission factors can provide clearer and more transparent impact estimates.

6. Scenario-based counterfactual emissions metrics
These measure the difference between with-project and without-project scenarios, integrating operational and investment effects. They are appropriate for system-shaping projects, portfolios, or policy-driven interventions.

7. Emissions intensity per unit of delivered service
Metrics such as gCO₂e per MWh firmed, shifted, or delivered allow comparison across projects that provide different grid services (e.g., storage, hybrid systems, electrification).

8. Lifecycle emission rates (LCA-based)
Lifecycle metrics capture emissions from manufacturing through decommissioning. While not suitable for marginal grid impacts, they are useful for technology comparison and strategic planning.

Conclusion
Selecting appropriate emission rates should depend on project characteristics, temporal and locational effects, data availability, and the strength of the claim being made. Using complementary metrics alongside OM and BM can improve relevance, transparency, and environmental integrity when applied consistently and conservatively.

In markets with nodal pricing (e.g., LMP-based systems), dispatch and prices are determined at the node level. Aligning marginal emission rates with the same spatial resolution ensures conceptual consistency between economic dispatch and emissions accounting.

Aggregated regions can combine low- and high-emitting marginal units, leading to systematic over- or under-estimation of emissions impacts, particularly in congested grids or weakly interconnected systems.

Best practice for high-impact or system-shaping projects
For large projects, storage, or load-shifting interventions where location materially affects outcomes, nodal marginal emission rates provide the highest analytical fidelity.

MRV safeguards still apply

Dispatch or SCED data are available,

Methods are transparent and reproducible, and

Results are subject to verification.
Where these conditions are not met, coarser levels (zonal or balancing area) may be more appropriate.

In addition to the approaches already listed, several alternative, defensible approaches could be used to assign build margin (BM) and operating margin (OM) weights for electricity projects, provided transparency and conservativeness are maintained.

1. Contract-based causality approach
OM and BM weights can be assigned based on contract characteristics, such as duration, firmness, volume, and risk allocation. Long-term, firm contracts (e.g., long-dated PPAs) that credibly support financing of new capacity would receive higher BM weighting, while short-term or non-firm arrangements would be weighted more toward OM. This approach directly links weighting to investment signals.

2. Dynamic or phased weighting over the project lifecycle
Rather than a static split, OM and BM weights can change over time. Early years emphasize OM impacts reflecting dispatch effects, while later years gradually increase BM weighting as investment and retirement responses materialize. This better reflects how electricity systems respond to interventions over time.

3. Materiality- or scale-based weighting
Weights can be determined based on the size of the project relative to the grid (e.g., share of peak demand or annual generation). Small projects with negligible investment influence would receive OM-heavy weighting, while large or system-shaping projects would receive higher BM weighting.

4. Reliability and peak-coincidence approach
BM weighting can be increased for projects that contribute to resource adequacy or peak demand reduction, such as firm renewables, storage, or demand-side projects that reduce capacity needs. Projects with little contribution to reliability would remain OM-weighted.

5. Empirical or econometric response approach
Where data are available, historical analysis of similar projects can be used to estimate the observed split between dispatch effects and capacity additions, with OM/BM weights derived from empirical evidence rather than defaults.

We welcome the opportunity to provide feedback on the GHG Protocol’s public consultation on consequential electricity-sector emissions impacts. We support, in principle, the development of consequential accounting methods for electricity-sector actions, recognising their potential to improve how organisations quantify and report consequential GHG impacts from electricity actions. However, we have not reviewed or formed a position on the specific proposed calculations or methodologies in this consultation. Our feedback focuses on overarching principles, practical considerations, and implications for New Zealand, rather than technical details.
Potential benefits
1. Better decision-making: Consequential accounting focuses on the estimated change in emissions from actions, not allocation by consumption. This could help New Zealand organisations prioritise actions that deliver decarbonisation, such as investing in projects that are outside New Zealand, or investing in flexible capacity or storage.
2. Alignment with New Zealand’s renewable grid: With ~80-85% renewable electricity, attributional methods can overstate the impact of buying renewable electricity. Consequential methods may provide more accurate insights into marginal impacts, for example, reducing fossil fuel generation during dry years or peaks.
3. Supports policy and investment: Consequential accounting could inform government and corporate strategies, ensuring investments target emissions-intensive marginal generation rather than simply claiming renewable attributes.
Challenges
1. Data availability and granularity: Consequential methods require marginal emissions factors and scenario modelling. In New Zealand, hydro variability and seasonal dry-year risks complicate marginal emissions estimation. Hydro variability and dry-year risks complicate estimation, as fossil backup use fluctuates.
2. Complexity and cost: Developing and maintaining models for New Zealand’s relatively unique hydro-dominated system would be resource-intensive for both regulators and companies. Smaller organisations may lack capacity to apply these methods.
3. Comparability: If organisations use different assumptions or datasets, claims may become non-comparable, undermining trust and complicating alignment with New Zealand’s mandatory climate-related disclosures.
Unintended consequences
1. Misinterpreting impacts: Actions that appear beneficial under attributional accounting may show negligible or negative marginal impact in New Zealand’s context. This could risk confusing stakeholders or discouraging activity if not communicated clearly.
2. Potential for gaming or selective baselines: Without standardised baselines and marginal factors, organisations might choose assumptions that maximise perceived impact.
3. Perception issues: Moving to consequential accounting could make some current claims (for example, “100% renewable electricity”) appear less meaningful, creating reputational challenges for organisations that have invested heavily in market-based instruments.
Practical considerations

The primary benefit of developing a consequential accounting method is that it directly aligns corporate climate accounting with the ultimate goal of climate action: maximizing real-world, atmospheric emissions reductions. It answers the question, "What was the change in grid emissions as a consequence of my action?" This moves beyond attributional accounting to focus on tangible impact, creating a powerful incentive for companies to invest in projects that displace the most fossil fuels.

The main challenge is methodological complexity. Calculating accurate marginal emission rates requires sophisticated modeling and robust data, which may not be available in all regions. This creates a risk of inconsistency and a potential for "cherry-picking" favorable methodologies if the rules are not rigorous and standardized.

The key unintended consequence to avoid is creating a system that is perceived as less credible or "auditable" than attributional methods. To prevent this, the methodology must be transparent, based on conservative assumptions, and rooted in peer-reviewed science. If developed correctly, a consequential method would be a powerful new tool. If developed poorly, it could lead to confusion and greenwashing concerns, undermining its potential.

The proposed formula, which quantifies impact as the difference between baseline emissions and project emissions, is a standard and appropriate structure for this type of analysis. It correctly identifies the core components of a consequential calculation. By separating the primary effects (direct displacement of grid electricity) and providing a framework to consider secondary effects, it is both comprehensive and flexible. This structure provides a solid foundation upon which the more detailed methodological components, such as the specific methods for calculating marginal emission rates, can be built. It is aligned with established principles of project-based GHG accounting and provides a logical and defensible starting point.

Secondary effects, such as grid infrastructure changes or long-term market responses induced by a project, should be considered, but likely as a qualitative or supplementary quantitative disclosure rather than part of the core calculation. For example, a large wind project might induce transmission upgrades that enable further renewables, a positive secondary effect. Quantifying these effects is extremely difficult and highly dependent on modeling assumptions. Including them in the primary impact claim could reduce credibility. A better approach is to focus the core, auditable claim on the primary effect (avoided generation emissions) and require a qualitative discussion of potential secondary effects, supported by modeling where feasible.

Impacts must be reported annually. Grid conditions are not static; the marginal emission rate of a grid changes from year to year as new generators come online and old ones retire. A project's impact in year one may be very different from its impact in year 10. Reporting annually provides a much more accurate and relevant picture of a project's ongoing contribution to decarbonization. Reporting a lifetime impact upfront would be based on a long-term forecast that is highly uncertain and would quickly become outdated. Annual reporting aligns with the standard corporate reporting cycle and provides stakeholders with timely, decision-useful information about the performance of a company's project portfolio.

Regulatory test (required): This is a fundamental, nonnegotiable test. If a project is required by law, it is by definition not additional.

Performance standard (required): This establishes a baseline of what is considered standard practice. Projects that outperform this baseline (e.g., are built in a grid with very low renewable penetration) can be considered additional. It is a robust and objective test.

Contractual/tenor test (required): The signing of a long-term (10+ year) PPA is strong evidence of "purchaser-caused" additionality. This long-term revenue certainty is what enables developers to secure financing for new projects. This is a key indicator of a buyer's direct contribution.

Optional tests: The other tests (financial, barrier, common practice, etc.) provide valuable alternative pathways for projects to demonstrate additionality under different circumstances. Not all projects will be able to show financial additionality, but they may face nonfinancial barriers that a corporate PPA helps overcome. Providing a menu of optional tests creates a flexible but rigorous framework.

All the listed tests are feasible to implement, as they are drawn from existing carbon market and project finance practices (e.g., the Clean Development Mechanism, voluntary offset standards). The key to feasibility is not the test itself, but the availability of clear guidance, standardized tools (e.g., financial models), and reliable data for applying the tests. For example, implementing a "common practice test" requires access to good regional data on renewable energy deployment rates. The feasibility challenge is in developing the detailed methodologies and data infrastructure to support consistent application of these tests globally.

The provided list is comprehensive and covers the main established approaches to demonstrating additionality. No additional tests are necessary at this stage. The focus should be on developing rigorous and clear methodologies for the tests already listed, rather than adding more complexity.

It's helpful to consider the significant role of regional context when assessing additionality. In a mature renewable energy market, a conventional wind farm might not demonstrate additionality based on a "common practice" test alone. In that context, it may be appropriate for a project to meet a more rigorous standard, like a financial additionality test or by representing a "first-of-its-kind" technology.

In contrast, for a nascent market with low renewable energy penetration, the first utility-scale wind farm would likely demonstrate high additionality. Here, a more streamlined set of tests (e.g., regulatory surplus and common practice) could be considered sufficient.

Applying a single, stringent financial test universally risks inadvertently creating barriers to investment in these emerging markets, potentially slowing progress where it is highly valued. Therefore, a framework that allows for regional customization of additionality requirements would likely be more effective and balanced.

A tiered approach to claims based on the rigor of the additionality demonstration would enhance credibility. For a strong causal claim, such as "Our investment caused X tonnes of emissions to be avoided," a project should be required to pass a stringent set of additionality tests, including financial or barrier analysis and the contractual/tenor test. For a softer, associational claim, such as "We support projects that contribute to grid decarbonization," a simpler demonstration, perhaps passing only the regulatory and common practice tests, might be sufficient. This allows for different levels of corporate ambition and provides clarity to stakeholders about the strength of the claim being made, linking the quality of the proof to the quality of the claim.

Methodologies based on security-constrained economic dispatch (SCED) models or sophisticated statistical analysis are the most appropriate because they most accurately reflect the complex reality of which power plants are displaced by new renewable generation on an hourly or sub-hourly basis. These methods capture the dynamics of the grid. Simpler methods, like capacity-factor-based or difference-based approaches, are less appropriate because they are proxies that can miss crucial temporal and locational details. For example, a simple approach may not capture the fact that solar power primarily displaces gas peaker plants in the afternoon, while wind power might displace baseload coal at night. The more sophisticated methods are needed to provide credible, investment-grade data for a consequential framework.

Capacity expansion models are the most robust method for quantifying the build margin, as they provide a forward-looking, economically grounded assessment of which future power plants are likely to be avoided or delayed due to the addition of a new renewable project. Analyzing recent capacity additions is a reasonable, simpler proxy, assuming future trends will resemble the recent past. Using a simple average emission rate is not appropriate as it does not reflect the "marginal" plant that is being displaced. Relying on policy scenarios is also problematic, as these are often aspirational and may not reflect the economic reality of what will actually be built.

The GHG Protocol could develop a set of minimum criteria or a "quality screen" for models to be considered credible. This could include requirements for the model to be peer-reviewed, use publicly available data, have transparent assumptions, and be calibrated against historical grid behavior. The applicability could also be tiered: for large, high-impact projects, the use of a sophisticated capacity expansion model could be required, while for smaller projects, a simpler, pre-approved methodology might be acceptable. This would balance rigor with feasibility.

Beyond avoided CO2 emissions, metrics related to other impacts could be valuable as supplementary disclosures. This could include avoided emissions of local air pollutants (SOx, NOx, particulate matter), which have significant public health benefits. Another metric could be water consumption avoided by displacing thirsty thermal power plants. While avoided GHG emissions should remain the core metric for a climate-focused consequential framework, disclosing these co-benefits would provide a more holistic picture of a project's positive impact.

The balancing area (or equivalent, like an ISO/RTO) is the most appropriate level of spatial granularity. This is the geographic region within which the grid is centrally managed and balanced in real time. It is at this level that the economic dispatch decisions that determine the marginal generator are made. Going more granular (e.g., nodal) introduces immense complexity and data volatility that is not necessary for this type of analysis and can be misleading. Going broader (e.g., grid region or country) can miss important regional constraints and differences in the generation mix. The balancing area represents the best balance of accuracy and practicality.

Hourly is the most appropriate temporal granularity. It aligns with the standard settlement period for electricity markets and captures the key diurnal patterns of electricity demand and renewable generation (e.g., the solar "duck curve"). While sub-hourly data exists, the incremental improvement in accuracy for annual reporting purposes is likely minimal and would come at a significant cost in data complexity. Monthly or annual marginal rates are too coarse and would miss the critical intra-day variations that determine a project's true impact. Hourly provides the right balance of precision and feasibility for a robust consequential accounting framework.

The existing GHG Protocol and UNFCCC guidelines provide well-established, internationally recognized methodologies that offer a credible starting point. More sophisticated approaches, like those based on resource adequacy or intervention lifecycle, are also appropriate as they can provide a more nuanced, forward-looking assessment. For example, a lifecycle approach can dynamically adjust the weighting over time, reflecting that a project's impact may be primarily on the operating margin in its early years but shift to influencing the build margin as it becomes part of the long-term resource plan. A flexible framework that allows for these different, credible approaches is the best option.

An alternative approach could be based on the "planning reserve margin" of the grid in question. In a grid with a significant capacity surplus, a new project is unlikely to defer the construction of another plant in the short term, so its impact would be almost 100% on the operating margin. In a grid that is capacity-constrained and actively planning new builds, a new renewable project is much more likely to have a build margin impact. The weighting could be determined by a formula linked to the publicly available planning reserve margin data from the system operator.

Research by organizations like the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) and various academic institutions on grid planning and resource adequacy could provide the foundation for developing such a methodology. Studies on capacity markets and their price signals could also inform how to quantify the likelihood of a new project displacing a future build.

We strongly support the development of a consequential accounting framework to estimate avoided emissions from electricity-sector actions. As a utility-scale renewable energy provider, our projects play a direct role in displacing fossil generation and reducing grid emissions. These impacts must be measurable and reportable.

We offer the following recommendations:

Standardized Methodologies for PPAs and Grid Investments
Corporate PPAs and renewable energy projects have quantifiable impacts on grid emissions. The framework should include clear, standardized methods for estimating these avoided emissions, grounded in marginal emissions data and dispatch modeling.

Temporal and Locational Accuracy
Avoided emissions estimates must reflect the time and location of generation and displacement. Marginal emissions rates, grid congestion, and dispatch order are essential to accurate accounting.

Decision-Usefulness and Transparency
Consequential accounting should empower companies to make informed decisions about procurement, investment, and climate strategy. Outputs must be transparent, comparable, and aligned with broader climate disclosure frameworks.

CRS welcomes the development of consequential accounting methods for electricity-sector actions outside of scope 2 but sees significant challenges in the current consultation draft because it does not clearly distinguish what type of consequential impact is being measured or for what purpose. Without these distinctions, requirements related to baselines, additionality, marginal emissions, and claims become unclear or internally inconsistent.

First, the consultation document does not differentiate between two fundamentally different uses of consequential accounting: (A) measuring system-wide avoided grid emissions (a consequential analysis that does not require additionality), and (B) supporting claims of beyond-business-as-usual (beyond-BAU) emissions reductions (i.e., offsets), which do require additionality tests and stricter criteria. These are not interchangeable. Consequential accounting can quantify grid impacts without implying offset claims, but if the intention is (B), additionality must be required and project-based baselines applied.

Second, the framework is ambiguous about whose action is being measured. It alternates between the action of the generator (building or operating a project) and the action of the purchaser or investor (buying clean electricity or financing a project). These actions involve different baselines and requirements.

Third, not only is the concept of additionality potentially misapplied, if it is required for reporting of avoided grid emissions associated with the operation of a generation project from which electricity is purchased, but it is also applied inconsistently. Additionality is discussed only for renewable projects, not fossil ones. A consequential accounting framework should apply across the electricity sector. If additionality tests were to be required (for offset claims, determining emissions reductions beyond BAU, and purchaser-caused emissions reductions), they must also be required for all generators of purchased generation. Otherwise, the framework would withhold accountability for reporting entities’ impacts unless they can prove additionality—an outcome that is neither desirable nor fit for purpose.

This confusion is reflected, for example, in the table comparing “existing additionality frameworks,” which mixes offset standards, renewable energy initiatives, and tax credit programs with different objectives.

To avoid confusion, the GHG Protocol should explicitly distinguish among several possible consequential outputs, each with different data needs, baselines, and requirements. Organizations could report more than one output, provided claims are clearly distinguished:
A. Short-term avoided grid emissions
• Operating margin × purchased MWh
• Immediate system impacts from purchased generation; no additionality requirement
B. Long-term avoided grid emissions
• Combined margin (operating + build margin) × purchased MWh
• Captures immediate and structural grid effects; no additionality requirement
C. Net consequential emissions impact of purchased electricity
• Induced emissions from load - avoided emissions from purchased generation
• Requires load data + marginal emissions; no additionality unless used for causal claims
D. Global emissions reductions suitable for “offset-like” claims
• Combined margin × purchased MWh - project emissions
• Requires project-based baseline and additionality tests; only category requiring additionality
The four metrics, which are specific to the electricity sector, can be adapted to other sectors using more generic terms such as: A. short-term changes in sectoral emissions, B. long-term changes in sectoral emissions, C. net consequential impact of purchase, and D. global emissions reductions.

GHG Protocol should specify which types of consequential impacts it intends to support or provide methodological pathways for several distinct outputs, each with appropriate requirements.

The draft on consequential accounting relies on a highly static view of the baseline. This assumption does not reflect the realities of electricity systems, which are influenced by numerous dynamic and interdependent factors. Relevant variables include: intraday and long term power pricing, technology dispatch preferences, access to baseload generation (e.g., nuclear or coal), node saturation constraints, thermal losses associated with grid loading, variability of renewable resources, grid stability requirements, regional or national technology preferences, availability and use of energy storage, among other factors.
In essence, establishing a baseline for a given year -representing the scenario in which the particular renewable project was not connected to the grid- is an inverse calculation. It requires estimating how the past would have looked absent the project, accounting for this multitude of interacting factors. When extending this analysis beyond a single project to multiple, often interdependent renewable projects -potentially connected to the same node or drawing from the same variable resource- the mathematical complexity increases substantially and begins to resemble a game theory problem.
Illustrative example of the complexity involved:
Current consequential accounting draft methodology is open to baseline estimation at grid node level, though similar challenges arise at national scale. Consider a photovoltaic project connected to node A, which also hosts nuclear (default baseload), combined cycle gas turbines, and wind generation. Due to node saturation, these technologies cannot always dispatch simultaneously. Under specific conditions -such as low renewable output or high gas prices- node A also imports electricity from other nodes, including nodes in neighboring countries.
Determining the baseline emissions for node A for the prior year requires estimating how the node would have operated without the photovoltaic project, taking all the above factors into account. This is already a highly complex modeling exercise. Allowing baseline calculation at multiple levels (node, regional, grid, national) introduces the possibility of divergent claims. For example, at the node level, if the photovoltaic project primarily displaces nuclear, it may deliver little to no Scope 2 benefit compared with the nuclear or wind already present at node A. However, if the node sits within a high carbon region or grid, the same project could appear to generate significant emission reductions.
Permitting multiple claimable baselines -especially when combined with the existing location based and market based Scope 2 options- risks confusing end users of electricity related claims and undermining the credibility of the methodology and GHG protocol overall.

Attributional accounting is the foundational approach for emissions accounting and life cycle assessment (cradle to gate), as it reflects emissions associated with activities that have actually occurred. By contrast, consequential accounting is typically incorporated within the Sensitivity Assessment portion of a full Life Cycle Assessment and has historically been used to justify carbon avoidance credits.
The track record of carbon avoidance credits illustrates the inherent challenges of defining an appropriate baseline—specifically, determining what emissions would have occurred in the absence of a project. This complexity, combined with the incentive to demonstrate a positive differential between project and baseline, has been widely scrutinized. The scientific literature underscores these concerns, particularly in the context of electricity systems, where baseline conditions evolve throughout a project’s lifecycle and where issues such as curtailment and strategic stakeholder behavior further complicate comparisons.
For these reasons, attributional modeling remains the core principle of carbon emission accounting and life cycle assessment: it is grounded in verified events rather than hypothetical scenarios. We therefore have strong reservations about approaches that resemble an early “third method” for Scope 2 within the GHG Protocol, as they risk facilitating the creation of marketing driven claims and enabling double counting.
The existing location based and market based methods—both already subject to misuse—provide sufficient flexibility for corporate claims, and the current Scope 2 update is explicitly aimed at reducing the prevalence of misleading or non physical representations of electricity use. Introducing an additional reporting method, or laying the groundwork for one, would further obscure the reality of actual electricity consumption and weaken the integrity of emissions reporting frameworks.
The development of a consistent and homogeneous framework for secondary effects is beyond the scope of this update. In the absence of such a framework, we recommend its exclusion.

Both options present significant challenges. Under option (a), the project itself may already influence the baseline, particularly given that the baseline is defined using a rolling annual window. Under option (b), there is inherently no reliable visibility into how the electricity grid will evolve over the multi decade lifecycle of a power project—especially in a highly regulated sector such as electricity generation and transmission and taking into account some of the Additionality Test suggested within this Survey Document.
These issues further underscore the scrutiny and uncertainty associated with consequential accounting. By contrast, attributional modeling offers a more robust and credible basis for emissions accounting, as it is grounded in observable events that have actually occurred rather than speculative future scenarios.

The proposal to discuss consequential electricity-sector emissions impact as a separate metric from attributional accounting, only counting towards mitigation of the scope 2 emissions inventory when the underlying procurement happens to meet the proposed hourly- and location-matching quality criteria for market-based instruments, is a detrimental design flaw. Emissions accounting per the GHG Protocol Scope 2 Standard has been successful thus far because enterprises around the world have chosen to adopt it as their standardized methodology, as it measured legitimacy alongside feasibility. The current proposal, wherein causation of new renewable energy is relegated to a separate consequential accounting rather than integral to attributional accounting itself, will not provide any motivational value to companies to leverage this voluntary standard and, more importantly, the voluntary procurement mechanism derived from the GHGP standards.

We have advised over 100 global corporations on a multi-year basis over the last 15+ years; each of those corporations were motivated towards driving an impactful renewable energy strategy, despite having cheaper and logistically easier options on the open unbundled EAC market, primarily by the fact that the consequential accounting currently implicit in the market-based method was a viable method of scope 2 emissions reduction. Removing and reallocating this primary incentive to a separate consequential accounting approach would obviate the reason all of our clients have chosen the “hard right” of causing new clean energy generation through long-term forward PPAs” over the “easy wrong” of buying unbundled EACs from long-existing projects in the spot market, that are coincidentally matched 24/7 with their demand.

If consequential impact were integrated into attribution accounting as a key quality criterion for market-based instruments whenever feasible, GHGP would have the unique opportunity to not only enhance momentum towards bringing new renewable energy onto the grid but also clarify how an off-site renewable energy procurement can be validated as causing new renewable energy capacity. SR Inc has long advocated for such criteria to be made clear through the establishment of a “purchaser-caused” tag when a procurement meets specific requirements, which we will articulate further in questions 26 & 27 of this survey. This is critical because companies marketing non-causative EACs as additional undermine the credibility of the EAC market, which cannot be afforded.

Undermining the Scope 2 emissions accounting incentive to serve as the proximate cause of new clean energy capacity is a mistake, especially if it is done to advance a specious “use claim” through a pseudo “deliverability” for a pseudo “inventory,” as is currently proposed by the hourly- and location-matching requirements. The current Scope 2 market-based method accounting is a consequential accounting that rightly recognizes procurement of clean energy generation, not consumption, and GHGP can further enhance this standard to legitimize the work of all the companies that have contributed to nearly 140 GW of new renewables on the US grid, momentum which must continue to reduce the most catastrophic effects of human-caused climate breakdown.

The human health impacts of renewable energy should be considered including, but not limited to, avoided pollution, public health, ecosystem and economic impacts. This analysis can include (1) Global perspective: Net benefits analysis integrating both pollution increases from infrastructure manufacturing and pollution decreases due to operation of the project; (2) Operational perspective: Avoided local and global air pollutants and resource use due to operation of the project; (3) Local perspective: Avoided local air pollutants and resource use in and around the project area due to operation of the project. In its first year of operation, the 1 GW portfolio of renewable energy capacity that SR Inc Member-Clients enabled through aggregated procurements for utility-scale renewable energy generated:

1. $925M in health systems cost savings
2. 1,600,000 MT CO2 emissions avoided
3. 3,694 disability-adjusted human life years saved
4. 7 distinct species saved.

These figures come from Quantum Energy’s TotalView Energy Platform, which considers the three aforementioned perspectives and uses metrics related to emissions to air, emissions to water, emissions to soil, and resource use to quantify the pubic health, ecosystem, and economic impacts of not only the addition of new renewable energy capacity to the grid but the displacement of fossil fuel infrastructure from the grid. These metrics are critical secondary effects of the addition of new renewable energy capacity to the grid and should be considered in impact criteria.

1. Timing test: For a project to be considered “additional,” the timing test is necessary to require a pre-financing contractual commitment to pay for the bundled new renewable energy generating capacity & EACs produced by the project. If the project is already financed, a buyer cannot claim to have “caused” new renewable energy capacity as the project would have come online without the financial backing brought in by the buyer. The contractual agreement should also come before construction, though financing almost always comes before construction. However, “under construction” should be defined as the actual physical construction of the project, after FNTP is achieved, not “under construction” by current U.S. tax incentive rules. It is unimportant whether the project was already planned, as many planned projects do not eventuate into operating plants.
2. Barrier test: Similarly to the above, and particularly if the timing test only applies to situations where the project is pre-planning or pre-construction, the barrier test should be used to demonstrate that lack of financing was a barrier to the project’s execution, and the contract for EACs along with the investment grade credit rating, or posted Letter of Credit, of the buyer(s) was the catalyst to overcome that barrier. The contractual commitment to pay for the RECs bundled with the new generation capacity must happen before the project is financed.
3. Contractual/tenor test: For a project to be considered additional, the EAC procurement term must be at least 10 years (as the market has empirically demonstrated), and the contract must bundle the cost of energy with the cost of the EACs. Long-term contracts are necessary to help demonstrate that buyers provided the financial certainty needed for financing, so the length of the term is critical in assuring that the project gets built, and the developer is guaranteed a long-term offtaker for the EACS in advance. The bundling of the EACs and the cost of energy is also necessary for ensuring that the buyer takes on the downside risk which enables potential financers to move forward with the project.

There are several pieces of data one could point to in order to prove that the contract for the EACs generated by a project came before financing was secured by the developer. 1) The date of the signed contract should be earlier than the date of “Final Notice to Proceed,” or FNTP. FNTP must be given in order for the financer to proceed with delivering the financing to the developer. 2) One could source anecdotal responses from developers describing their process for obtaining financing, and any notice they received from financers about the level of downside risk they would have to mitigate through long-term EAC contracts in order to proceed with financing.

A financial analysis test would be infeasible because determining a universal threshold level of financial attractiveness that is acceptable to a wide range of developers and financing institutional funds (which demonstrate an array of risk/return thresholds for investing funds), as well across different markets and transaction types would be impossible.
d. Depending on the barrier being evaluated this test may or may not be feasible, and this is also dependent on who is trying to claim additionality. If a solar panel manufacturer wanted to claim additionality on a project because it wouldn’t have been possible without the supply of solar panels, this would be a dubious claim. However, in the case that lack of financing was the barrier to preventing a project from moving forward, and the long-term contract for EACs was the incentive to overcome it, this can be proved through the same methods described for the timing test.
e. While the common practice test is theoretically feasible to prove, it is not practically desirable. Even if many solar projects are already implemented in a given region, each one of them certainly took significant effort to bring into operation, which justifies the tag of additionality. Second, as EACs are used to claim renewable energy, and the EAC is itself an incentive, there are very few examples today of renewable energy projects, let alone many in a given region or market, that are entirely without incentives. This criterion might be better evaluated in a market closer to achieving real zero (e.g. Costa Rica). Furthermore, given the current state of the market, the goal of an “additionality” tag is to incentivize adding new renewable energy capacity to the grid. So, even if the solar had achieved cost-parity with non-renewable alternatives without EACs or tax credits, these standards should still consider new solar capacity as “additional.”
f. Depending on the criteria included in the positive list test, it could be feasible to implement, but other tests are more relevant.
g. Performance standard: While the performance standard test might be feasible, it is muddied by the arbitrary nature of a baseline emissions rate or energy efficiency level which have nothing to do with whether a project adds new renewable energy capacity to the grid.
h. Given that nearly all legal contracts have a defined “term,” it would be straightforward to test for tenor of a project. Also, given the clarity necessitated by legal contracts, it should also be easy to prove whether a contract bundles the EACs with the cost of electricity through a fixed price, flat price, or some other pricing structure.
i. A first-of-its-kind test is immaterial in whether a project adds new capacity.

Optional project capacity test: The standard could include an optional minimum capacity test that is region-specific, allowing for that amount to be procured individually or in aggregate (e.g. 50MW for U.S. solar). This scale encourages the addition of utility-scale capacity to the grid. The size is included because it helps ensure that the developer couldn’t finance the project on their own, so the other tests should cover this. Not all renewable energy procurements generate equal impact. There is an important distinction to be made between EACs bought from an existing system that a corporate buyer had no influence in causing, EACs bought from a system that a corporate buyer contributed to the financing of, and EACs bought from a system that would not have existed without the role of the corporate buyer in the procurement process.
The first option, unbundled EACs purchased from the spot mark, represent the lowest value option. They are often bought from projects that were developed years earlier. While inexpensive, they do not impact the greening of the grid whatsoever.
The second option, “Contributing EACs,” offer a modest improvement over the above but fall well short of maximal impact. Typically, corporates provide incremental capital to renewable energy projects primarily financed by other sources. They are more expensive, and more impactful, but they still cannot claim to proximately cause new renewable energy deployment to the grid. Attributing the same value to these “Contributing EACs” as one would to “Purchaser-caused EACs” or “Causal EACs,” would threaten market credibility.
The third option, “Purchaser-caused EACs” or “Causal EACs,” represent genuine “additionality.” These procurements directly cause new renewable energy projects to be built by meeting three key criteria:
1. Bundled prefinancing commitment: Procurements that contract to cover the cost of a clean energy project’s development AND its resulting EACs.
2. Sufficient duration: Procurements that commit to a term of ten or more years.
3. Optional - Sufficient volume: Procurements that commit to 40 MW or more of capacity (alone or with others’ simultaneous matching contracts).
When procurements meet these three thresholds, companies demonstrably cause renewable energy capacity that wouldn’t otherwise exist to be added to the grid. This difference matters enormously for the world to achieve its climate goals. The COP28 UAE Consensus identified the tripling of renewable energy deployment by 2030 as essential to avoiding climate catastrophe and achieving this goal necessitates corporate procurement that actually builds new capacity, not just redistributes EACs from existing projects.
Industry consensus surrounding what constitutes causation is clear among experienced corporate buyers, so companies serious about climate impact must be incentivized by the market and the standards they follow to prioritize causation over contribution.
