Consequential accounting methods are essential for aligning electricity-sector emissions reporting with actual climate outcomes. One of their clearest benefits is accurately characterizing the system-level impact of energy storage, which is consistently misrepresented under attributional methods like the location-based method (LBM) and market-based method (MBM).

Attributional approaches assign emissions to energy storage based solely on round-trip losses, regardless of when or how it operates. This leads to uniformly positive Scope 2 emissions for storage, even when its operations lead to net emissions reductions on the grid. It penalizes grid-beneficial behavior and provides no recognition for storage's ability to displace high-emissions generation.

Real-world operational experience with utility-scale battery storage has demonstrated the value of consequential accounting. When batteries are operated with explicit emissions optimization using marginal operating emissions rates in bid strategies and compared to baseline operations focused purely on economic dispatch, important patterns emerge:
• Adding an emissions signal to battery optimization can substantially improve emissions performance under operating margin-based accounting.
• Introducing build margin can reduce or reverse the apparent incremental emissions benefit, showing a trade-off between how short-term and long-term impacts are valued.
• Under build margin-dominant frameworks, dispatch optimized for immediate emissions reduction can appear less beneficial than baseline economic dispatch even when it demonstrably reduces real-time grid emissions.

These patterns show that build margin-dominant metrics can perversely reward behavior that increases short-term emissions, while penalizing efforts to reduce them. This creates misaligned incentives and erodes the scientific credibility of emissions claims.

Moreover, MBM does not correct this. As a stand-alone asset, storage's emissions impact is linked to its losses in allocational accounting methods. The emission reduction potential of storage is only recognized under MBM when it is contractually linked to a load, and even then, only if it participates in REC arbitrage frameworks that require verification and validation of dispatch schedules and reservoir accounting for RECs. Merchant storage, or grid-interactive assets operating independently of specific load, are not recognized for the emissions impact due to timeshifting under the MBM.

Consequential methods meaningfully recognize storage's contribution to decarbonization by evaluating:
• Induced emissions during charging (when the battery adds load to the system),
• Avoided emissions during discharging (when it offsets fossil peakers), and
• Net emissions outcomes over time.

Without consequential accounting, storage may be operated in ways that increase emissions and receive credit for doing so if incentives are based solely on build margin or REC-based frameworks. Consequential accounting corrects this misalignment and ensures that energy storage that does not participate in REC arbitrage, validation, and verification, are still appropriately accounted for.

We urge the GHG Protocol to incorporate consequential accounting alongside attributional methods. It is essential for emissions integrity, grid-aligned investment decisions, and recognition of technologies that enable deep decarbonization.

The proposed formula is incomplete and inappropriate as a standalone method for quantifying emissions impacts from electricity projects, especially when applied to energy storage. The formula only accounts for avoided emissions (via marginal emission rate × procured electricity) and ignores induced emissions, which are equally important in determining net impact.

The omission of induced emissions is particularly problematic because storage introduces new load to the grid when it charges. Because storage shifts energy temporally, it inherently induces emissions when it charges and avoids emissions when it discharges. Therefore, the net impact depends on differences in marginal emissions between periods.

If the formula only counts avoided emissions (e.g., only discharging hours), it will overstate the benefit of storage unless it also subtracts the emissions caused during charging. In fact, without accounting for charging-induced emissions, storage that increases net grid emissions can appear as a source of avoided emissions under the current formula, presenting a credibility risk for emissions impact claims.

For example, a battery that charges at night on a coal-heavy grid and discharges during the day when solar is already plentiful may increase emissions overall. Under the proposed formula, it would be credited for avoided emissions during discharge hours, without induced emissions from charging.

Even with “hourly matched” MBM procurement, energy storage is not required to demonstrate that clean energy used to charge is physically deliverable at the time or place of discharge. This can lead to misleading emissions claims if storage is charged in emissive periods. Unless the marginal generator at the time is a zero-emission resource, this added demand typically causes fossil-fueled generators to ramp up to meet it even if renewables are producing electricity simultaneously.

This is why methods like the Marginal Impact Method, originally proposed by the Consequential Scope 2 TWG subgroup members, explicitly calculate both:
• Induced emissions: Charging MWh × Marginal Emission Rate_charge
• Avoided emissions: Discharging MWh × Marginal Emission Rate_discharge
• And then determine the net impact: Avoided - Induced

Notably, the GHG Protocol Project Guidance and CDM methodologies reflect this more robust structure by measuring changes relative to a baseline, including additions and subtractions. The proposed Scope 2 TWG subgroup formula departs from this precedent and risks significant bias if used in isolation.

To ensure environmental integrity and applicability to modern grid-interactive technologies like storage and flexible demand, the formula must be expanded to include both:
• Electricity consumed (including round-trip losses), and
• Electricity delivered or displaced, with each component evaluated against the relevant marginal emission rate for its time and location.

Yes — both primary effects and certain methodologically robust secondary effects should be required, while speculative or assumption-heavy secondary effects should be optional.

Primary effects such as emissions induced by electricity consumption (e.g., charging storage) and avoided through delivery or generation (e.g., discharging storage or adding clean supply) are direct and essential. These must be required in any routine consequential accounting framework. Established consequential methodologies provide a practical and transparent methodology for calculating these effects using marginal emissions rates.

In addition, some secondary effects should also be required, specifically those that are methodologically robust and standardizable. For example:
• Consequential methods can include long-term dispatch effects through build margin emissions factors, which reflect how new clean electricity displaces future fossil capacity. This is a legitimate and meaningful secondary effect that can be quantified consistently using public data and modeling assumptions.
• These build margin effects provide important insight into the structural, long-term climate benefits of procurement and grid interventions and are essential for strategic planning.

By contrast, other secondary effects such as life cycle emissions from construction of generation or infrastructure are often too dependent on variable and project-specific assumptions to standardize. These should remain optional disclosures, suitable for ad hoc assessments or lifecycle studies but not required in Scope 2 routine impact accounting.

For energy storage, both primary and build-margin secondary effects are relevant:
• Charging induces marginal emissions.
• Discharging avoids emissions.
• Long-term deployment of storage can reduce curtailment and defer fossil peaker capacity, which should be captured using standardized secondary methods where appropriate.

In summary, our recommendation is to (i) require primary effects, (ii) require standardized, robust secondary effects (e.g., build margin), and (iii) allow optional reporting of complex or speculative secondary effects (e.g., life cycle emissions).

Emissions impacts should be reported each year on an ex post basis vs once at the outset on an ex ante basis. This ensures consistency with the core principles of the GHG Protocol, including comparability, consistency, and transparency across reporting entities and time periods.

Annual reporting enables accrual reporting of emissions impacts that reflect real-time grid dynamics, including changes in marginal emissions, dispatch patterns, and operational behavior. This is especially important for technologies like energy storage, whose emissions impact varies significantly depending on when and where it charges and discharges.

The Marginal Impact Method (MIM) provides a standardized, transparent way to estimate year-over-year emissions impacts using observed consumption and generation data. Confining MIM results to a single reporting year ensures alignment with the rest of a company’s GHG inventory and makes results more actionable and comparable.

If companies wish to disclose longer-term or broader project impacts — such as estimated lifecycle emissions or multi-year structural changes — these can be reported separately under a project-based or ad hoc consequential method, but they should not replace standardized annual reporting for Scope 2 emissions impact accounting.

Energy storage requires a two-pathway approach to additionality:
1. Behavioral Additionality: Existing projects can generate additional avoided emissions when operational behavior changes due to interventions like carbon arbitrage incentives or dispatch optimization tools. Even if these assets were originally built under regulatory incentives or without offtake from a reporting entity, they may still be additional under consequential accounting if the emissions-avoiding operating mode is new and attributable to the reporting entity's action.
2. Greenfield Additionality: New storage projects that would not exist without the intervention (e.g. tolling, offtake, revenue guarantee) must demonstrate their dependency on the reporting entity's action. These can be rigorously assessed using a combination of tests that demonstrate financial and contractual causality.

Regulatory Test (Required): Should be required only for greenfield projects to determine whether they were mandated or already incentivized through policy. If a project was built solely to fulfill a regulation, it should not be claimed as additional. However, this test should not disqualify behavioral interventions applied to already existing assets, even if they received regulatory support.

Timing Test (Not Required): While helpful in some contexts, timing alone cannot determine causality for behavioral change. Storage assets may operate in new, lower-emission patterns long after construction in response to new market incentives or partnerships.

Financial Analysis Test (Optional): The financial analysis test should only substitute for the positive list when the storage project does not fall within the positive list criteria but can quantitatively demonstrate economic infeasibility without the intervention. This substitution route must be tightly defined to avoid inconsistent or overly subjective applications of the financial test. Substitution should require:
• A detailed pro forma showing inadequate IRR or NPV under baseline conditions,
• Documentation that the intervention (e.g., contract) closes the financing gap,
• Third-party or auditor verification if used to justify claims.

Positive List (Required): The positive list should be the default, required test for establishing additionality in greenfield storage projects. This approach provides a standardized, low-burden screen for determining whether a storage project is in a context or use-case likely to be additional. This test ensures scalability and comparability across entities while retaining environmental integrity. The list could include:
• Markets with limited policy incentives for storage,
• Non-commercially viable applications (e.g., long-duration storage),
• Projects that rely on third-party offtake or tolling arrangements to move forward.

Contractual/Tenor Test (Required): Essential for greenfield storage. Storage projects require revenue certainty to attract financing. Offtake contracts or tolling agreements are typically the mechanism that enables construction. This test should be a core part of the positive list criteria for storage.

First-of-its-Kind (FOAK) Test (Required): Should be interpreted as dynamic baselining which calculates the emissions impact of an operating storage facility if it was NOT considering any incentive to reduce emissions.

Barrier, Common Practice, and Performance Standard Tests (Not Required): These add limited value for energy storage additionality when better alternatives (positive list, contractual, FOAK) are available. They may still serve as optional evidence.

Of the available options, the following tests are feasible for use in avoided emissions accounting for electricity projects (especially energy storage) because they are either already applied in existing methodologies or can be standardized with clear implementation criteria:

Regulatory Test: Feasible for greenfield storage projects. It can be implemented as a binary screen to ensure projects built solely to meet compliance obligations (e.g., mandated capacity targets) are excluded from additionality claims. This test is straightforward and relies on public regulatory documentation.

Timing Test: Feasible for both greenfield and behavioral additionality, provided it is used in support of but not as a strict gatekeeper for additionality. It helps establish temporal correlation between the intervention (e.g., contract execution) and a change in project development or behavior but should not be the sole test.

Financial Analysis Test: Feasible only as a substitution pathway when a project does not qualify under a positive list. It requires access to project-specific pro formas and financing assumptions. While more subjective than other tests, it can be implemented with standardized documentation requirements (e.g., pre/post IRR analysis, third-party attestation).

Positive List: Highly feasible and recommended as the primary test for greenfield additionality. It provides clarity, reduces burden, and is scalable across markets. The list should be developed based on market penetration levels, regulatory context, and contractual dependencies. Updates can be made periodically to reflect evolving norms.

Contractual/Tenor Test: Feasible for greenfield projects where offtake contracts, tolling agreements, or long-term service agreements provide the financial foundation for construction. This test is objective and easily documented. It is essential for assessing whether the reporting entity’s intervention was enabling.

First-of-its-Kind Test: Feasible for existing assets under a dynamic baselining framework. It compares an asset’s dispatch behavior after accounting for an intervention against dispatch behavior without accounting for the intervention. This test enables recognition of behavioral additionality, particularly when emissions-reducing operations are induced by a reporting entity.

Barrier Test, Common Practice Test, Performance Standard: These are not recommended due to high subjectivity, limited transparency, inconsistency across jurisdictions and technologies, and redundancy with more precise tests like contractual dependency or dynamic baselining.

A critical additionality test that should be included in the framework is dynamic baselining, particularly for existing dispatchable assets like energy storage, or new assets that don't meet traditional greenfield tests but still result in meaningful emissions reductions through behavioral change.

Dynamic baselining involves simulating how an energy storage system would have operated under identical real-world conditions absent an environmental intervention. For example, the counterfactual could be a dispatch strategy that maximizes market revenue (price arbitrage), while the observed operation reflects an emissions-optimized dispatch. This baselining approach is outlined in detail in the consequential methodology available here via the Energy Storage Solutions Consortium's website: https://www.ess-consortium.org/home/#methodology

This test is important for the following reasons:
• Storage dispatch is highly flexible, and its emissions impact depends entirely on when it charges and discharges.
• Marginal emissions rates are often uncorrelated with electricity prices, meaning a system optimized to reduce emissions can behave very differently from one optimized to earn revenue.
• A battery can be non-additional from a build perspective yet still abate substantial emissions due to operational changes directly induced by the reporting entity.

This is not just theoretical: operational experience with utility-scale energy storage has demonstrated this approach in practice. When emissions-aware dispatch is applied and compared against modeled revenue-maximizing dispatch scenarios, dynamic baselining can quantify both the incremental behavioral impact and the absolute emissions impact of the asset.

Real-world application demonstrates that dynamic baselining is practical, credible, and technically feasible. It offers a standardized path to recognize behavioral additionality for storage and similar assets, which might otherwise be overlooked in a framework focused only on new builds.

We recommend that GHG Protocol define and include a standardized methodology for dynamic baselining in its consequential guidance appendix to ensure rigor, comparability, and auditability.

For the purposes of maintaining comparability and consistency across reporting entities and through time, the additionality tests should not vary regionally. We believe additionality tests should be structurally standardized, even if region-specific data inputs are used to populate them. This approach ensures that emissions claims are comparable across geographies, fair across market participants, and consistent with the global role of the GHG Protocol. While we acknowledge that some regions may require stricter data inputs (e.g., in markets with high renewable penetration), this does not justify changing the underlying tests. Instead, regional differences should inform how the tests are applied not whether they are applied.

The level of rigor in additionality testing should be standardized across all reporting entities, regardless of whether a claim is characterized as "causal" or "associative." The GHG Protocol should not create multiple claim types with differing credibility thresholds. Instead, it should establish a single, transparent framework for consequential emissions impact accounting.

That framework must include the following:
• Both induced and avoided emissions, ensuring that reported impacts reflect net change to atmospheric GHG levels.
• Consistent, independently verifiable methodologies.
• Consistent accounting rules to all reporters to enable comparability across companies and over time.

Such standardization provides the market with a more accurate picture of climate impact. Entities can be assessed and compared using the same yardstick, enhancing credibility and reducing confusion.

Moreover, with an appropriately constructed positive list, informed by technical experts and based on robust market data, it is entirely reasonable to expect that actions meeting this threshold are causing real change. Projects that pass the positive list and meet required tests (like contractual dependency) are more likely to result in new clean energy deployment unlike unbundled EACs, which have not demonstrated a reliable causal link to new builds. Despite their widespread use, EACs alone have failed to drive sufficient renewable capacity additions to support credible "net zero" claims.

By focusing on rigorous, standardized accounting and effective eligibility screens, the GHG Protocol can shift the market toward recognizing real impact rather than reclassifying claims based on ambiguous or subjective tests.

These three methods are not appropriate for the following reasons:
1. Scenario Modeling: While valuable in research or policy evaluation contexts, scenario modeling introduces too much subjectivity and variability for routine accounting. It relies on complex counterfactuals that require numerous assumptions about what the grid would have done under alternative conditions. The lack of a consistent baseline scenario across entities undermines comparability and transparency. It is also difficult to validate externally, making it poorly suited for standardized emissions reporting.

2. Capacity Factor Based: This method oversimplifies grid dynamics by assuming that low-capacity factor generators are always marginal. In practice, marginal units change hourly or sub-hourly depending on dispatch constraints, demand, and transmission congestion. Using capacity factor as a proxy does not reflect real-world dispatch and is inconsistent with how modern grids operate.

3. Difference-Based: While this approach attempts to calculate marginal emissions by observing total system emissions before and after a change, it fails to isolate the specific impact of the intervention. Grid emissions fluctuate due to many factors (weather, fuel prices, outages, etc.) making it nearly impossible to attribute observed changes solely to a specific action without robust modeling controls. This method lacks the granularity and attribution accuracy required for credible consequential emissions accounting.

In contrast, methods based on SCED sensitivity analysis and statistical inference from observed grid behavior (e.g., Marginal Impact Method, originally proposed by the Consequential Scope 2 TWG Subgroup Members) offer higher rigor, verifiability, and alignment with system operations, and are better suited for routine implementation.

For consequential emissions accounting to be valid, it is critical that the marginal generator be causally linked to the change in grid operations. That is, emissions attribution must reflect not merely that 1 MWh was injected or withdrawn, but that the generator actually changed output as a direct result of the intervention (e.g., a change in load or dispatch). Including non-causal generators (generators that do not respond to the intervention) introduces noise and undermines the fidelity of the emissions estimate.

Duration-limited resources such as batteries or other storage should not be included in the set of marginal generators. These assets do not operate continuously, and their dispatch is inherently constrained by state of charge and time-shifting behavior. For any observed dispatch, there are infinite possible counterfactuals for how the energy storage could have operated instead (i.e., it could have dispatched earlier, later, or not at all). This makes it impossible to establish a credible counterfactual against which to measure the marginal impact of an intervention.

Including such resources in marginal emissions calculations distorts the causal relationship between grid actions and emissions, and risks double-counting or misattributing avoided emissions. A robust accounting framework should limit marginal attribution to resources that are continuously dispatchable and causally responsive to load changes within the modeled time interval.

The only appropriate methodology for build margin estimation is the recent capacity additions approach. This method is empirical, transparent, and validated against historical build behavior. It bases emissions factors on the mix of fossil generation that has recently entered commercial operation, which is a strong proxy for what clean energy additions are most likely to displace.

Validation work from the Global Energy Monitor (see: MBERs validation) shows that using recent build data accurately reflects market behavior, avoids speculative assumptions, and provides a credible benchmark for estimating long-run avoided emissions from clean energy procurement.

In contrast, the following methodologies are not appropriate for build margin estimation:
• Policy scenarios and capacity expansion models are speculative and rely heavily on assumptions about policy implementation, market design, and fuel prices. These models are difficult to standardize and often reflect idealized futures rather than actual investment behavior.
• Average emissions rates (e.g., grid-average emissions) misrepresent marginal displacement by blending baseload, intermittent, and peaking resources. This dilutes the signal needed to understand what fossil generation would truly be avoided.

Therefore, to ensure consistency, transparency, and causal alignment with actual emissions reductions, recent capacity additions should be the sole method endorsed for build margin estimation.

Rather than tailoring different build margin models to different project types, the GHG Protocol should adopt a single, consistent build margin dataset across all projects with variation in build vs. operating margin weighting used to reflect differences in project characteristics such as dispatchability or operational flexibility.

Using a uniform build margin dataset supports the GHG Protocol's core principles of comparability, consistency, and transparency. When all projects apply the same emissions factor for build margin, stakeholders can compare emissions impact across technologies and reporting entities without introducing variability from modeling assumptions or data sources. The differentiation in emissions attribution should come not from different models, but from the weighting applied to build vs. operating margin.

To ensure accuracy and scientific integrity, the selected build margin model should include the following:
• Backward-looking and empirical, reflecting actual capacity additions on the grid.
• Low in assumptions, avoiding speculative forecasting, modeled policy scenarios, or capacity expansion projections.
• Transparent and replicable, using public data sources and standardized methodology.

Among the options considered, recent capacity additions best meet these criteria. This approach directly ties emissions factors to observed market behavior and structural changes in the generation mix. In contrast, models based on policy scenarios or expansion modeling are too sensitive to input assumptions and vary significantly by user, making them unsuitable for standardized reporting.

In summary, we recommend the following:
• Use a single, centralized build margin emissions dataset across all projects.
• Allow differentiation via project-specific BM/OM weightings, not separate build margin models.
• Favor recent capacity additions as the modeling basis for build margin, due to its empirical foundation, transparency, and alignment with GHGP principles.

One of the most critical metrics missing from current frameworks is a net marginal emissions metric that distinguishes between the emissions impact of electricity consumption (induced emissions) and the emissions impact of electricity procurement or generation (avoided emissions). Established consequential methodologies formalize this distinction and enable standardized, time-resolved accounting, which is essential for dispatchable technologies like energy storage.

However, this approach is not only important for energy storage. It is also essential for any consumer of electricity, because load itself has a causal emissions impact. Reducing load to zero is one of the clearest ways to reduce grid emissions which means that any decision to maintain or increase load induces emissions that are observable at the margin.

Without capturing the induced emissions from consumption, we ignore half of the equation. This limits the ability of emissions accounting to reflect the full causal impact of a reporting entity's actions on the grid. It also creates the risk of overstating climate performance by reporting only avoided emissions without accounting for the emissions induced by electricity use.

This distinction becomes particularly important in a world where entities may:
• Procure clean power but operate high-emissions equipment at carbon-intensive times,
• Invest in renewables while simultaneously increasing electricity-intensive operations,
• Shift loads in ways that unintentionally worsen system emissions.

It's also essential to clarify that consequential metrics should not be netted against MBM or LBM attributional inventories, which are based on allocational accounting principles. These two approaches serve fundamentally different purposes and cannot be combined without compromising their integrity. Attributional metrics tell us "how much" of which kind of electricity was procured; consequential metrics tell us "what changed" on the grid because of those choices.

By including both procurement and consumption-based marginal emissions (i.e., avoided and induced impacts), organizations can be evaluated based on their actual emissions impact, not just their sourcing claims. This provides a foundation for more credible disclosures, more informed decisions, and more effective climate action.

We do not support any of the proposed approaches for assigning build and operating margin (BM/OM) weights. They fail to account for the most important determinant of emissions impact: operational flexibility, i.e., a project's ability to influence system emissions in real time through dispatch decisions. The current methods, including those based on resource adequacy, capacity value, or default rules, conflate reliability attributes with emissions causality.

We recommend GHG Protocol develop a new framework where BM/OM weights are based on dispatchability. This ensures emissions attribution reflects a project's actual influence on system dispatch and short- versus long-term emissions outcomes. The framework could follow this logic:
• Dispatchable resources (e.g., batteries, gas peakers): Primarily assessed using operating margin, as their emissions impacts depend on hourly operational decisions.
• Non-dispatchable resources (e.g., wind, solar, nuclear): Assessed using a combination of operating margin and build margin, since their emissions impact comes from both short-term and long-term structural displacement of fossil fuel capacity.
• Semi-dispatchable resources (e.g., coal, demand response): Assigned blended weights depending on ramping capabilities and price/emissions responsiveness.

Operational experience with utility-scale battery storage has revealed how different weighting frameworks can mischaracterize emissions impacts. When comparing baseline economic optimization to emissions-aware optimization scenarios over extended operational periods, clear patterns emerge:
• Batteries operating purely for revenue can appear more beneficial under build margin-dominant frameworks despite potentially increasing near-term emissions.
• Batteries explicitly optimized to reduce emissions can receive less credit under build margin than under operating margin even when delivering greater actual abatement.

This creates a perverse incentive: systems may be operated to maximize cycling and long-term "build displacement," even if it means raising actual emissions in the near term. Operating margin provides a more reliable signal for operational emissions control. Experience also suggests that build margin value may be largely "locked in" upon asset construction and should not guide ongoing dispatch incentives.

The resource adequacy approach, which uses metrics like ELCC to weight BM/OM, is also flawed. For example, batteries and nuclear both have high-capacity value, but only storage can modulate output to align with real-time grid needs. ELCC is useful for system planning, not emissions impact accounting.

We recommend the GHG Protocol abandon default or resource adequacy-based weightings and adopt a dispatchability-based model selection framework. While this differs from some proposed approaches, it is consistent with causal principles and backed by real-world data.

These approaches are not feasible to implement consistently or transparently across different project types and reporting entities for the following reasons:
• The GHG Protocol Guidelines and UNFCCC CDM Tool07 rely on complex or subjective input variables (e.g., capacity value, capacity factor, planning horizon assumptions) and assign weights that can change over time. This introduces uncertainty, lack of comparability, and risk of manipulation.
• Resource adequacy approaches, while grounded in real planning metrics, assign build margin weights based on a project’s contribution to firm capacity (e.g., ELCC). However, this conflates capacity value with emissions impact potential. For example, both nuclear and battery storage have high ELCC, but only storage can dynamically respond to system marginal emissions. The approach is therefore misaligned with actual emissions causality.
• Intervention lifecycle approaches attempt to time-weight build and operating margin attribution depending on whether a project was anticipated in planning. This introduces significant complexity and subjectivity, particularly across jurisdictions with varying planning transparency. It also risks creating inconsistent incentives across technologies and geographies.

Across all four methods, the core issue is that they introduce time-varying, project-specific weighting schemes that undermine the GHG Protocol’s foundational goals of transparency, comparability, and consistency.

We recommend a new approach that assigns build and operating margin weights based on a project’s measurable dispatchability, which is its ability to respond to grid conditions and alter output or consumption in real time.

Rather than relying on static categories like “firm” or “intermittent,” or changing weights over time based on planning status, this approach evaluates how much control a project has over its operations — and how directly it can affect marginal system emissions.

Dispatchability can be measured using three key criteria:
1. Control over timing of output or load - Can the project decide when to inject or consume electricity? Example: Storage and demand response can shift behavior across hours; wind and solar cannot.
2. Responsiveness to price or emissions signals - Does the project adjust operations in response to real-time prices or marginal emissions data? This can be assessed by: Operational records, Integration with emissions- or price-optimized dispatch platforms, Simulation using emissions signals as dispatch inputs.
3. Granularity of dispatch flexibility - At what time resolution can the asset adjust (e.g., 5-minute, hourly)? Projects with finer control over dispatch timing have greater emissions impact potential on the operating margin.

Using these attributes, projects could be classified on a dispatchability spectrum, from fully dispatchable (e.g., batteries) to non-dispatchable (e.g., nuclear, solar). This classification would then determine:
• High OM weight for dispatchable projects that affect real-time emissions.
• High BM weight for fixed-output or inflexible projects that affect long-term capacity mix.

This approach would preserve transparency, comparability, and standardization, while aligning emissions accounting with actual system behavior, a core goal of consequential methods like the Marginal Impact Method (originally proposed by the Consequential Scope 2 TWG Subgroup Members).

Consequential accounting methods for electricity-sector actions offer a valuable complement to attributional Scope 2 inventories by better reflecting how specific actions may influence system-level emissions over time. Their main benefit lies in impact signaling: they can help distinguish actions that plausibly drive additional low-carbon generation, storage, or flexibility from those that primarily reallocate existing attributes. This can improve policy relevance, support system planning, and better align corporate actions with real-world decarbonization pathways.

However, consequential methods introduce significant methodological and practical challenges. Causal attribution is inherently uncertain, particularly in complex and interconnected power systems where marginal effects depend on dispatch order, market conditions, policy constraints, and counterfactual assumptions. Results can vary widely depending on modeling choices (e.g., marginal vs average factors, short-run vs long-run effects), reducing comparability across organizations and over time. From an assurance perspective, this uncertainty makes it difficult to define what constitutes sufficient, appropriate evidence.

Data and cost considerations are also material. Consequential approaches often require system-level modeling, scenario analysis, and forward-looking assumptions that are not consistently available, especially in lower-maturity markets. This raises barriers for smaller organizations and risks creating inequitable reporting expectations. Without strong governance, there is also a risk that selectively chosen assumptions could be used to justify favorable outcomes, increasing skepticism and perceived greenwashing.

An important unintended consequence could be claim confusion. If consequential results are mixed with attributional Scope 2 inventories, users may misinterpret modeled impacts as firm-level emissions reductions. This could undermine clarity and comparability unless claims are clearly labeled, scoped, and disclosed.

At a structural level, the proposed formula is appropriate as an initial framework for quantifying emissions impacts from electricity projects. It clearly separates the activity being assessed from the emissions response of the electricity system and avoids embedding specific methodological assumptions directly into the equation itself. This makes the formula flexible enough to be applied across different market structures and project types while allowing methodological refinements to sit outside the core structure.

From a practical standpoint, the formula is also consistent with how consequential impacts are typically evaluated in energy system analysis: it links an incremental action to a modeled change in system emissions over a defined boundary and time horizon. This is conceptually sound and avoids conflating attributional inventory accounting with impact-based assessment.

However, while the structure is suitable, its usefulness will ultimately depend on clear guidance around boundaries, timeframes, and assumptions applied outside the formula. Without that supporting guidance, different users could apply the same formula in materially different ways. That said, this concern relates to implementation rather than the structure of the equation itself.

Secondary effects should be considered, but in a clearly bounded and transparent way. Relevant secondary effects may include changes in dispatch patterns, induced changes in grid emissions due to storage or demand response, and longer-term impacts on investment or retirement decisions where there is a plausible causal link to the project.

In practice, secondary effects are more uncertain than primary effects and should not be treated with the same level of precision. A pragmatic approach would be to quantify primary effects as the core result, with secondary effects reported separately, using scenario-based or sensitivity analysis rather than a single deterministic value. Clear disclosure of assumptions, time horizons, and uncertainty ranges is essential.

From an assurance perspective, secondary effects should be optional or clearly labeled as modeled estimates, so users understand they are indicative rather than directly measurable outcomes.

Annual reporting better reflects how electricity systems and project impacts evolve over time. Grid emission intensities, dispatch order, and system constraints change year to year, meaning a single lifetime estimate produced at project outset can quickly become outdated or misleading.

Annual reporting also improves transparency and alignment with existing reporting cycles, allowing users to track how the emissions impact of a project changes as the grid decarbonizes or as operating conditions shift. From an assurance and governance perspective, it is easier to review and contextualize annual estimates than to rely on a long-term projection made under assumptions that may no longer hold.

Lifetime estimates may still be useful for planning or internal decision-making, but for public reporting, annual impact reporting provides clearer, more decision-relevant information and reduces the risk of overstated or static claims.

Regulatory test (Required)
This should be mandatory, as it establishes a clear baseline: projects that are already required by law or regulation cannot reasonably be considered additional. This test is generally objective, verifiable, and well understood by auditors and regulators.

Timing test (Required)
The timing of project commitment relative to policy changes, incentives, or procurement decisions is fundamental to additionality. Without this test, it is difficult to demonstrate a causal link between an organization’s action and the project’s development.

Financial analysis test (Optional)
Financial analysis can be a strong indicator of additionality, but it is sensitive to assumptions, confidential data, and counterfactual modeling. It should be allowed as an option rather than required, particularly to avoid disadvantaging smaller developers or projects in emerging markets.

Barrier test (Optional)
Barrier analysis is useful where non-financial obstacles (e.g. permitting risk, grid access, technology maturity) are clearly documented. However, it can be subjective and should not be mandatory.

Common practice test (Optional)
This test helps distinguish genuinely incremental projects from business-as-usual development. It is most useful when supported by credible market data, but its relevance varies significantly by region.

Positive list / performance standard (Optional)
These approaches improve scalability and reduce administrative burden, especially in early-stage or underserved markets. They should be optional and periodically reviewed to avoid becoming outdated.

Contractual / tenor test (Optional)
Longer-term commitments can support additionality claims, but contract length alone is not sufficient proof. This test should be supplementary.

First-of-its-kind test (Optional)
This can be relevant for innovative technologies but is too narrow to be required across all renewable projects.

1. GHG Protocol Guidelines are appropriate because they provide a clear conceptual basis for combining short-run dispatch effects (operating margin) with longer-run structural effects (build margin). They are also familiar to many practitioners, which helps with interpretability and consistency.

3. UNFCCC CDM Tool07 is appropriate because it has been widely applied across jurisdictions and project types, and it offers a standardized approach that many auditors and regulators recognize. Even where the exact parameters need updating, the structure is practical and can be adapted.

4. Resource adequacy approaches are appropriate because they link weighting to a grid’s investment condition (e.g., whether the system is capacity-constrained, in expansion, or in surplus). In markets where capacity adequacy is the binding constraint, build margin effects are likely more relevant; where short-run dispatch dominates, operating margin effects tend to be more informative. This approach is conceptually aligned with power system planning.

5. Intervention lifecycle approaches are appropriate because they recognize that the relative importance of operating vs build effects can change over time. For example, early years of a project may primarily shift dispatch, while longer-run effects may include deferred fossil additions or accelerated retirements, depending on the system. This framing is useful when the goal is an impact metric rather than an inventory number.

I do not support a fixed 0.50 build margin default as a general rule because it can be arbitrary across regions and may misrepresent systems that are clearly expansion-driven or clearly dispatch-driven.

Resource adequacy approaches depend on reliable and comparable planning data (reserve margins, adequacy assessments, capacity credit methodologies, reliability standards), which are not consistently published or comparable across markets. In some regions, the data exists but is not transparent or updated regularly. This creates implementation burden and inconsistent outcomes.

Intervention lifecycle approaches can be methodologically sound but are often difficult to operationalize at scale because they require assumptions about future grid evolution, policy changes, and investment responses. Without strong governance and standardized scenarios, results will diverge significantly across users. From an assurance standpoint, it becomes difficult to evaluate “reasonable assumptions” in a consistent way.

By contrast, GHG Protocol Guidelines and CDM Tool07-type approaches are generally feasible because they can be implemented with more standardized inputs and clearer audit trails.

A practical alternative is a tiered, market-readiness weighting framework with explicit default weights and justified departures. For example:
- Tier 1 (limited data markets): default weight set (e.g., OM-heavy) with conservative assumptions and required disclosure.
- Tier 2 (moderate data markets): weights based on a small set of objective indicators (e.g., multi-year net capacity growth, reserve margin band, observed fossil build/retirement trend).
- Tier 3 (high data markets): weights derived from published system operator planning outputs or standardized capacity expansion modeling scenarios.

This reduces burden where data are thin, while allowing more tailored weights where the system information is credible and publicly verifiable. It also improves comparability because users operate within a defined tier structure rather than inventing weights case-by-case.

The tiered concept is consistent with how several electricity and carbon accounting practices handle uneven data maturity: use standardized defaults where necessary, then allow more precise methods where system data and governance support it. Relevant supporting references include:
- GHG Protocol guidance on grid-connected electricity project reductions (for OM/BM concepts and combining effects).
- UNFCCC CDM Tool07 (combined margin approach and practical implementation precedent).
- IEA electricity sector analyses and grid transition reporting (for the concept that marginal impacts depend on system adequacy, expansion dynamics, and dispatch conditions).
- Academic power systems literature on marginal emissions and investment response (showing that OM/BM relevance differs by market structure and stage of transition, supporting a tiered approach rather than one fixed weight).

Consequential accounting represents a critical and necessary evolution of electricity emissions reporting because it directly addresses the question that ultimately matters: whether corporate actions reduce global emissions in the real world. Unlike attributional Scope 2 methods, which focus on allocating emissions within a reporting boundary, consequential methods explicitly evaluate system-wide impacts relative to a counterfactual baseline, making them far more decision-useful for procurement, investment, and policy engagement.

The principal benefit is that consequential accounting correctly rewards actions that displace high-emitting marginal generation or influence long-term grid evolution, regardless of whether those actions occur within a reporter’s local grid. This avoids perverse incentives created by attributional approaches, where organizations may prioritize local or time-matched procurement that looks favorable in an inventory but delivers limited or zero net emissions benefit at the system level.

Key challenges include data availability, methodological complexity, and the risk of false precision if results are over-interpreted. Marginal emission rates vary by time, location, and modeling approach, and additionality assessments require judgment. However, these challenges are preferable to the false confidence created by highly granular attributional metrics that do not measure causal impact. Transparency, conservative assumptions, and clear disclosure of uncertainty are therefore more important than uniformity.

A significant unintended consequence to avoid is allowing consequential accounting to be treated as a secondary or optional supplement to attributional reporting. If positioned merely as an “impact metric,” organizations may continue to optimize against attributional Scope 2 outcomes that do not reduce emissions in practice. To be effective, consequential accounting must be clearly framed as the primary tool for evaluating whether electricity-related actions meaningfully contribute to global decarbonization, with attributional inventories serving a more limited bookkeeping role.

At a structural level, the proposed Scope 2 TWG subgroup formula is an appropriate and necessary starting point for quantifying consequential emissions impacts from electricity projects. The formula correctly shifts the focus from attributional allocation toward causal impact by comparing a project’s effect against a counterfactual baseline, which is essential for assessing whether an action actually reduces emissions in the electricity system.

We support the distinction between primary effects and potential secondary effects, as well as the explicit recognition that emissions impacts depend on changes to system dispatch, capacity, or investment decisions rather than on contractual or geographic attribution. This structure is directionally correct and aligned with the core purpose of consequential accounting: informing decisions that reduce real-world emissions.

That said, the usefulness of the formula will ultimately depend on how it is applied and disclosed. Overly rigid or prescriptive implementations risk undermining its value by introducing false precision or by privileging methodological complexity over decision relevance. The formula should therefore be treated as a flexible framework that accommodates different data availability and modeling approaches, with transparency about assumptions and uncertainty, rather than as a single deterministic calculation.

Secondary effects should be considered where they are material and decision-relevant, particularly when electricity projects influence longer-term system behavior beyond immediate dispatch effects. These may include impacts on capacity expansion or retirement decisions, changes in marginal generation over time, interactions with transmission constraints, price-induced demand or supply responses, and indirect effects on fossil generation utilization.

For example, long-term procurement or investment decisions may reduce emissions not only through short-term displacement of marginal generation, but also by accelerating the retirement of high-emitting assets or altering future capacity build-out. Ignoring these effects risks systematically understating the true emissions impact of projects that meaningfully influence grid evolution.

Quantification of secondary effects should be proportional to materiality and supported by transparent assumptions rather than overly complex modeling. Scenario analysis, sensitivity ranges, or standardized conservative proxies may often be more decision-useful than highly granular models that are difficult to audit or replicate. Where uncertainty is high, disclosure of ranges and qualitative explanation should be favored over exclusion of secondary effects altogether.

Emissions impacts should be calculated and reported on a recurring, annual basis rather than as a one-time lifetime estimate. Annual reporting better reflects the dynamic nature of electricity systems, where marginal emissions, dispatch patterns, grid mix, and counterfactual conditions evolve over time. A single upfront lifetime estimate risks becoming rapidly outdated and may misrepresent the actual ongoing impact of a project.

Annual reporting also improves decision-usefulness and accountability by allowing stakeholders to observe whether a project continues to deliver emissions reductions as expected, and under what system conditions those reductions occur. This approach aligns with how corporate decisions are revisited, adjusted, or expanded over time, and it allows consequential metrics to inform real-world operational and procurement choices.

While lifetime estimates may still be useful for internal planning or ex ante investment analysis, they should not substitute for ongoing reporting. If lifetime impacts are disclosed, they should be clearly distinguished from annually reported realized impacts and accompanied by transparent assumptions and uncertainty ranges.

Additionality frameworks must strike a careful balance between rigor and feasibility. The objective should be to identify actions that genuinely change system outcomes, not to impose a narrow set of tests that exclude impactful projects due to methodological rigidity.

The regulatory test should be required, as it establishes a clear and widely accepted baseline: activities already mandated by law or regulation should not be credited as additional. This test is objective, relatively easy to apply, and foundational to maintaining credibility.

All other tests should remain optional, allowing projects to demonstrate additionality through multiple plausible pathways. Electricity systems vary widely by region, maturity, and policy context, and no single test reliably captures causality across all settings.

Timing tests can be informative where a project clearly precedes expected market or policy-driven deployment, but are not universally applicable.

Financial analysis and barrier tests can demonstrate that a project required incremental support, but rely on assumptions that may be difficult to audit consistently.

Common practice and performance standard tests are useful in mature markets but risk excluding high-impact projects in rapidly transitioning or emerging systems.

Positive lists can improve feasibility and consistency where well designed, but must be regularly updated to avoid becoming stale.

Contractual/tenor and first-of-its-kind tests can provide strong evidence of causality in some contexts, but should not be mandatory.

Allowing multiple optional pathways better reflects real-world decision-making and avoids false negatives that could deter investment in emissions-reducing projects.

For example:

In highly regulated or vertically integrated markets, regulatory and contractual tests may be most informative.

In liberalized markets with deep renewable penetration, common practice or performance standards may be more appropriate.

In emerging markets or high-emissions regions, financial or barrier tests may be critical to identifying projects that genuinely shift investment outcomes.

A rigid, globally uniform set of required tests would either exclude impactful projects in some regions or dilute rigor in others. Regional flexibility is therefore essential to preserve both integrity and climate impact.

The level of additionality rigor should scale with the strength of the claim being made.

Association or contribution claims (e.g., “this procurement supports low-carbon electricity development”) may reasonably rely on fewer or simpler tests, provided claims are clearly framed and disclosed.

This distinction allows organizations to pursue meaningful climate actions without overstating certainty, while preserving credibility for claims that assert quantified emissions impacts. Aligning rigor with claim strength improves transparency, reduces greenwashing risk, and supports decision-useful reporting.

Operating margin emissions reflect how incremental changes in generation or load affect real-time system dispatch. Methodologies that directly or indirectly capture which resources are actually displaced at the margin are therefore appropriate.

SCED-based approaches (both fuel-on-the-margin and locational) are highly appropriate where system operator data are available, as they directly represent dispatch outcomes. Heat-rate/LMP methods provide a credible proxy when SCED data are unavailable, particularly in organized markets.

Statistical and difference-based methods can also be appropriate, especially in regions without transparent dispatch data, provided they are empirically grounded, well documented, and validated against observed system behavior.

Scenario modeling is appropriate when used transparently and calibrated to realistic system constraints, particularly for forward-looking or non-dispatchable projects.

In contrast, capacity-factor-based approaches are not appropriate for operating margin impacts, as they do not reflect marginal displacement and risk reverting to attributional averages rather than consequential effects.

GHG Protocol guidance should explicitly allow multiple operating margin methodologies, conditioned on transparency, data quality, and fitness for purpose, rather than mandating a single approach.

Build margin emissions represent how projects influence future investment and capacity decisions, not current dispatch. Accordingly, methodologies must reflect counterfactual capacity outcomes.

Capacity expansion modeling is the most conceptually robust approach, as it explicitly captures how incremental supply or demand affects long-run system build decisions. Policy scenario analysis is also appropriate, particularly where capacity expansion models are unavailable or where policy constraints strongly shape investment outcomes.

Recent capacity additions can serve as a reasonable proxy in some contexts, especially where market signals are stable and recent builds are representative of marginal investments.

Unless they are used as part of carefully constructed time and location generation modeling scenarios Average emission rates are not appropriate for build margin impacts, as they fail to represent investment causality and do not capture how projects influence future system evolution.

As with operating margins, methodological pluralism is essential. Guidance should focus on methodological integrity and disclosure rather than prescribing a single global approach.

GHG Protocol should assess applicability based on project characteristics and system context, rather than applying uniform methodological requirements.

Relevant factors include:

Project size relative to the system

Temporal generation profile (e.g., solar vs. wind vs. storage)

Capacity factor and shape

Degree of correlation with system peaks or constrained periods

Market structure and availability of dispatch or planning data

Smaller or highly intermittent projects may warrant simpler statistical or proxy methods, while large projects or aggregated portfolios may justify more sophisticated dispatch or expansion modeling.

Clear guidance on method selection criteria, coupled with transparency and uncertainty disclosure, would be more effective than rigid method mandates.

Additional metrics that may be appropriate include:

Locational marginal emissions (LMEs) derived from nodal or zonal dispatch data

Time-weighted marginal emissions for projects affecting specific hours or seasons

Forward-looking marginal emissions incorporating expected policy or fuel-price changes

Hybrid operating/build margin metrics for projects that affect both dispatch and investment decisions

These metrics can improve decision-usefulness when clearly scoped and transparently reported, particularly for demand-side measures, storage, and flexible load projects.

In principle, nodal granularity best reflects how electricity systems actually operate, particularly in organized markets with locational dispatch and congestion.

However, the appropriate spatial resolution should be bounded by data quality and interpretability. Where nodal data are robust and transparent, they provide the most accurate representation of marginal impacts. Where such data are unavailable or unreliable, zonal or balancing-area approaches may be more appropriate.

GHG Protocol should treat nodal granularity as an upper bound rather than a universal requirement, emphasizing fitness for purpose over formal precision.

Electricity dispatch and emissions outcomes often change at sub-hourly intervals, particularly in systems with high penetrations of variable renewables, storage, and fast-ramping resources.

Sub-hourly marginal emission rates are therefore conceptually appropriate where supported by system data. That said, temporal granularity should scale with data availability and analytical rigor. When they are used as part of carefully constructed time and location-specific generation modeling, well constructed high-resolution estimates can be useful if facility-specific granular metering data is not available. However, poorly constructed estimates can create an illusion of precision without improving accuracy and should be avoided.

GHG Protocol guidance should emphasize that higher temporal granularity is preferable when it materially improves representation of system behavior, but should not mandate granularity beyond what data quality can credibly support.

Multiple approaches to assigning build and operating margin weights are appropriate because the emissions impact of an electricity intervention depends on how it changes the global power system, not solely on where electricity is consumed or contracted. A single universal weighting rule would systematically misrepresent impacts in many contexts and would bias decision-making away from interventions that deliver the largest real-world emissions reductions.

The existing GHG Protocol guidance and UNFCCC CDM Tool07 appropriately recognize that electricity projects can influence both short-run dispatch and long-run investment outcomes, and that the relative importance of these effects varies by system conditions, technology type, and policy environment.

A default 0.50 build margin weight is appropriate as a pragmatic and conservative baseline where project-specific evidence is limited, provided it is treated as a default rather than a normative benchmark and is accompanied by transparent disclosure. Defaults should enable participation without foreclosing more rigorous approaches where data supports them.

Resource adequacy approaches are particularly appropriate where interventions plausibly affect system capacity needs, reliability margins, or long-term investment signals. In such cases, build margin impacts often dominate operating margin effects, and weighting should reflect this reality rather than impose symmetry for accounting convenience.

Intervention lifecycle approaches are also appropriate where emissions impacts evolve over time. Many interventions have near-term operating effects and longer-term structural effects, especially as grids decarbonize. Recognizing this evolution improves decision usefulness by aligning reported impacts with how emissions reductions actually occur in the real world.

Overall, weighting approaches should be selected to reflect causal impact on system emissions at scale. The Protocol should therefore support multiple credible approaches, with clear guidance on applicability and disclosure, rather than mandate a single weighting structure that may be precise but wrong.

Resource adequacy and intervention lifecycle approaches can be methodologically strong but are not broadly feasible in many regions today due to data limitations, lack of transparent planning models, inconsistent access to capacity and reliability information, and significant implementation and assurance burden.

In many markets, the evidence required to credibly parameterize these approaches (e.g., system planning assumptions, reserve margin drivers, transmission constraints, forward capacity outlooks, and policy evolution) is not publicly available or is not available at sufficient resolution to support consistent and auditable application.

For this reason, these approaches should be supported as advanced options where credible inputs exist, but the framework should also include simpler defaults for broad global applicability.

A more decision-useful alternative is a tiered, impact-oriented weighting framework that links build and operating margin weights to observable indicators of how an intervention affects emissions at the system level, regardless of where electricity is consumed or contracted.

Such a framework could assign weights based on:

System context (e.g., capacity-constrained vs. energy-constrained grids; growth vs. saturation)

Intervention type (e.g., new renewable capacity, firming resources, storage, demand flexibility, or load shifting)

Evidence of investment causality (e.g., whether the intervention plausibly enables incremental capacity that would not otherwise be built)

Marginal emissions intensity of affected regions, recognizing that emissions reductions in higher-emitting systems can have substantially greater global impact than equivalent actions in already low-emissions grids

Temporal dynamics, including whether impacts are primarily short-run displacement, long-run structural change, or a combination of both

This approach avoids privileging geographic proximity or contractual deliverability over emissions impact. It also prevents false precision by standardizing weight tiers where data is limited, while allowing more rigorous, project-specific weighting where credible evidence exists.

By anchoring weighting decisions in causal impact rather than accounting symmetry, this framework better aligns consequential reporting with the core objective of the GHG Protocol: accelerating real, additional emissions reductions at the scale and locations where they matter most.

Overall, the Protocol should prioritize decision usefulness and integrity through transparent, well-justified method selection rather than a single prescriptive weighting rule.

A tiered, impact-oriented approach to assigning build and operating margin weights is supported by empirical research showing that consequential emissions impacts depend on how interventions alter system dispatch and investment outcomes, not just accounting conventions.

First, research on marginal emissions factors establishes that avoided emissions differ materially from average emissions and vary significantly by time and region. Siler-Evans et al.’s foundational work Marginal Emissions Factors for the U.S. Electricity System systematically calculates short-run marginal emissions factors using regressions of hourly generation and emissions data, finding that average emission factors can misstate avoided emissions by large margins — and that avoided emissions benefits differ greatly across regions.
🔗 https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/es300145v

Second, System-level impacts of voluntary carbon-free electricity procurement strategies (Xu et al., Joule 2024) uses capacity-expansion and dispatch modeling to examine how different procurement strategies affect overall emissions and system mix. It finds that annual matching approaches have little impact on long-run CO₂ emissions, whereas temporal (hourly) matching — which alters dispatch and investment signals — can drive significant system-level emissions reductions and incentivize advanced clean generation and storage that would not otherwise be adopted.
🔗 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2023.12.007

Supporting this, working papers such as System Effects of Carbon-Free Electricity Procurement (Bistline, arXiv 2025) find that clean electricity procurement strategies that align generation with load (e.g., hourly matching) produce larger emissions reductions system-wide than volumetric or annual approaches, especially when they influence capacity investment decisions.
🔗 https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.03049

Empirical grid-transition literature also distinguishes short-run (operating margin) from long-run (build margin) effects. For example, studies on long-run marginal emission factors (Hawkes 2014) show that long-run marginal emissions can diverge significantly from short-run rates as systems decarbonize, indicating the need to weight these effects differently when estimating emissions impacts over time.
🔗 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2014.03.060

Taken together, these sources support a flexible, impact-focused approach to weighting build and operating margins that reflects real system behavior — recognizing that interventions can affect both dispatch and investment in ways that vary by region, technology, and time horizon. Such a framework better aligns with the core objective of consequential accounting: accelerating real-world emissions reductions rather than optimizing attributional symmetry.

• Consequential accounting methods can serve as helpful tools to analyze the system-wide emissions impacts of projects or interventions; however, they can suffer from serious technical challenges and result in unintended consequences for investments in the voluntary clean energy market.
• GHG Protocol’s Public Consultation Draft for Consequential Electricity Sector Emissions Impact (Draft) notes that additionality is a key component of consequential accounting methods. According to the Draft, projects that can demonstrate additionality—wherein the project scenario differs from a baseline scenario—are considered to reduce system-wide emissions. Yet, a key methodological challenge is how a baseline is established, and which projects are deemed eligible to be analyzed in a project scenario. If additionality rules narrowly consider only certain kinds of projects as eligible under the project scenario (e.g., only a brand-new solar project) and include all existing facilities in the baseline—no matter their performance, role in grid decarbonization, or economic needs—then these stringent rules can unnecessarily limit the number of recognized GHG reductions and in some cases exclude projects that are additional and highly desirable.
• In the U.S., hydropower, including pumped storage hydropower, serves as a case in point. Hydropower has unique grid attributes that are essential for grid decarbonization. Hydropower can displace fossil-fuel-based generation, given its ability to operate at all hours of the day and ramp up when wind and solar are unavailable. Hydropower is also routinely called upon for its ancillary services including black start capabilities, regulation, and spinning reserves (see, https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2021/01/f82/us-hydropower-market-report-full-2021.pdf). Despite hydropower’s essential contribution to advancing grid decarbonization, flexibility, and reliability, this resource is often excluded under narrow definitions of additionality (e.g., when only new resources count) since a large number of facilities in the existing U.S. fleet are multi-decade old. This narrow view of additionality ignores the capital-intensive nature of hydropower: facilities require long payback periods for their initial capital investment and continue to need additional investments throughout their life for their upkeep, maintenance, refurbishment, and repowering (see, https://docs.nrel.gov/docs/fy24osti/87470.pdf; https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2021/01/f82/us-hydropower-market-report-full-2021.pdf; https://atb.nrel.gov/electricity/2024/hydropower). The U.S. has both regulated and deregulated electricity markets that affect ownership structures of hydropower projects and their ability to access necessary investments. Simply slating existing resources, such as hydropower, in a baseline scenario disregards their ongoing investment needs at best and, at worst, assumes their continued operation despite economic realities—with particularly detrimental outcomes for independently owned projects in deregulated markets. This treatment for existing hydropower could inadvertently chill necessary investment in this strategic resource at a critical point in time: 40% of the U.S. non-federal hydro fleet is coming up for relicensing in the next few years and projects will likely need new investments to upgrade facilities and extend the life of assets.
• The pitfalls outlined in the aforementioned example underscore the need for a careful development of additionality rules in the consequential accounting method. As a rule of thumb, consequential accounting should not disincentivize investments in renewable resources at a time when we need every electron to achieve societal decarbonization goals.
• Broadly, consequential accounting should complement attributional accounting and not replace it.

•Hydropower facilities, like all energy systems, can emit greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions over their entire lifecycle (See https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1364032111001924; https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/17/13/5794)
•Human-made reservoirs can emit GHGs, and for hydropower facilities with a reservoir— regardless of whether hydropower generation is the primary purpose of the reservoir—the creation and unique characteristics of the reservoir along with its ongoing operation play a key role in influencing the overall rate of GHG emissions from individual facilities (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2005GB002457; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1364032122003161). In other words, hydropower facilities with a reservoir may have not only one-time secondary effects (i.e., GHG emissions that occur during the construction, installation, and decommissioning or a project), but also ongoing secondary effects resulting from the operation of the water reservoir. Reservoirs can also serve as GHG emission sinks.
•Individual reservoir characteristics, such as the age, location, size, and morphology of the water reservoir, operational patterns [e.g., run-of-river, storage/peaking], water quality and stratification in the reservoir, external environmental factors etc. can all affect the rate and pathways of GHG emissions from water reservoirs. (See, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32801383/; https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/17/13/5794)

A Draft of the Guidance that was released in 2022. This draft notes that “[c]ompanies that purchase electricity from hydropower [should] report CH4 emissions from the hydropower reservoirs used to generate electricity as scope 2 emissions.” Final guidance is expected to be released at the end of January 2026.

The narrow perspective of these tests disregards the capital-intensive nature and economic reality of hydropower projects, and misunderstands how projects operate in practice. Hydropower facilities require long payback periods for their initial capital investment and continue to have ongoing maintenance and repowering expenses throughout their life (see, https://docs.nrel.gov/docs/fy24osti/87470.pdf; https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2021/01/f82/us-hydropower-market-report-full-2021.pdf; https://atb.nrel.gov/electricity/2024/hydropower). The timing test notes that if a project was already planned or under construction before an incentive was available (e.g., tax credit), then the facility would fail the test. Most of the existing hydropower projects in the U.S. would fail to meet this simplistic timing test; yet the reality is that incentives are but one part of a capital stack for existing projects, and they are critically necessary to keep projects operational and online. In other words, simply because a hydropower project is already built does not mean that it does not need continued investment to prevent decommissioning or license surrender [from 2010 to 2022 alone, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued 68 surrenders for hydropower licenses (and exemptions) with a combined capacity of 322 MW, and the most frequently reason cited for surrender was economic infeasibility, see https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2023-09/U.S.%20Hydropower%20Market%20Report%202023%20Edition.pdf]. Moreover, hydropower projects often perform repowering and upgrades on a turbine level, not project level. So, simply the pre-existence of a project for a timing perspective would fail to qualify turbine-level upgrades as additional even though the upgrades would in fact result in extending the life of the project as a whole. When it comes to the financial test, if the test is solely looking at a single contract (e.g., PPA) to assess whether that contact turns a project from being financially unattractive to attractive, then that too fails to acknowledge that hydropower projects often require multiple offtakes (and price premiums) across regions and diverse revenue streams to stay operational—a single investment alone would likely not change the financial outlook of a project and would be an improper way to assess additionality.
