Consequential methods may better reflect how electricity-sector actions actually change the system, capturing investment/retirement responses, technology substitution, and time- and location-specific operational effects, which EPRI has shown may matter for rooftop solar (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y), energy storage (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902), and end-use electrification (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33902-9). Used appropriately, consequential accounting may improve decision usefulness, avoid double-counting, and clarify co-pollutant/air-quality co-benefits alongside GHGs.

Key challenges include, but may not be limited to:
• Temporal volatility and evolution: Short-run marginal signals are instantaneous and may diverge from both short-run and long-run mix a multi-decade project will face.
• Spatial heterogeneity: Margins differ across nodes and balancing areas, as EPRI work shows (EPRI 2025; 3002031420; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002031420). Using coarse regional averages may potentially mis-rank options, while overly granular inputs can reduce comparability.
• Mechanism mismatch: Operating margin approaches may omit structural change when actions scale, biasing results, as discussed in earlier EPRI work. (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2211624119).
• Data and cost: Hourly, locational inputs and transparent documentation of counterfactuals may raise the analysis burden but are often necessary where material.
• Methods: There are a variety of approaches that have been explored to estimate locational marginal emission rates, but they all suffer from methodological and empirical problems that may render them unusable for conducting marginal electric sector impact analysis. (EPRI 2024; 3002030179; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002030179).

Unintended consequences for consideration:
• Perverse siting signals if instantaneous snapshots are treated as long-run project factors (EPRI 2025; 3002031420).
• Potential “over-crediting” of estimated abatement when substitution or policy constraints mean a project is infra-marginal (https://www.aeaweb.org/conference/2025/program/paper/NEDSnTBF).
• Loss of comparability if methods mix operating margin snapshots with build margin effects without disclosure or sensitivities.

The formula incorporates the use of marginal emissions rates, which may be inappropriate to apply to electricity procurement actions that are not marginal. By definition, a marginal rate is the change in system emissions for an increase or decrease of 1 MWh of demand or supply. Any procurement action that is more than “incremental” to the system will not correctly be quantified using a marginal rate (EPRI 2025; 3002031420; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002031420).

EPRI modeling indicates that consequential emissions estimates may be: 1. Influenced by investment and dispatch feedbacks; 2. Better informed by using power system models or long-run marginal emission rates where structural change is material. Studies that link capacity planning/dispatch to interventions like electrification, rooftop solar, and energy storage adoption show that simplified short-run marginal factors miss structural substitutions and misstate system responses.

Links to studies: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33902-9, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902

In addition to short-run dispatch effects, consequential estimates may be more effective when considering (where material):
• Investment and retirement responses: EPRI research suggests that these structural responses can dominate consequential emissions impacts, which makes power system models or long-run marginal emission rates better-suited to capture these effects (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33902-9, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902).
• Technology interactions in the power sector: Representing substitution across resources and temporal correlations can alter impacts (e.g., rooftop solar displacing utility-scale solar, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y).
• Cross-sector feedbacks: EPRI research indicates that integrated energy system modeling may be important for quantifying consequential impacts in areas like end-use electrification (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33902-9) and electrolytic hydrogen production (https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002028407).
• Co-pollutant emissions and air quality effects: Changes in generator operations, entry, and exit as well as upstream/downstream emissions sources can alter non-CO2 pollutants (NOx/SO2/PM), which has air quality impacts (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33902-9).
For each category, the research above indicates the importance of materiality-based inclusion (i.e., based on context-specific factors), transparent disclosure of methods, and sensitivity analysis to key drivers (e.g., policy, fuel prices, technology costs).

In theory, for interventions that plausibly change the capacity mix or system operations over time, EPRI research indicates that forward-looking consequential methods may alter assessed emissions impacts. Evidence from EPRI studies show that:
• Investment/retirement responses dominate emissions outcomes for energy storage: Dispatch-only, year-by-year snapshots may mislead; evaluating impacts across the asset’s lifetime better reflects potential consequential impacts (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902).
• Simplified short-run rates can underestimate electrification’s benefits due to grid decarbonization over time, which electrification facilitates: This dynamic may make lifetime, scenario-consistent accounting more accurate than single-year snapshots (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-33902-9).
• Rooftop PV impacts depend on substitution with grid additions over time and evolving hourly margins: Lifetime modeling (or long-run rates) may better capture these dynamics compared with annual fixed rates (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y).

However, in practice, this research suggests that calculating the emissions impact over the expected lifetime of the proposed project may raise implementation challenges. Because marginal rates are constantly changing and can be expected to change with structural changes to the electricity system (e.g., new loads, changes in generation supplies), using a fixed marginal emissions rate that is estimated at the time a proposed project is being evaluated can negatively impact decision making. In addition, approaches that account for structural changes (e.g., capacity expansion modeling, long-run marginal rates) entail uncertainty at the project’s outset, which may suggest reasons for limiting analysis to the reporting year only.

Additionality is a component of GHG offset programs that ensures that offset projects are not granted tradable carbon credits for non-additional actions. In general, there is no analytic method that can be used to definitively “prove” the additionality of a proposed offset project (EPRI 2011; 1023122; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000000001023122).

However, the use of additionality tests may not needed to evaluate the potential GHG emissions impact of proposed grid-connected electricity projects, unless these projects are envisioned to be eligible to receive carbon credits. Any new investments in new electricity infrastructure or changes in electricity demand may be expected to impact system-wide GHG emissions, so it may be sensible to develop methods to estimate the GHG emissions impact of new grid-connected projects regardless of whether they are additional.

The CDM and other offset programs have determined additionality using a case-by-case approach for each project (i.e., a “project-based” approach), involving the use of multiple additionality tests. Standardized approaches credit reductions on the basis of uniformly applicable criteria. These include performance standards (e.g., emission rates, energy use rates, market penetration rates) and technology benchmarks (e.g., specific technologies in certain sectors and locations that are automatically deemed additional) (EPRI 2011).
A standardized approach to baseline setting can incorporate default assumptions (e.g., BAU emissions factors) established by the regulator, thereby streamlining the baseline calculation process and reducing the amount of project-specific data required to calculate the baseline. In contrast, RGGI’s offset system requires the calculation of project-specific baselines and provides methodologies for doing so. This approach is similar to the one used by the CDM. It may be the case, however, that even under a standardized baseline approach, some project categories will require a significant amount of project-specific data and assessment (EPRI 2011).

EPRI has been engaged in developing approved carbon offset protocols related to reducing nitrogen fertilizer applications in agricultural crop production (EPRI 2013; 1023669; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000000001023669). This research indicates the difficulties in implementing a financial analysis test, particularly when a proposed project such as reduced nitrogen use may actually be profitable for farmers that engage in this activity. This EPRI research also suggests that farmers tend to continue to fertilize their lands beyond the economic optimum level because of “common practice.” This research suggests that it does not seem feasible in all instances to use a financial analysis test.

The EPRI research referenced above suggests that the “Common Practice” test may be used effectively to assess the additionality of certain types of offset and GHG abatement projects. In the MSU-EPRI Methodology (ACR and VCS versions), the performance test is passed at a project site if the N fertilizer rate is below a threshold that represents the business-as-usual (BAU) rate. This BAU rate is based on the yield-goal approach (historical and current common practice), and is identical to the calculated baseline N rate of the project, using either Approach 1 or 2. In the CAR NMPP, the performance standard for a project activity is based on a N use efficiency (NUE) metric termed the ratio of Removed to Applied Nitrogen (RTA) calculated as a ratio of the amount of N removed by crop biomass to the amount of N available to the crop as a function of how much total N was applied to the crop. production (EPRI 2013).

When using the ACR and VCS versions of the MSU-EPRI Methodology, project proponents must pass a Practice-Based Performance Standard Test. This standard equates the BAU baseline scenario for N fertilizer application with the common practice of producers to apply N fertilizer rates based upon recommendations derived from yield goal estimates. Project developers pass the Performance Standard Test by reducing their N fertilizer rate below the BAU rate, which is also the baseline value for N fertilizer rate for the proposed project. Reducing the N fertilizer rate (and therefore N2O emissions) below the BAU rate (Approach 1 or 2) results in project additionality. Brief evidence for the wide-scale historic and continued use of the yield-goal approach in U.S. crop agriculture, and therefore its legitimacy as a Performance Standard for testing additionality is provided un the original EPRI published report. More information can be found in Annex E of the VCS version of the MSU-EPRI Methodology (EPRI 2013).

One major reason the EPRI-MSU team proposed a Performance Benchmark was to create a site specific (project-scale) test for additionality that could act as a sectoral baseline for agricultural crop N management projects in the U.S. The research expected this approach to reduce the current need to conduct costly and time-consuming site-specific evaluations of additionality for each proposed emissions reduction project. Project developers pass the Performance Benchmark by being below a threshold value that represents a BAU application of N fertilizer – identical to the baseline N application rate at a project field. Reductions in rate, and therefore N2O emissions, below the BAU value result in project additionality. In other words, the additionality benchmark is identical in value to the crediting benchmark (EPRI 2013).

EPRI research shows emissions impacts and additionality may vary by region owing to differences in resource mix, policies, infrastructure, and other factors:
• Policy and market context: EPRI research illustrates how electricity generation resource additions are inframarginal in U.S. states that have binding emission performance standards, which implies that these “new” generation projects would otherwise have been built due to state policies (https://www.aeaweb.org/conference/2025/program/paper/NEDSnTBF). EPRI analysis also illustrates regional differences in power sector planning and relative cost-effectiveness of different resources, which alters project additionality (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435124004239).
• Technology substitution varies by region: EPRI research indicates that impacts of energy storage may be region-dependent and may raise or lower emissions depending on the regional fleet, prices, and policy (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902). Rooftop solar often substitutes for utility-scale solar in high-solar regions; consequential emissions impacts differ across regions (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y).
• Financial viability and local practices: Additionality may be region specific in that what may be additional in one region may not be additional in another region. For example, it may be common practice for farmers to over-fertilize corn grown in the Upper Midwest of the United States, but this may not be common practice in other regions of the U.S. or in other parts of the world. A good example of the need for different regional approaches to determining additionality are GHG emissions offset projects designed to destroy methane (CH4) emitted from landfills. In this case, the California Air Resources Board (CARB) does not recognize landfill gas offsets implemented anywhere in the United States as being “additional,” because under existing laws and regulations in California, operators of landfills are required to capture and destroy methane emissions from landfills. However, a number of landfill gas offset projects have been successfully implemented in other U.S. states and Canada that have been granted tradable carbon offsets because these activities were deemed to be additional as these activities are not required to be done by law or regulation in these jurisdictions (EPRI 2022; 3002025723; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002025723).

EPRI research indicates that “appropriate” approaches match the mechanism and scale. Operating margin (OM) approaches that hold the fleet fixed (short-run dispatch response) are most appropriate for small, transitory operational changes that do not induce new builds/retirements (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2211624119). Several ISOs/RTOs publish locational marginal emissions rates (LMERs) that can inform these operational questions (EPRI 2025, 3002031420, https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002031420). When projects plausibly affect the capacity mix (e.g., large-scale rooftop solar deployment, energy storage, widespread electrification), operating-margin-only methods can misstate impacts by omitting structural change, especially since the build margin can influence the operating margin, as shown in EPRI research on energy storage (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902).

Practical considerations limit OM/LMER use as standalone factors for long-lived projects:
• Temporal variability and evolution: OM/LMER signals are instantaneous and constantly changing with dispatch, congestion, and policy/fleet evolution. A factor observed today may not represent the margins faced over a multi-decade project horizon (EPRI 2024; 3002030179: https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002030179)
• Spatial heterogeneity and multiple marginal units: In large systems (e.g., PJM/MISO), there is nearly always congestion somewhere, so multiple resources share the margin with location-specific shift factors. This produces highly variable and sometimes large marginal rates across nodes and five-minute intervals (EPRI 2024; 3002030179: https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002030179).
• Forecasting limits: Because dispatch can flip between intervals (e.g., wind on the margin in one period and coal on the margin the next), OM snapshots describe what happened, not necessarily what will happen. They are ideally treated as operational indicators, not long-run project factors.

Comments on specific methods:
• A difference-based approach can be highly granular but reportedly is subject to bias since changing grid conditions confound the effect of varying load. Also, this approach may lead to extreme values based on coincidence, especially in situations where load is changing more slowly (EPRI 2024; 3002030179; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002030179).
• One challenge with using binning-based regression models is that using multiple bins of historical data for each hour may result in regression analyses producing different rates for different grid conditions. These models also can be inaccurate if grid conditions within a bin are not similar along a confounding dimension. The most common confounding bias is in marginal renewables (EPRI 2024; 3002030179).
• Using a heat-rate modeling approach, one may calculate a resulting MER. This approach may be both highly granular but also highly variable. EPRI research suggests that these models may perform best in power grids where there is a clearly defined fuel type on the margin (EPRI 2024; 3002030179).
• Experiment-based models reportedly can have low bias, but implementing this approach requires access and manipulation of very large, high-quality datasets. In general, EPRI research indicates that this approach may have low statistical power, and it may be difficult to produce a wide range of treatment effects under various grid conditions (EPRI 2024; 3002030179).
• One advantage of developing MER estimates based on the actual emissions of marginal generation unit is that grid operators may have access to data about the grid that is not readily available to the public, but MER estimates developed this way can be highly variable and highly granular (EPRI 2024; 3002030179).

Build margin factors may be most useful when they reflect the mix of new capacity economically induced or displaced by an action, which can be technology- and region-specific. EPRI modeling shows displacement weights vary and may not be well represented by fixed global heuristics. For instance, for rooftop solar, build margins can dominate because it frequently substitutes for utility-scale additions in many regions (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y).

Several factors can be considered when evaluating model applicability for different projects:
• Mechanism: If a project plausibly influences investment/retirement decisions (structural), due to its persistence and policy context, approaches that capture long-run system response may be more appropriate, including capacity expansion models or long-run marginal rates (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2211624119). EPRI research indicates that energy storage (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902) and rooftop solar (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y) are technologies where emissions impacts can be dominated by investment effects rather than dispatch alone.
• Penetration level and system feedbacks: As penetration rises, projects may alter prices, curtailment, future builds, and displaced resources, especially given correlations in output across installed capacity (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0301421521002949). For rooftop solar, including these dynamics reduces implied benefits by 41-98% in a U.S. case study, relative to short-run rates (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y).

Marginal emissions factors may differ at different geographic locations on the power grid. Given this, EPRI research indicates the importance of using locational marginal emission rates, where material, instead of marginal rates related to larger geographies (EPRI 2025; 3002031420; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002031420).

“Appropriate” temporal resolution likely varies based on the application, but EPRI research suggests that, where output/load co-varies hourly with marginal emissions (e.g., solar profiles, EV charging), operating margin estimates are most accurate/useful when they are at least hourly and region-specific (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902). EPRI research suggests that annualized emissions rates can over-/under-estimate effects and mis-rank options (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y). ISO locational marginal emissions rate data illustrate substantial intra-hour volatility, which reinforces the need for higher temporal resolution treatments for some applications (EPRI 2025; 3002031420; https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002031420). However, data availability may limit temporal granularity based on the time interval of dispatch.

EPRI research suggests several considerations for selection:
• Endogenous/model-based weighting may be appropriate when projects can change the capacity mix. EPRI modeling shows investment (build margin) effects may dominate dispatch (operating margin) effects for technologies like battery storage, where evaluating investment and dispatch simultaneously changes the sign and magnitudes across technologies and regions (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306261920301902). This finding supports approaches that derive weights from capacity expansion modeling or long-run marginal methods for specific technologies, geographies, and scenarios rather than fixed splits.
• Weights may be most useful when they reflect technology-specific substitution. EPRI’s detailed systems modeling suggests that rooftop solar often displaces utility-scale solar rather than fossil, yielding 41% lower benefits in 2035 and 98% in 2050 versus simplified a “combined margin” approach that places 0.75 weight on the operating margin (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02459-y).
• Program design and incentives may shift build versus operating contributions for electricity-consuming projects. For EPRI analysis of hydrogen tax credits, the stringency of temporal matching, additionality, and deliverability changes power sector buildout and dispatch, which alters the relative importance of build margin and operating margin channels (https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002028407).

Green Strategies welcomes the Protocol’s efforts to develop consequential accounting, and Green Strategies has advocated for consequential accounting to become a key component of updating and modernizing Scope 2 reporting[1][2]. Consequential accounting enables reporting companies to distinguish transactions that have higher GHG reduction impact from those with lesser impact and to target transactions and investments at locations and times that are most GHG-intensive. Consequential accounting can complement the preparation of location-based and market-based inventories. Actions that may lower a Scope 2 market-based inventory, such as matching a zero-emission EAC to a megawatt-hour of consumption, may have varying real-world impact depending the time and location of the EAC’s underlying generation. Consequential accounting considers how and the extent to which a clean energy project achieves incremental reduction in fossil generation and takes into account project characteristics (e.g. new build) and the timing and location of the project’s generation.

In 2025, Green Strategies surveyed a group of leading corporate clean energy buyers to understand their perspective and interest in consequential accounting [3]. The survey found that approximately 60% of respondents would procure outside of their existing market boundaries. Respondents stated interest in procurement opportunities that would displace more GHG emissions (e.g. they operate in relatively clean grids already) and pointed to procurement challenges within their current market boundaries, such as restrictions on customer access to clean electricity.

ACORE supports the development of a consequential accounting method for electricity-sector actions. Establishing this pathway could encourage additional participation from voluntary purchasers by enabling corporates to report on investments that fall outside the parameters of the market-based method of the Scope 2 inventory. However, a consequential accounting methodology for electricity-sector actions should not be viewed as a replacement for the market-based method or used as justification to implement new requirements to the Scope 2 quality criteria.

The consequential method provides an additional information stream for stakeholders. A net impact metric, included in the proposal from the Scope 2 Technical Working Group Consequential Subgroup, would allow stakeholders to assess a company’s overall emissions impact against a baseline. Both the induced consumption and avoided emissions are fundamental to understanding the overall picture of a company’s impact.

Providing a reporter with the ability to disclose the total emissions that their actions have avoided could be a fundamental driver for additional action. However, to maximize incentives for companies, and to provide critical context for readers of sustainability reports, this must be paired with an induced consumption metric. This methodology would enable companies to disclose their impacts on a percentage basis, in addition to the absolute basis, allowing readers to compare a company’s level of spurred avoided emissions to the emissions it is responsible for inducing.

Most members of the general public do not have, and should not be expected to have, the in-depth understanding necessary to contextualize the quantity of avoided emissions that a company reports. By reporting its induced consumption, a company provides a benchmark against which stakeholders can measure its actions to spur additional development of clean energy. Accordingly, it provides a minimum threshold for companies to achieve to demonstrate that they are avoiding as many tons of CO2e as they are inducing. This also provides the foundation for companies to go above and beyond and demonstrate clear leadership in power sector decarbonization. Thus, a consequential accounting method could serve as a key pathway alongside the Scope 2 inventory.

Annual reporting of the emissions impacts for projects is fundamental to providing consistent, comparable, and contextualized information to readers. Reporting the impacts only once could make it harder to compare companies’ performance internally across years and externally to other reporters. From year-to-year, there could be significant variability in the number of projects that commence operations and thus significant swings in the emissions impact one year to the next. For stakeholders, this makes it more difficult to discern the overall impact that an individual reporter has on power sector decarbonization. Additionally, an annual disclosure cadence for the consequential methodology would sync better with the annual inventory reporting, providing a more useful supplementary information stream for readers.

There is no one-size-fits all approach to additionality that would be appropriate for all interventions. ACORE suggests a technology/intervention-specific approach to additionality.

ACORE considers the regulatory test and the timing test to be relatively feasible and important guardrails to prevent greenwashing. For the timing test, beginning of construction could be the metric against which additionality is measured. Most U.S. clean energy projects without a long-term commitment from a credit-worthy offtaker cannot secure efficient financing and will not achieve a Final Investment Decision (FID). [See Norton Rose Fulbright’s Cost of Capital 2026, https://tinyurl.com/36cv4ht9]. However, project sponsors must begin planning a project long before an offtaker comes in, but often with the understanding that the project would not proceed to construction without offtake. Basing the timing test off of earlier hurdles in the planning process would not reflect real-world conditions and introduce significant barriers to meaningful offtake. When implementing the timing test, it is fundamental to ensure that reporters can claim credit for actions that enable repowers, uprates, and delayed decommissionings, in addition to new-build generation. Repowers, uprates, and delayed decommissionings are pivotal actions that ensure the sustained success of clean energy buildout, and preventing companies from reporting on their credit here could create adverse incentives that lead to inefficient, more carbon-intensive outcomes.

ACORE considers the positive list test to be a more feasible option to determine additionality. Articulating a set of parameters under which contracts could qualify as additional allows buyers a clear framework of the procurements that would be eligible. However, to implement a successful positive list test, there must be a delineation of criteria that reflect real-world contract structures that drive clean energy deployment and include solar and wind. Implementation of clear rules could thus spur further levels of clean energy procurement by enhancing buyer confidence that they will receive credit for the duration of the contract.

While the positive list test would be the most feasible to implement, having the financial analysis test as another pathway to prove additionality, as proposed by the Consequential Subgroup, could be a way to include corporate activity that plays a meaningful role in spurring new clean energy infrastructure that would otherwise be unlikely to reach commercial operations.

Requiring the first-of-its-kind or common practice tests in the electricity sector may discourage investment away from projects that need corporate procurement to achieve FID. Projects of many varieties, including more established technologies, may need a long-term commitment from a credit-worthy offtaker to attain financing. One of the most impactful actions corporates can take is to leverage their creditworthiness and capital to mitigate the revenue risk present in clean electricity projects. While clean electricity projects are increasingly cost-competitive, financiers make investment decisions on whether they expect project revenues to cover project obligations, rather than whether a project generates cheaper electricity on a levelized basis. Thus, while merchant solar and wind projects may be providing cheaper electricity for the ratepayer, the actual return that the project receives will be dependent on the marginal clearing price in the wholesale market. With a long-term power purchase agreement in place, tax equity and debt providers can expect consistent revenue generation and are able to offer viable terms that enable project construction.

The barrier and performance standard tests appear highly subjective and complex to understand, with potentially high compliance costs. Requiring these tests could discourage procurement.

Benefits:
- Measurable Impact and Defensible Claims. Consequential accounting allows companies to demonstrate measurable, real-world climate benefits.
- Long-term Planning. Consequential accounting aligns corporate actions with national decarbonization targets and offers more consistency between private and public efforts.
- Capital Efficiency and Innovation. By linking emissions outcomes to time and location, companies can compare interventions by cost per tonne of CO2 avoided and focus investment on technologies/solutions that maximize system value.

Challenges:
- Cost. High-quality consequential analysis is data- and expertise-intensive, which raises costs for users, especially outside well-modelled markets. To avoid “pricing out” organizations that would otherwise voluntarily participate in renewable/clean energy purchases and GHG accounting/disclosure, the data for avoided emissions must be widely available.

- Reporting Complexity. If consequential impacts are calculated annually, emission accounting will require updated marginal emission rates as the grid (and models) evolve. The additional complexity may discourage firms from action. This challenge is avoided if the “avoided emissions” (impact) is calculated once at the time of contract/COD and applied consistently over the contract term.

- Eroding Benefit. If consequential impacts are calculated annually, the impact of a purchase/investment erodes as the grid decarbonizes. Long-term commitments needed to finance new renewable energy projects may be difficult for many firms. This challenge is avoided, if the “avoided emissions” (impact) is calculated once at the time of contract/COD and firms have confidence in the emission benefit over the contract term.
- Standardization and Governance. Without a standard and common approach to modelling “avoided emissions” (impact) of a purchase/investment, organizations may be reluctant to enter long-term agreements or make significant investments in regions where the accounting methodology is less certain or less viable.

Regulatory test - Required
Renewable purchases that are required by law or market design are not to be considered “additional.” However, the regulatory test is not comprehensive, as the voluntary purchase of energy attribute certificates from existing/merchant generators does not provide the financial commitments necessary to bring new generation to market.
Timing test - Required
Simple, objective, and politically neutral. Ensures operational projects are not counted as newly additional.
Contractual / tenor test - Optional
Term length does not necessarily define “additionality.” For example, firms that install solar generation through capital investments do not have a term as those installations are purchased outright. These systems would not exist without the firms’ commitment, but they also do not carry an applicable term length. Further, the purchase of a 5 or 10-year contract for EACs from an existing clean energy asset does not offer “additionality,” as that asset is already producing energy and in the current generation stack.
Positive list – Optional, highly feasible.
Positive lists are already used in formats like RE100, so for many buyers it is straightforward to show that a project falls into an approved category. However, because not all regions or actors are covered by existing lists, and lists can become outdated as markets evolve, it is better to treat them as an easy optional route to demonstrate additionality rather than a universal requirement.
Financial, barrier, common practice, and performance standards – Optional and feasible in many instances. Any purchase/investment made prior to a project’s financial close can be considered “additional,” as it provides the revenue certainty to secure the internal or third-party financial commitments necessary to build the project.

Common practice/performance standard, both require market data and careful boundary setting but are widely used in carbon standards and can be implemented where robust statistics exist, but not in all markets.

Financial and barrier tests demand granular project data, developer cooperation, and expert judgement, which can be costly and inconsistent across regions.

The definition of additionality should be consistent across markets. However, the method to demonstrate additionality may differ based on available information. A hierarchy of testing methods may be appropriate to allow organizations that support additional projects to demonstrate the additionality in circumstances where data/documentation may not be as readily available.

The only way to measure impact.

- Attributional inventories, including LBM and MBM, do not measure impact. Their purpose is to accurately account for usage, as stated by GHGP (June 2025). Send the right investment signal to the market.

- Decision-useful data to guide procurement choices for the most impactful projects by accounting for the emissions impact of electricity projects. As the GHGP noted, a solar

project in Georgia or Poland on a carbon-intensive grid would displace more emissions than one deployed in California or Spain on a cleaner grid.

- This data guides buyers to projects with the greatest emissions impact, providing long-term offtake agreements for impactful projects and sending an investment signal to generate projects where they have the highest emissions impact. Collectively, this accelerates grid decarbonization.

Growing feasibility.

- As the GHGP already noted, a broad and growing base of data is available for build and operating margin from ISOs and other organizations.

Accuracy: most accurate view into system changes.

- Consequential accounting captures grid realities (i.e. impact on the grid from changes in generation or consumption) and assesses the marginal impact of a decision to increase or decrease consumption at a specific time and place.

Cost effective / lowers electricity costs overall.

- Consequential accounting does not rely on deliverability boundaries, opening investment to high impact but lower cost regions, including potential to drive $85B into emerging markets by 2040.

PURPOSE:
The GHGP has long recognized the need for BOTH inventory (attributional) accounting and impact (consequential) accounting. These report different elements which, taken together, provide the full picture to drive maximum climate impact. The purpose of consequential accounting for the electricity sector should be to provide visibility to where actions drive the greatest emissions impact, supporting progress against targets. Specifically, it should capture routine impacts of consumption and generation (positive and negative procurement emissions impacts) that drive decision-useful data for stakeholders. This is not the same purpose as a full project accounting assessment.
For consequential metrics to provide decision-useful information to reporting entities, buyers, policymakers, investors, and other stakeholders on routine impacts of consumption and procurement (both positive and negative emissions impacts), they need to be recognized by target setting bodies.
For target bodies to recognize an impact metric, it has to be REQUIRED by the GHGP as the premiere global GHG accounting body.
Specifically, target setting bodies require accounting guidance on what an avoided emissions metric must be compared against (e.g. comparing consumption and procurement emissions impacts at the same time and location).
The approach proposed by the GHGP in this consultation document does not achieve the above objectives. It aligns with the Project Protocol which:
- Is not used by target setting bodies
- Includes no guidance for what an avoided emissions metric must be compared against
- Is not required accounting by the GHGP
- Has been rarely used by companies since its inception in 2005.

Accuracy: most accurate view into system changes.

RNG COALITION believes consequential accounting methods for electricity-sector actions can provide a mechanism for highlighting projects and procurement decisions that drive system-level decarbonization outside of pure emissions ownership. The challenge is ensuring the accounting is structured in a way that it incentivizes impactful projects in a technology-agnostic way. Historically, carbon accounting and target-setting frameworks have disadvantaged impactful decarbonization solutions like renewable gases and clean fuels. It is for those reasons that the proposed consequential methods present significant challenges. Results are highly sensitive to assumptions about counterfactuals, deliverability, quality criteria, etc., which can vary by region and over time and are often difficult to validate. Without clear methodological guardrails and standardized claims guidance that is informed by science and experts within the renewable gases and clean fuels space, there is a risk that consequential results could be misinterpreted and lead to confusion or understated impact. RNG COALITION does not support mandatory consequential accounting for reporting entities, but rather as a beneficial tool for those entities to describe their electricity-consuming operations.

RNG COALITION agrees the proposed Scope 2 TWG subgroup formula is structurally appropriate for quantifying emissions impacts from electricity projects, as it clearly distinguishes between project activity, counterfactual grid emissions, and project emissions. This difference-based structure can consistently capture system-level impacts across technologies, including dispatchable resources, provided that underlying assumptions and parameters are robustly defined.

RNG COALITION believes including secondary effects can provide a more complete view of the system-level emissions impact of electricity projects, particularly for dispatchable, low-carbon resources. For example, biogas generation can reduce reliance on high-emission peaker plants and influence future grid investment decisions, such as delaying new fossil capacity, which would not be captured by primary effects alone. Accounting for these indirect impacts better reflects the true marginal climate benefits of biogas projects and aligns reported emissions impacts with the real-world decarbonization they enable. Examples of these secondary effects that should be considered include displacement of high-emission marginal generators during peak hours, avoided future fossil capacity build, methane reductions from feedstocks, and shifts in market dispatch or system reliability. These can be quantified using marginal emissions factors, lifecycle emissions for feedstocks, scenario modeling of future capacity, or market simulation of dispatch impacts. Including these effects provides a more accurate representation of the true system-level climate benefits of biogas/biomethane-to-electricity projects.

We support the addition of consequential accounting within the Scope 2 guidance to allow companies to assess their interventions based on their decarbonization impact rather than solely MWh matching. This supports the GHGP’s stated goal of providing a standard that supports decision making which drives ambitious global climate action. Retaining attributional accounting alongside use of consequential accounting for the market-based standard maintains scientific integrity and GHG accounting and reporting principles.
Consequential accounting enables (1) users to seek out the highest impact projects, (2) captures the decarbonization value of grid-supporting projects such as batteries, and (3) provides a flexible approach that encourages action by stakeholders, irrespective of the size of their electricity procurement.

Seek out the highest impact projects
· A MWh attributional approach only measures the matching of consumption with generation, and not the carbon impact of those respective actions. Consequential accounting provides users with data on the carbon impact of their decisions for consumption and generation which enables better decision-making in line with the GHGP objective of driving ambitious global climate action. Consumers are then incentivized to procure energy from projects which have an impact equal to their consumption and provides them with the option to support high impact projects in regions with higher marginal emissions to displace fossil power, rather than continuing to procure in grids which may already be rich in renewables or where curtailment is becoming a challenge.

Captures the decarbonization value of grid-supporting projects
· Consequential accounting enables all potential electric sector actions to be evaluated on a level playing field using a single metric. This allows organizations to effectively assess different potential interventions, vs. only carbon free generation today. This incentivizes solutions such as energy storage, load shifting, renewable development, consumption siting, and transmission development. This significantly improves the grid investment challenge that is currently holding back CFE scale-up.

Broad stakeholder acceptance
· Consequential accounting provides stakeholders with a market-based option irrespective of their geography, size, or preferred method of decarbonization. Rather than limiting stakeholders to one set of market actions, stakeholders are empowered to evaluate what actions are best suited to their operations and use the consequential approach to quantify the carbon impacts of their operations and abatement actions. This supports acceleration of global climate action by aligning actions with reported outcomes.

Practical considerations
· The data and calculations for a consequential metric are available, feasible, and comparable. Operating marginal emissions data is available globally (WattTime, October, 2024) and build margin emissions rates inferred from recent capacity expansions and aligned with the existing GHGP project accounting protocol are also available. The methods proposed for calculating avoided emissions from carbon free generation in the consequential proposal can be equally applied to induced emissions from power consumption, and these results are comparable across reporting entities.

Clarity of claims
· Companies today procure energy close to their load consumption for business reasons (such as enabling new business capacity and adherence to local regulation) and this is not expected to change with adoption of a consequential metric. A consequential metric provides options for companies who are procurement-constrained or who have greater ambition to procure impactful projects outside of their core operations, which accelerates global climate ambition. This flexibility reflects the true intent of market-based mechanisms, which is to drive global optimization of electricity sector carbon emissions in a cost-effective manner.

Regulatory test: Regulations can change (RPS standards in Texas and Ohio for example) and in times of policy uncertainty, power purchase agreements provide stability for project developers. If a regulatory test is to be considered, it should be optional.

Timing test: This test should be optional, and the sale of a PPA from one party to another should not prevent the buying party from claiming the project as additional. Further, it should be clear that a company coming in to support a distressed project should still be able to claim the project as additional.

Financial Analysis test: It is unclear how to put a financial test in practice, as different project developers and buyers value projects differently. There will also be a confidentiality issue and this could create complications about financial dislcosures for private transactions.

Barrier test: We recommend the barrier test be optional - for some projects, proving a barrier is possible (financial barrier, unfavorable policy environment). For items such as limited access to technology, proof may be difficult or impossible and as such should be optional.

Common Practice test: This test should not be required due to vagueness (what constitutes a region or a sector) and conflating business-as-usual as equivalent to "will always occur".

Positive list: An optional positive list, refined by geography and policy environment, would be an implementable option that could cater to a broad range of stakeholders in identifying additional projects.

Performance standard: This test should not be required due to the difficulty of standardizing "performance" and setting a fair bar across technologies. For example, how do you measure the performance of a new wind turbine type vs. the performance of a new geothermal plant and ensure that both are adhering to a high-performance standard in their own field/metric?

Contractual tenor: We agree that making an impact claim should be supported by a contract providing financial stability to the project.

First of its kind test: We recommend this test as optional, as limiting this solely to first of a kind projects would reduce the number of projects to a very small number.

As noted above, we only recommend that a contractual additionality test be required under this metric. We do not believe that regional differences need to be considered for a contract to be in place between parties. However, if the GHGP moves ahead with other additionality tests then regional differences will be necessary and increasingly complicated.

Different regions have different financial market conditions and regulatory incentives. As a result, a rigid regulatory test or financial test could not be impartially applied across regions. For example, the recent regulatory decision from the Irish energy regulator for large energy user grid connections applies an additionality test for a requirement that new connections be matched with CFE. In reviewing that additionality test, it can be seen that jurisdiction specific requirements were necessary. In the decision, the regulator set specific timelines and identified projects that didn’t qualify through the national procurement auction process as being considered additional (see, Commission for Regulated Utilities, CRU/2025236, December 2025). This example illustrates the complexity and jurisdictional specific variations that are necessary for applying an additionality requirement to CFE procurement.

Another example can be found in the variation between clean energy policies in U.S. states when compared to Germany. U.S. state-level renewable portfolio standards typically require utilities to purchase and retire a renewable energy certificate to meet their obligation, but the regulation does not provide a financial incentive (financial incentive determined by market value of the certificate). In Germany, regulation the EEG (Erneuerbare-Energien-Gesetz) provides a floor price in the form of a feed-in-tariff and preferential connection to the grid, but these projects cannot create guarantees of origin (and hence derive no financial value from sale of GOs, vs. projects in compliance markets in the US).

An association claim states that two variables are related, but not necessarily that one causes the other, while a causal claim asserts that one variable is directly responsible for changing the other. Impact accounting is closer to a “causal” claim, (Project A caused X tCO2e in carbon avoidance) rather than an “association claim” (Project A, a solar project in Mississippi, may be associated with X tCO2e in carbon avoidance). It doesn’t make sense to use an additionality test to only make an association claim. If we are to subject impact accounting to an additionality test at all, it should result in a causal claim.

Operating margin data should be derived from data which is (1) available and (2) relies on a minimum of assumptions. SCED, Heat-rate/LMP, Capacity Factor, and Difference-Based methodologies rely on measured activity and the methodologies are straight-forward linear transformations of the underlying activity into an operating marginal emissions rate. On the other hand, Scenario Modelling and Statistical approaches use both empirical data as well as assumptions to estimate the impact of a change in the grid. Scenario modelling requires assumption of a counterfactual, and statistical modelling such as the EPA AVERT model includes assumptions such as “low-cost renewable energy (RE) and energy efficiency (EE) resources are dispatched first, displacing more expensive fossil fuel generation. The model assumes that an equivalent reduction in demand is modeled by comparing a scenario with a new RE resource to one without it.”.

Build margin data, while less knowable than operating margin data, should follow the same principles: (1) available and (2) relies on a minimum of assumptions. The two datasets which best fit this description are ‘Recent capacity additions’ and ‘average emissions rate’. Both datasets are available and research indicates they are a good proxy for future builds on the grid.

Use of policy scenarios or capacity expansion modeling require heavy use of assumptions and are not suitable for a standardized approach across geographies for impact assessment. For example, policy scenarios often include cost assumptions based on favorable (or unfavorable) policy, and capacity expansion models include assumptions on future electricity demand, projected technology costs and adoption, and also policy impacts themselves.

The maximum appropriate level of spatial granularity, interpreted as the largest geographic region under which application of marginal emissions rates can be applied, is at the balancing authority/area level. Balancing authority regions are defined as the region in which a balancing authority dispatches electric generators to balance supply and demand. There may be imports/exports between balancing authorities, but each balancing authority is responsible for tracking the marginal generator (whether within the grid region or as part of an export) within their own region of operations.

Grid Region in some instances aligns with balancing authority but not always. For example, US eGRID boundaries are a hybrid boundary between the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) regions and the smaller balancing authorities (BAs). The NERC boundaries are large regions across which imports/exports could occur, but the regions are too large to reliably point to a single marginal generator (e.g., WECC covers most of US West, British Columbia, and Alberta.

The marginal generator can be measured as often as the five minute (sub-hourly) interval, but can be time-averaged and aggregated to the hourly, daily, monthly, or annual values. Research and published values (IFI, IGES) for weighted-average marginal emission rates at the annual grain exist.

More information is needed to understand if a ‘resource adequacy approach’ is appropriate. However, we would not expect a resource adequacy approach in determining build margin weighting to result in significant differences vs. the GHGP guidelines, as the predictability of a project’s output is already considered within those guidelines.
All methods are feasible, in that the data required to estimate a build margin weight exists, or a set of assumptions that is easy to evaluate exists.

The potential benefits of robust consequential accounting methods for electricity sector actions are significant, including providing recognition and incentives for more impactful or cost-effective GHG mitigation actions inside and outside of organizations’ Scope 2 footprints. But there are significant risks associated with their use, and it is likely that a poorly implemented approach would do more harm than good. These risks stem primarily from the fact that the results of consequential accounting are by definition unverifiable, being assessments of the difference in outcomes between unobservable counterfactual realities. This means that consequential assessments will always be subject to deep uncertainty, and the best we can do is to craft methodologies that appear as theoretically robust as possible.

At the same time, corporations can be expected to utilize consequential accounting to identify and pursue actions that enable the largest GHG mitigation claims at the least cost. While this is often presented as a benefit, it also makes the challenge of ‘baseline setting’ in consequential accounting more difficult. Because the lowest-cost mitigation efforts are also the least likely to have needed additional financial support, there is a thin line between a system that accurately incentivizes the most cost-effective actions, and one that incorrectly rewards non-impactful actions. The challenge in determining whether interventions are additional and impactful compared to a baseline is one that has plagued the carbon offset market (which is also based on consequential accounting and has attempted to implement methods similar to those proposed here in the electricity sector), leading to a collapse in public trust in offset impact claims.

Developing sufficiently robust consequential accounting methods is a worthy goal, but many challenges must be overcome. Above all, electricity sector consequential accounting must be sufficiently credible and conservative in its handling of baseline setting, additionality, and market leakage, to minimize the likelihood that it becomes a vehicle for greenwashing. The chosen system should also be flexible and detailed enough to retain accuracy across the diverse global tapestry of electricity system regulatory and market structures, while at the same time remaining standardized enough to be practically usable and comparable across organizations.

GHGP must also ensure that GHG impact claims resulting from electricity sector consequential accounting practices are made with appropriate acknowledgement of the uncertainties involved. Consequential claims should be clearly presented as estimates rather than measurements, and should be kept separate in public communication from the fundamentally verifiable measurements that underpin attributional Scope 2 accounting. A balanced approach that acknowledges the advantages and shortcomings of both consequential accounting and Scope 2 inventory accounting will be most effective at driving real impact and maintaining public trust over the long run.

Finally, we recommend that GHGP consider the incentives created by the promotion of consequential accounting alongside traditional inventory accounting. Proposed revisions to GHGP’s Scope 2 inventory guidance, which CATF supports, may make it more difficult for organizations to report zero inventory emissions. If a consequential accounting approach is developed that is not robust, and makes it easy for organizations to claim net-zero emissions impact, companies may de-emphasize inventory reporting and elevate better-looking consequential reporting in its place. We therefore recommend that GHGP require reporting of inventory results alongside any consequential reporting, to give the public an accurate picture of the extent to which companies are both decarbonizing their own operations and driving global impact. This ensures that both goals remain at the forefront of corporate sustainability efforts.

Secondary effects should at the very least include impacts on the deployment, retirement, and operation of other electricity sector assets. These would ideally be quantified by estimating the expected behaviors of these other assets in a ‘status quo’ world where the intervention did not take place and comparing those estimates to observed outcomes.

While it would also be technically accurate to include a host of other secondary impacts (e.g. economic, political, technology development) these are likely too abstract to quantify with any degree of confidence.

Impact estimates are likely to change substantially as new information becomes available over the lifetime of a project and new operational decisions are made. While reported impacts will always be uncertain, they should not be based on information that is potentially decades out of date.

Regulatory and timing tests should be required because they are easy to implement and are obvious disqualifiers if failed. Projects that were already mandated or in progress prior to a buyer’s participation should not be considered additional.

A common practice test should be required because it is feasible to implement and addresses perhaps the greatest challenge in consequential accounting – ensuring that actions which are already widely economical are not credited with outsize impact.

A contractual/tenor test should be required because long-term contracts are well understood to be key enablers of project finance. While spot market purchases of instruments like EACs can theoretically incentivize growth in clean generation, the connection is much more tenuous and disputed compared to direct long-term offtake.

Tests that define clear, objective thresholds and rely on information that is widely publicly available are generally feasible.

A financial analysis test is likely not feasible because it requires disclosure of sensitive financial information and relies on standards that are not easily provable (i.e. that a project’s value to any other buyer would be lower than a certain threshold).

Both the barrier test and performance standard test are fairly complex and subjective, and would be very difficult to implement in a credible manner.

Regional factors will almost certainly play a role in the validity of certain additionality tests. For example, some regions may have carbon cap regulations that make it difficult for any individual intervention to drive impact, while others may have forms of top-down planning or programs to incentivize private sector clean energy procurement. At the same time, it is important that whatever system is adopted be as globally consistent as possible, so that bespoke practices that harm comparability do not need to be developed for each region. Ideally, there will be a clear set of global guidelines determining which tests are applicable under which sets of policy or market conditions.

If an organization merely procures clean power that is provably non-additional, they should be able to advertise this procurement but not claim any emissions impact. Any claims of impact should be contingent on high confidence in the additionality of the intervention in question, and even then should be presented as estimates.

Options (a) through (c) are generally appropriate methodologies because they are based on the same essential SCED logic that governs the operation of real grids. They should in theory produce relatively consistent results, though this assumption would ideally be tested before any set of methodologies is officially adopted. The remaining methodologies rely on various sets of assumptions that are more tenuously connected to the actual practice of grid operation.

One glaring gap in these methodologies as presented is the absence of any clear solution to quantifying the marginal emissions associated with discharge from energy storage, which is increasingly becoming a short-run marginal resource in grids worldwide. Even if storage can successfully be identified as a marginal generator (and this will be difficult under some methodologies given that storage bids based on opportunity cost rather than a predictable variable cost of operation), it is very difficult to calculate the emissions rate that should be assigned to that storage discharge. Appropriately tracking marginal emission rates during hours when storage is charging and assigning those emissions to discharge, while assessing the uncertainty involved, will be essential for the success of any operating margin methodology.

A build margin methodology that tracks recent capacity additions may be the only appropriate option, because it is based on empirical evidence. It is not a perfect approach, since the build margin implied by recent additions likely lags the instantaneous build margin if the pace of additions is changing rapidly, but it reflects a reasonable view of the resources whose deployment decisions might be affected by the intervention being assessed. In addition to capacity additions, this metric should also aim to take into account the impacts of avoided or accelerated capacity retirements.

The other proposed methodologies are generally unsuitable. The policy scenario option is based on national pledges rather than evidence of actual outcomes. Capacity expansion modeling is a useful tool for assessing potential future electricity system outcomes or comparing counterfactual scenarios, but it cannot predict actual system outcomes with high accuracy. An average emission rate approach is inappropriate because this metric has no relationship with either short- or long-run marginal emission rates.

Finally, if a build margin methodology based on recent additions is adopted, it must reflect the shape of the intervention being assessed in relation to the shape of the generation types on the build margin. For example, if the intervention is a new solar farm, its build margin impacts should be based on recently-built resources that generated at the same time as the solar farm’s expected generation (likely other solar farms). If this is not the case, interventions would be credited for displacing resources with which they do not directly compete.

There should be a single universal methodology for assessing the impacts of all projects. A usable, comparable methodology should allow as little user choice and subjectivity as possible, and should not incentivize pursuit of certain classes of projects due to their accounting advantages. Factors such as production shape are relevant to all generator types.
Any consequential method should adopt a level of spatial and temporal granularity that is at least equivalent to that of the proposed Scope 2 market-based method revisions.

Any consequential method should adopt a level of spatial and temporal granularity that is at least equivalent to that of the proposed Scope 2 market-based method revisions. Given the central role that variable renewables are likely to play in impact claims, time of generation and the resources with which an intervention competes are particularly critical factors to capture. A simple example illustrates the importance of hourly resolution: a grid where midday electricity demand is increasingly or entirely supplied by solar power, while demand at night is supplied by fossil power. If build and operating marginal emissions rates (and therefore impacts) are calculated at daily or higher resolution, it will appear that new solar power has a significant impact on emissions since the grid in question is still largely fossil-powered. Hourly resolution would reveal that new solar power largely displaces other solar on the build (and possibly operating) margin, and therefore has much less impact on emissions. This visibility is necessary to ensure that participants target times and locations where their interventions are most likely to be impactful.

Of the options listed here, an intervention lifecycle approach is likely the most appropriate. This option recognizes that in most cases, build margin impacts are likely to dominate over the long run as a project’s existence is factored into investment decisions in similar projects. The option is not without its flaws though, as it may not adequately capture the impacts of projects that adjust their operational approach on an ongoing basis (e.g. storage and demand-side management). More work will be needed, ideally in the form of both empirical investigation and energy system modeling, to assess the accuracy of this option.

It may be reasonable to assign weights differently depending on whether an intervention is primarily operational (e.g. demand shifting or storage operations) or capacity-based (e.g. installation of a solar or wind farm that will operate predictably over its life). Capacity-based interventions should trend toward 100% build margin weighting, while it may make sense to maintain a higher operating margin weighting for operational interventions.

There is a dire lack of supporting evidence for any of the potential approaches listed here. Without some form of validation (e.g. analysis of a methodology’s accuracy in the controlled setting of an electricity system capacity expansion model as in https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5985015, or case studies showing what projects deployed in different contexts would report), the chosen approach cannot be considered scientifically accurate or credible. This is of critical importance because an inaccurate weighting, e.g. giving operating margin a 50% weighting in a context where it should be 0%, could allow a completely non-impactful project to receive significant credit. This would directly incentivize the same behaviors that have plagued voluntary carbon markets in recent years, and would open GHGP to accusations of enabling greenwashing. The working groups responsible for developing any consequential metrics should consider building an affirmative evidence base to be a critical part of their work.

Additionality: as a Renewable Energy Certificate (REC) supplier, we are beginning to hear from prospective corporate customers that in anticipation of the upcoming Greenhouse Gas Protocol Scope 2 changes, they will begin requiring the procurement of RECs that can demonstrate “additionality”. When I request their definition of “additionality”, the prospective customer clarifies that by “additionality”, they mean a project that is not yet operational and will represent a new source of renewable electricity on the grid. I have heard this definition from many prospective customers that purport plans to continue following Greenhouse Gas Protocol guidance. At this definition’s level of simplicity, RECs purchased under these customers’ definition of “additionality” would not pass any of the tests described in Section 7 of the Consequential Electricity-Sector Emissions Impacts Consultation document. Therefore, it seems that aligning corporate procurement practices with Greenhouse Gas Protocol guidance is already proving to be a challenge.

Alternative Impact of Electricity Project Incentives: our company works closely with Native American tribes, which are often located in rural areas that make renewable energy development infeasible due to supply chain limitations. I am familiar with dozens of renewable energy projects owned and operated by tribes. None would have been built without philanthropic support from government or nonprofit sources. Based on my experience and that of my colleagues, I can confidently state that tribal renewable energy projects cannot be built without philanthropic support. While philanthropic capital is the sole factor enabling project development, this does not mean that the incentives generated by the project, such as RECs, cannot be impactful once the project is operational. REC revenue can provide real monetary benefits to tribal project owners over the operational life of the project; for example, eliminating the need to raise grant funding for unexpected operations, maintenance, and decommissioning costs if REC revenues are held in a fund dedicated to those activities. These costs are typically not feasible to fund in advance of project construction due to strict government and foundation grant application requirements. It does not appear that the full scope of impact that incentives such as RECs are considered in the consequential accounting methodology. Even if they cannot demonstrate additionality in a new renewable energy project being constructed, it is still possible to demonstrate additionality in a project’s continued operation. My company sees this as an unintended consequence of the structure of this methodology.

The most appropriate temporal granularity for emission factors is the smallest interval for which accurate data is available, and marginal emissions rates vary materially hour-to-hour due to diurnal and seasonal variations, as well as from impacts of congestion.

1. Enhanced accuracy and alignment with grid operations:
The core defense of hourly rates is that they accurately reflect the high frequency of changes in electricity generation and instantaneous grid dispatch. It is typically preferable to use hourly data or finer temporal granularity, as coarser data (e.g., annual) degrades the accuracy of the analysis due to diurnal and seasonal variations in marginal emissions rates.

Preventing misestimation: Relying on coarse accounting methods, such as annual averages, can lead to wildly inaccurate estimates of carbon emissions, potentially over- or under-estimating emissions. This gap is expected to increase as renewables saturate the grid, making hourly measurements necessary for accurate accounting.

Unlike attributional approaches, consequential accounting has the potential to highlight how incremental actions affect overall grid emissions. When used appropriately, these methods could complement existing Scope 2 frameworks by helping companies understand broader market impacts while preserving customer procurement flexibility. Importantly, RPS-compliant in-market procurement should continue to qualify under Scope 2 accounting, and voluntary procurement—both in-market and out-of-market—should remain additive, supported by feasibility safeguards and legacy protections for multi-year customer contracts. This is particularly relevant for those with long-term power contracts that were entered into under existing accounting rules.

While we support the creation of a consequential metric, the relationship between attributional and consequential accounting needs to be more clearly defined. Without clear guardrails, consequential metrics could introduce confusion in Scope 2 claims, reduce consistency in reporting, and increase compliance burdens, especially if used to justify mandatory requirements such as hourly matching or strict deliverability constraints. Applying consequential accounting without understanding the interplay with attributional accounting could unintentionally constrain customer choice, limit procurement options, and undermine voluntary market participation rather than encourage it.

Some methodologies have disadvantaged solutions such as renewable natural gas (RNG) and other lower carbon fuel types, despite their ability to deliver measurable, near-term emissions reductions by displacing higher-carbon fuels. For consequential accounting to be credible and effective, it must treat all energy sources fairly and recognize the full system value of diverse decarbonization pathways, including RNG. Overall, while the development of consequential accounting can be a valuable tool for impact assessment, it should remain optional and should not be used to impose more prescriptive procurement requirements within Scope 2 that reduce flexibility, clarity, or participation in clean energy markets.

The proposed Scope 2 TWG subgroup formula does not address the emissions impact from actions that produce incremental emissions, such as building a new natural gas-fired power plant to serve load. Instead, the proposed formula assumes all electricity projects are clean electricity projects. Failing to enable measurement of actions that both induce and avoid emissions will significantly limit the usefulness of the proposed framework.

The full lifecycle emissions impacts of electricity projects - akin to upstream and downstream Scope 3 emissions – should be accounted for elsewhere in a comprehensive consequential method, if applicable. The electricity sector consequential method should focus on emission impacts that directly result from changes to the electricity grid.

Calculating and reporting emission impacts for each reporting year, rather than estimating the entire lifetime of impacts at the outset of the project, best satisfies the GHG Protocol’s core principles of integrity, accuracy, comparability, feasibility, and decision usefulness by grounding the calculation in known, observable data.

The GHG Protocol should remain focused on accurate measurement of emissions and emissions-related metrics, rather than dictating the types of projects that qualify for measurement. Assessing the suitability of clean energy projects is the purview of target-setting organizations, such as SBTi and RE100. However, a regulatory requirement should be included as part of the framework – not as a test for additionality but as a threshold requirement for determining whether a clean energy project is actually voluntary.

It is feasible to include a regulatory requirement – independent of additionality tests – because it is a necessary threshold requirement for determining whether a clean energy project is actually voluntary.

In contrast, none of the other proposed additionality tests are feasible because defining additionality through the GHGP's current process is not feasible. While we support the development of an impact metric, defining and incorporating additionality tests as part of the proposed updates moves the Protocol beyond its traditional role of measuring emissions. Aside from its conceptual and historical incompatibility with the Protocol’s mission, taking on the challenge of defining additionality creates significant practical difficulties. Underlining that challenge is that none of the additionality frameworks referenced by the GHG Protocol - UNFCCC, Verra, US DOE 45V, RE100, Ever.Green, and TCAT – share a common requirement, option, or exclusion for even one of the listed additionality tests (see section 7.2 of the public consultation document). This is because, in practice, there can be no universally agreed-upon approach to additionality. Different approaches to additionality reflect a subjective balancing of stringency, accuracy, and feasibility that reflects each standard’s perspective, needs, and context because the fundamental question – is this action additional? – relies on a counterfactual claim. The GHG Protocol should resist calls to codify one perspective on additionality as part of a measurement standard. Failure to do so will divert resources, delay work, undermine consensus, and ultimately reduce the usefulness, credibility, and scalability of the final revisions.

Greening electric grids is a fundamentally different challenge from preserving rain forests.
