Based on peer reviewed research, SCED - locational and Statistical models are the best options to use for Operating Margin. For example, Steinsulz et al (2024) https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2753-3751/ad72f6/pdf analyzed generation data in ERCOT to estimate a benchmark Marginal Emissions Factor (MEF) and evaluated a number of classes of MEF models. They found that both dispatch and statistical MEF models have a high degree of agreement with the benchmark MEF, while heat rate and average emissions do not.

Models that use a single value for a large grid region, such as SCED - fuel on the margin, are not appropriate. Heat rate/LMP models are effective at identifying times of very low marginal operating emissions due to curtailment, but they do not accurately predict the operating margin at higher emissions rates. Scenario modeling methods are not appropriate for accounting for real world actions as they require oversimplifying real world conditions.

Although build margin is less knowable than operating margin, we support models that are 1) accessible and 2) minimize use of assumptions. Recent capacity additions and average emissions rates fit these criteria, supported by research from Pieter Gagnon (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2022.103915), which indicates average emissions rate are a good proxy for build margin, and WattTime/VERACI-T (http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5425615) analyzing recent capacity additions for build margin using a 50% weighting factor.

Stronger stance: Policy scenarios and capacity expansion modeling are unsuitable for standardized greenhouse gas impact assessment because they rely on layers of speculative assumptions that vary widely across geographies. Policy scenarios often embed cost projections tied to favorable or unfavorable policy environments, while capacity expansion models depend on uncertain forecasts of future electricity demand, technology costs and adoption rates, and policy impacts themselves.

In an integrated national REC market where REC buyers are responsive to REC prices (like the US voluntary market), the supply response and therefore emissions impact will be determined in the aggregate, not by the details of individual procurement details. As a result, it is inaccurate to think of different marginal emissions impacts for each procurement during a period of time. Any new procurement Q will add to aggregate demand that will raise REC prices nationally and stimulate new renewable projects on the aggregate supply curve. Therefore, all the procurements should receive the same marginal emissions impact during the year, equal to the average marginal impact of all the procurement.

The complete long-term emissions impact of the procurement should be considered at the time of the procurement. The impacts include:
1. The immediate price impacts: higher spot and futures prices for REC's, lower spot and futures prices in electricity markets where new generation is likely to be built, higher variance in electricity prices
2. The long-term change in generation mix and emissions: in response to the change in prices, new renewable generation comes on line, storage/DR/transmission capacity increases, new fossil fuel plants are delayed and/or existing fossil fuel plants are retired, and emissions are permanently lowered from the alternative baseline.

There should be a common marginal emissions impact for all procurement each year. The marginal emissions impact wouldn't change much each year, reflecting gradual changes in the mix of coal vs natural gas impacts.

The REC market, like other markets, is inherently additional and does not require separate additionality tests. Every procurement increases aggregate demand which raises prices to a market-clearing level that stimulates a matching quantity of new supply. Some have assumed that REC markets stop working because of "oversupply", disrupting "additionality". But this assumption is not supported by the market evidence (all REC's sold at positive prices) and inconsistent with standard economic assumptions (i.e.; that buyers and sellers respond to prices, which causes markets to find an equilibrium and clear).
There could be one market-wide test to check that the market is in fact clearing normally: Do suppliers tend to sell their REC's at a positive price?

Consequential accounting (which is different from "marginal impact") is a promising tool to help decarbonize the power sector in combination with other approaches. It can help direct investment to emissions hotspots around the globe and provide insight into decisionmaking on how we interact with and use the grid. If grounded in the well-established science of lifecycle assessment, it can provide a complementary perspective to Scope 2 accounting. However, it also comes with substantial risks that should not be brushed aside. Ignoring the "consequential" foundation of this science and instead focusing on just its "marginal" aspects, or just treating this approach as a feasibility release valve for more complex and robust Scope 2 accounting opens the door to greenwashing and erodes its impact. Consequential accounting, when done right, is quite complex and nuanced, and in many ways may be as equally if not more challenging to implement as the proposed scope 2 changes: it requires temporally and locationally granular accounting of activity and emissions factors, it requires strict quality criteria, and consideration of nuanced interactions with local policy and market environments. The current lack of standardized or verifiable emissions factors may make comparability, verification, and credibility difficult. Without strict guiderails, it has the potential to lead to widespread greenwashing and deviate from its theoretical promise to accelerate grid decarbonization. I am excited by the potential of consequential accounting, but it is equally important to consider and manage its risks so that it lives up to its potential.

If the goal is just to quantify impact from a generation project, then this formula is appropriate in that it considers both hour-specific and location-specific emission factors and activity data, which is critical for accurate calculation, since marginal impacts vary both in time and space. However, this formula is secondary to the initial determination of whether there is any consequential impact at all, which depends on factors such as additionality and interaction with other policy environments such as cap-and-trade systems or RPS. This formula also ignores impact of demand side actions on the grid.

If the goal is to quantify and minimize "global emissions impact", then consideration of all secondary effects would be appropriate, not only including upstream and downstream Scope 3 emissions, but also any secondary grid impacts beyond the marginal generators (which may or may not be included in the MER).

If the goal is to just provide a first order approximation or incentive signal, and not account for global atmospheric emission changes, then including secondary effects may not be necessary. However, some proximate lifecycle information may still be relevant (eg fugitive methane emissions for natural gas, which in some cases makes natural gas generation more GHG intensive than coal, which would affect decision and investment outcomes).

Example 1: Cap and trade region. As explained by the Clean Energy Buyer's Institute: "When a project activity is located in a region with a cap-and-trade program, such as the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, California’s Cap and Trade Program, and the European Union Emissions Trading System, there is a risk that the indirect emissions reductions at the marginal generator caused by the activity may allow for increased emissions at other times or at other generators, resulting in no net emissions reductions in the long term. In cap-and-trade programs, a regulatory cap is set on total emissions, and emitters must buy and trade emissions allowances to cover all their emissions. When the emissions cap is binding, taking an action that reduces power sector emissions may free up emissions allowances that can be used to pollute at a later time or be sold to another emitter that allows them to emit more. This risk can be mitigated by purchasing and retiring cap-and-trade allowances equivalent to the estimated emissions impact of a decision or reporting the activity as a voluntary set-aside in the cap-andtrade program (if such set-asides exist)."

Metrics such as net qualifying capacity (NQC) and effective load carrying capacity (ELCC) have been used commonly to establish how well a resource contributes to reliability needs during peak hours. Since peak hours tend to drive capacity expansion needs, these factors could be a reasonable approximation of a build margin weight.

An NQC/ELCC-like approach could potentially be used to establish build margin weights for each resource

CAISO splits these factors by geography and month of the year to reflect temporal and spatially-varying values of capacity. These values are typically calculated per season/month, region, and resource technology.

CAISO uses a specific (publicly documented) modeling approach to determine these factors, although similar factors could be potentially calculated using a simpler method (eg average capacity factor in the peak hour window for each grid region.

One feature of pure ELCC calculations is that they reflect “diminishing returns’: the more of a resource that is built, the more it meets system peak needs and pushes the peak to another time period that may be not as well served by that resource. This means that over time, the build margin weight of an oversaturated resource would decrease, putting more of an emphasis on the operating margin.

Another feature of an ELCC value is that if a storage project is operated economically, and prices are correlated with peak times, the storage device may have an ELCC near 100%, meaning that storage would primarily affect the build margin rather than the operating margin, although over time, that may decrease.

ELCC values have been widely used/explored by many of the major grid operators in the U.S., so ELCC values may already be publicly available in many regions. Support with Caveats: Support the introduction of a distinct Statement 3 on Impact, provided that this is clearly defined as a separate (3) "Impact Statement" as a part of a new "3-Statement" framework for the GHG Accounting Report incorporated in the revised GHG Protocol Corporate Suite of Standards and not as a separate voluntary metric with its own guidance. Explicitly define this Consequential framework as "Statement 3: GHG Impacts of Actions". It must be reported alongside but separately from the Physical and Contractual inventories.

The primary benefit of Consequential Accounting is that it is the only method that measures decarbonization. The challenge is that the GHG Protocol currently proposes keeping this separate from the main standard. If Impact Accounting is optional or secondary, it will be ignored in favor of the easier 'check-the-box' compliance of MBM. To ensure rapid decarbonization, this standard must be elevated to equal status with Scope 1, 2, and 3. It should be the 'Third Statement' in a complete GHG inventory

• Integrity: Claiming physical accuracy for financial instruments (MBM) violates the principle of integrity. Acknowledging them as "Market/Contract Footprints" restores integrity.
• Relevance: To be relevant in a climate emergency, a standard must measure whether emissions are actually decreasing (Impact). An inventory that balances to zero via contracts while global emissions rise is not "relevant" to the decision-making needs of saving the planet.

The primary objective of the AMI Standard should be to serve as the 'Integrity Filter' for the Corporate Inventory. It should not just be an optional 'extra' report. It should provide the methodology for determining which Market Instruments (Statement 2) are valid for decarbonization claims. If an action shows 'Zero Impact' under the AMI standard, it should automatically invalidate any corresponding reduction claim in the Scope 2 Market-Based inventory.

The primary objective should be to establish a rigorous, standardized methodology for quantifying Consequential Impact (Statement 3) that stands equal to, but separate from, the attributional inventory.

A neutral accounting standard must report Physical Reality (Statement 1), Market Action (Statement 2), and System Consequence (Statement 3) as distinct, non-fungible datasets. This 'Three-Statement Report' empowers target setters and validators with the clarity they need to assess true net-zero alignment, rather than forcing the accounting system to conflate these distinct concepts into a single, muddied number.

By formalizing this as a distinct 'Impact Statement,' the GHG Protocol remains neutral—it simply provides the math for calculating 'avoided emissions.' This allows external programs (like SBTi) to set specific 'Contribution Targets' based on this metric, rather than forcing the GHG Protocol to dilute the physical inventory to accommodate these claims.

The GHG Protocol's move to a Three-Statement Framework (Physical, Market, Impact) provides the most robust basis for the ISO 14060 and SBTi standards. It offers a 'Menu of Metrics' that allows you to set precise, science-based targets without compromising accounting integrity:
1. Abatement Targets: Must be validated against Statement 1 (Physical) to ensure absolute emissions are reducing in line with planetary boundaries.
2. Procurement Targets: Can be validated against Statement 2 (Market) to drive demand for clean energy instruments (e.g., RE100).
3. Contribution Targets: Must be validated against Statement 3 (Impact) to verify that Beyond Value Chain Mitigation (BVCM) claims are real and additional.
This separation allows your standards to set the rules (e.g., 'Target 1 must be met before claiming Target 3') while the GHG Protocol remains the neutral scorekeeper providing the unmixed data for each category.

The proposed formula correctly identifies that consequential impact is a function of the marginal unit displaced at a specific time and location (Emissionality). This aligns with the "Truth of Causal Change" required for Statement 3. It accurately captures the delta between the baseline (what would have happened) and the intervention.

The formula focusing on marginal emission rates is superior to the MBM's average rates for measuring change. However, for this to be 'fit for purpose,' it must be framed not just as a project assessment tool, but as a corporate reporting standard. Companies should be required to report the 'Emissions Impact' of their Scope 2 procurement alongside their inventory. Without this, MBM remains a 'feel-good' metric that disconnects corporate claims from atmospheric reality.

To serve as a robust basis for target-setting standards, the AMI formula must produce a metric that is auditable and distinct from the corporate inventory.
I recommend framing this as a 'System Impact Statement'. This provides a neutral, quantified value (tCO2e avoided/induced) that validates whether a company's market choices (Statement 2) actually drove decarbonization. This separation protects the Protocol's neutrality by reporting what happened (Impact) separately from who is responsible (Inventory), allowing policymakers to decide how to incentivize each

Secondary effects, specifically "leakage" (emissions increasing in a neighboring grid) and "embodied emissions" (construction impacts), must be included if they exceed a materiality threshold (e.g., 5%). Ignoring upstream fuel emissions distorts the "avoided" benefit and risks overstating the climate impact of interventions. A lifecycle perspective is required to prove true fossil fuel displacement.

Annual reporting based on ex-post marginal emission rates aligns with corporate financial cycles and reflects the actual grid reality. "Lifetime" reporting relies on uncertain 20-year forecasts that are prone to manipulation and inaccuracy. Statement 3 must be dynamic and verifiable annually to maintain credibility alongside the annual inventory.

I support a rigorous Additionality Framework because it is essential for the 'Impact-Adjusted' reporting model. If we are to use Statement 3 to validate Statement 2 claims, the additionality tests must be robust enough to distinguish between 'passive' procurement (buying existing RECs) and 'active' decarbonization (funding new capacity). I recommend a tiered system: 'High Impact' (proven additionality, 100% claimable) vs. 'Low Impact' (no additionality, 0% claimable for targets)."

A company can claim "100% Market Alignment" in Statement 2 based on contracts, but can only claim "Progress toward Net Zero" if Statement 3 confirms those contracts were additional. If a contract has no additionality (0% impact), it should have 0% value for emission reduction targets. This creates a "Race to the Top" for high-quality instruments.

Propose a "Surplus Test" to prevent double counting with regulatory obligations like RPS. Furthermore, an "Emissionality/Locational Marginal" test should be explicitly recognized to quantify the higher impact of projects in "dirty" grids (e.g., Poland) versus "clean" grids (e.g., Norway).

Additionality is inherently context-dependent. A solar project in a coal-heavy grid has a fundamentally different consequential impact than one in a solar-saturated grid where it might lead to curtailment. Regional baselines are essential for credible Statement 3 accounting; global averages must not be used here. If "Positive Lists" are used these should be regional.

Statement 3 requires higher rigor because causal claims ("I reduced emissions") demand a higher evidentiary bar than association claims in Statement 2 ("I bought attributes"). The risk of greenwashing is highest in Statement 3, so the verification standards must be stricter.

SCED-locational is the gold standard as it reflects the actual physics of dispatch and congestion. Average Emission Rates must be explicitly deemed inappropriate for consequential accounting (Statement 3) as they reflect attribution, not the causal chain of dispatch (the marginal unit). Using average rates here would duplicate Statement 1 logic and fail to measure impact. Methods used need to reflect real-time grid physics.

"Recent capacity additions" look backward. In a rapidly transitioning grid, what was built yesterday (e.g., gas) may not be what is built tomorrow (e.g., storage/wind). Capacity Expansion Models are necessary to capture the forward-looking structural response of the grid to new demand.

GHG Protocol should provide a "Methodology Hierarchy" similar to the LBM data hierarchy. Projects should use the most granular model available (e.g., Nodal SCED) and fallback to zonal models only if data is unavailable.
Curtailment Risk: Metrics that assess the probability of renewable curtailment should be considered, as adding capacity to a constrained node yields zero impact.

Nodal pricing reflects physical transmission constraints, which is the reality of the grid. Nodal pricing/emissions reflect physical transmission constraints. However, it may be difficult to get data on a nodal level which suggest balancing area might be a good compromise.

Electricity markets dispatch on 5-minute or 15-minute intervals. Matching this granularity captures the ramping of peaker plants accurately. It should at least be hourly, with exceptions if data is not available. For consequential impact (Column 3), hourly marginal data is required to accurately quantify avoided emissions. This differs from the contractual inventory (Column 2) where annual matching may still be legally valid. Marginal emissions vary by hour. Impact claims must be hourly to be credible in Pillar 3.

A static "50/50" weight (as used in CDM) is arbitrary and obsolete. The weighting should reflect the time horizon. Operational interventions (e.g., demand response) primarily affect the Operating Margin (100% OM). Long-term capacity additions (e.g., new wind farm) affect the Build Margin. 3Degrees supports consequential accounting as a valuable tool for assessing the real‑world emissions impacts of corporate actions. This approach shifts focus from inventory metrics to actual emission reductions, enabling companies to identify and disclose interventions that produce tangible decarbonization outcomes. However, realizing this potential requires more than revised calculation methods. Without clarity on how reporters would apply these methods—or how results would connect to existing corporate inventories—it is difficult to evaluate their implications or provide meaningful feedback.

Adopting standard approaches always involves trade-offs, where the benefits provided by the standardized approach are weighed against the cost, level-of-effort, constraints, practice changes, data availability, and other factors that implementing the standard would require. With this in mind, examining an accounting method in isolation with no commentary on its purpose or use, leaves us stymied as to how to evaluate these tradeoffs. Furthermore, a consultation structured in this way risks failing to attract appropriate stakeholder attention such that potentially important points of view are never heard.

As such, 3Degrees is concerned that the GHGP proposed Consequential Accounting Methods for Electricity-Sector Emissions lacks sufficient guidance and clarity regarding its intended purpose for a productive consultation.

Mature consequential accounting methods for the electricity sector already exist, including those within the GHG Protocol. It is unclear what additional value a new method adds or how it fits within current reporting frameworks. Given ISO’s 2024 reaffirmation of ISO 14064‑2:2019 as a still-current standard for project accounting—and ongoing ISO/GHGP harmonization—introducing a new GHGP method now seems unnecessary and poorly timed.

Third, while the issue of “mutual exclusivity” is not addressed in the proposed Consequential Accounting Methods for Electricity-sector Emissions, we understand the topic is still being considered within the Actions and Market Instruments discussions. As such, we here posit that the contractual ledger and the impact ledger do not need to be mutually exclusive.
Many companies seek to understand the impact of their actions in both attributional and consequential terms, as the two expressions convey distinct but critical information about intervention impacts. Companies should be able to claim and report both kinds of information to their customers and stakeholders, provided it is clear that the two ledgers are not additive.

By using the consequential Scope 2 methods, companies can identify where to pursue PPAs or source RECs from specific suppliers to maximize impact and should be able to quantify and disclose those benefits. At the same time, they should retain the ability to report a full market‑based inventory using allocational accounting. The two approaches provide distinct yet complementary insights into real‑world impact and overall GHG performance. Limiting reporting to one ledger would restrict transparency and flexibility.

Lastly, 3Degrees is concerned about the sequence of decisions leading up to this consultation, as the materials in the GHGP’s Standards Development and Governance Repository appear misaligned with this first public consultation, and there has been insufficient transparency and accountability regarding how and why this shift occurred. Per GHGP’s strengthened governance model, trust and transparency are foundational because the standards only function effectively when market actors and regulators can see that the rules are fair, stable, and applied consistently across all users. We recommend that GHGP clearly explain how and why the content of this consultation diverges from the direction previously discussed in the Scope 2 TWG and the consequential accounting subgroup, including the rationale for any substantive changes.

The Section 6 proposal language is, frankly, confusing so we are uncertain how best to comment and simply cannot affirm that the proposal is appropriate. Here are central points of our confusion:

The text in 6.1 states that the TWG proposal is intended to “capture the emissions impacts of electricity projects” while the headline statement in 6.0 states the proposal is intended to “quantify consequential emissions impacts from electricity procurement.” Further, the formula itself uses the variable “MWh procured.”

Procurement assessment and new-built project assessment are different aims. Not every procurement involves a new project, not every procurement is a low-carbon initiative, not every procurement is specific to the time and place of specific generation resources. As worded, the formula could be interpreted as attempting to sum up the emissions associated with all electricity purchased by a reporter in the reporting year. This interpretation aligns with the language “emission impacts from electricity procurement.”

We suspect however that the TWG’s intention is to provide a formula representing the reporting-year benefits of low-carbon MWhs procured and claimed in a company’s market-based Scope 2 inventory. In this case, the formula provides an “avoided emissions” calculation pertaining to these procured MWh. We note that the word “impact” can have either positive or negative connotations, so our interpretation is uncertain. As to scope, the formula’s intended use might be limited to certain kinds of procurements (Whole projects? New projects (new when?) Do tariffs count? etc. We note the phrase “electricity project generation” in the middle of page 8 and in the text of Question 19, but we are not clear on the specifics here.

Without a clearer understanding of the TWG’s intention and, as noted in our response to Question 18, without an idea of the proposed use of these calculations, we are unable to provide tuned commentary and cannot affirm the formula’s appropriateness.

The types of secondary effects we’d recommend considering would depend on the purpose of the calculation method. That said, we’d encourage the GHGP to consider including recurring upstream secondary effects. These recurring effects could be substantial in some instances, particularly for renewable energy projects that displace fossil-generated electricity because of ongoing upstream emissions from fuel extraction, processing, transport, and methane leakage associated with fossil-generated electricity. In the first year, the effects may appear modest once you include the emissions from manufacturing renewable energy assets (e.g., solar panels), but in subsequent years, as the renewable project continues to avoid fuel‑cycle emissions, avoided emissions are significant. Ignoring this dynamic, or failing to recognize it explicitly for solar and other renewables, leads to an incomplete and potentially misleading picture of their true emissions benefits. Some additional relevant secondary effects GHGP could consider include the year‑by‑year changes in project economics as renewable penetration increases, which in turn create incentives to add storage to both existing and new projects.

Emissions impacts should be calculated and reported each reporting year, with ex post data. Annual reporting allows year-specific generation and grid emissions data to be reflected in results and aligns with annual corporate inventory cycles. Reporting a project’s lifetime impacts at the outset would require assumptions about lifetime generation and grid conditions, which may diverge from measured generation and grid emissions data in later years.

Note that without an understanding of the purpose and use of these calculations, we cannot be certain that our answer here is firm. For example, estimating emission benefits to be derived from forward-looking, long-term procurement contracts is a common feature of many buyer decision-making processes. For this purpose, only a forward-looking, whole-life estimate is appropriate.

For what it’s worth, it is not obvious what stakeholder actions will be influenced by an annual procurement impact metric that sits alongside inventory metrics. Especially with a scope 2 market-based proposal that severely narrows the geographic range of qualifying electricity procurements - hence precluding reporters from pursuing high-emissions-impact options if their load is in a clean-grid location - it is just not clear what decision-useful information the metric will convey.

3Degrees does not support the inclusion of any additionality standard in the consequential accounting guidance. This is for programmatic reasons, electricity system reasons, and to maintain the integrity and transparency of the accounted emissions.

Programmatic role:
The GHGP should offer guidance similar to ISO 14064‑2, where they require the project to define and justify a baseline scenario representing what would reasonably have happened without the project and to quantify the emissions impact relative to that baseline, without passing judgment on the project’s key causal factors. This is because there are many legitimate ways to apply project accounting and the resulting emission calculations, not all of which require proof of causation.

Instead, the standard should leave additionality questions to programs and users to layer in where and when appropriate to their purposes.

Electricity System:
In most of the world, electricity project development is enabled by a large ecosystem of stakeholders, often competing for development opportunities. While corporate offtakers can play an important role in bringing new projects to fruition, it is a dynamic market and it now stretches credibility to assert that any one company’s particular action was causal; another buyer would be right behind, and in any case the developments are economically advantageous for their developers, financiers, and other participants. It is for this (and other) reasons that carbon credit program authorities stopped validating new renewable energy-based carbon projects in developed countries, several years ago.

Integrity and transparency

Even if programmatic and electricity system factors were not at play, we would not recommend additionality tests in this standard. Additionality tests purport to confirm or prove the level-of-importance a specific actor plays in a complex transaction involving many parties. Even when prescriptive, they are prone to error and controversy.

Rather than attempting to prescribe the ideal additionality test, we believe it is more credible and transparent to avoid them altogether, and make clear that the emissions impact calculations represent the impact of the project without asserting any causal relationship between the reporter and the project’s realization. In this way, stakeholders can decide whether to embrace the emission benefits as important and relevant to the reporter’s performance, or not. As they see fit.

As a leading independent power producer with a portfolio of wind, solar, storage, and transmission projects, we support the development of consequential accounting methods for electricity-sector activities within Scope 2. A robust framework, particularly the TWG subgroup's proposed impact-based accounting that nets avoided emissions from clean energy procurement against induced emissions from consumption using marginal rates, would better align Scope 2 with actual GHG reductions, incentivizing high-impact investments over allocational matching. Overall, benefits likely outweigh challenges if GHGP adopts the subgroup's full formula, emphasizing marginal frameworks for both procurement and consumption.

Potential Benefits:
Focus on GHG Outcomes: Consequential methods prioritize emissions impacts while driving real decarbonization. This supports Emissions First Partnership principles by rewarding projects in dirty grids, potentially increasing corporate demand for high impact projects.
Transmission Integration: Methods could quantify avoided emissions from infrastructure that enables clean energy flow to fossil-heavy grids, fostering investment in underserved areas.
Market Growth: By creating comparability in impact claims, it could expand voluntary procurement to support deployments in more challenging, high-impact locations.
Additional information for stakeholders: A net impact metric would allow stakeholders to assess a overall emissions impacts against a baseline. Both the induced consumption and avoided emissions are fundamental to understanding the overall picture of a company’s impact.
A consequential accounting method could serve as a key pathway alongside the Scope 2 inventory: Paired with the induced consumption metric, this methodology allows for companies to disclose their impacts on a percentage basis, in addition to absolute basis, allowing stakeholders to compare a company’s level of spurred emissions avoidance to the emissions it is responsible for inducing.

Challenges:
Data Needs and Feasibility: Marginal emission rates require standardized, accessible data (e.g., hourly SCED-based rates from system operators). While tools like WattTime or REsurety exist, global inconsistencies could raise costs and feasibility barriers in emerging markets.
Comparability and Clarity: Without clear GHGP guidelines on additionality or weighting (e.g., build vs. operating margins), claims risk inconsistency and undermines trust. Phased implementation with registries could mitigate this.

Unintended Consequences:
Project Shifts: Low-impact projects in clean grids might see reduced demand, potentially slowing deployments in those locations, but this could redirect capital to higher-emissions regions, amplifying net GHG reductions.
Equity Issues: Smaller reporters or regions without granular data might face exclusion; GHGP should provide free, credible sources (e.g., via partnerships with ISOs/RTOs) to ensure broad adoption.

We recommend revising the underlying project accounting standards (e.g., the GHG Protocol Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Reductions from Grid-Connected Electricity Projects) to explicitly account for avoided emissions from transmission lines and battery storage. For transmission, quantify reductions when connecting a dirty grid (e.g., coal-heavy) to a cleaner one, estimating displaced fossil generation via energy flows across the line (using OM/BM methods adjusted for interconnection capacity). For storage, account for emissions avoided by shifting output to high-emission hours. This enhances feasibility for developers enabling inter-regional decarbonization, while improving comparability through standardized data (e.g., flow monitoring). Challenges include data access for marginal dispatch; unintended consequences could be over-crediting without additionality safeguards. Benefits are that it accelerates the deployment of transmission and storage for real-world impact.

The formula currently only illustrates the emissions avoided by procurement. There should also be a component to also allow the netting of emissions caused by consumption to show the net emissions impact. For existing projects, this could be the comparison of their Scope 2 location-based emissions compared to the avoided emissions. For projecting the impact of proposed projects, we think more clarity is needed.

While hourly, nodal granularity is crucial for measuring marginal emissions and congestion accurately at the generator level, this level of granularity may not be possible for reporters aiming to quantify the aggregated avoided emissions of the clean energy they generated over a period of time, such as annually. Therefore, evaluating impacts at the node to ensure credible and precise net emissions impact claims for a particular project should be encouraged, but companies should not be prohibited from reporting the avoided emissions benefits of their operating fleets using regional marginal grid factors and/or credible sources, such as the U.S. EPA AVERT tool. This is still an important piece of information to communicate the benefits of renewable energy and having GHGP guidance to add credibility to reporters' approaches would be helpful, especially in light of emerging anti-greenwashing regulations that require claims be tied to credible international standards or methodology.

Below is rationale for hourly temporal granularity in marginal emission rates. However, similar to the previous comment related to grid regions, companies should still be able to report their estimated avoided emissions as a result of their operational renewable energy fleet's production in the preceding year using credible sources for emissions factors, such as the U.S. EPA AVERT tool. The GHG Protocol should account for this nuance in reporting as long as reporters are transparent in the methodology used.

Appropriate Interval Selection: The most suitable temporal granularity for emission factors is the smallest interval for which accurate data is available. Marginal emissions rates can vary significantly from hour to hour due to diurnal and seasonal changes, as well as the effects of grid congestion. Therefore, selecting a granularity that captures these variations leads to more precise measurement, where such granularity is reasonable feasible.

Enhanced Accuracy and Grid Alignment: Hourly rates are favored because they accurately reflect the high frequency of changes in electricity generation and the real-time nature of grid dispatch. Using hourly data—or even finer intervals—is generally preferable, as coarser temporal resolutions, such as annual averages, can diminish the accuracy of emissions analysis. This loss of accuracy is particularly pronounced due to the regular fluctuations in marginal emissions rates throughout the day and across different seasons.

Preventing Misestimation of Emissions: Utilizing coarse accounting methods, such as annual averages may result in either overestimation or underestimation of actual emissions. As renewable energy sources become more integrated into the grid, the need for hourly measurements becomes more critical to ensure accurate accounting, since the variability in generation and emissions increases.

Alignment with GHG Protocol Recommendations: The Greenhouse Gas Protocol recommends in its revisions to the Location-Based Method (LBM) that hourly intervals be considered the most precise form of temporal granularity. We support this recommendation being voluntary for LBM reporters or for reporters with impacts over a certain threshold and advocate for reporters having the option to apply the same level of precision to consequential metrics.

By their definition, locational marginal emissions (LMEs) describe how system emissions change with respect to marginal changes in power demand/production and thus we believe the operating margin consequential emissions are truly described by the locational marginal emissions (LMEs) derived from the economic dispatch problem. If data describing LMEs is not available with a good temporal or spatial granularity, we believe the other selected approaches - particularly the Heat-rate/LMP based estimation and fuel-on-margin approaches can serve to approximate this. An accounting scheme should use a hierarchy of data availability as proposed in the market based methods consultation, for example (1) LME - hourly, (2) fuel on margin - hourly, (3) heat-rate/LMP - hourly, (4) LME - daily, etc. Regarding the difference based approach we believe that this is a poor approximation of LMEs as the system emissions can have significant changes across dispatch periods not just from load changes but also from (VRE) resource availability which leads us to believe such an approach could poorly approximate LMEs in some scenarios. Furthermore, it seems that the difference based approach assigns a single marginal emission rate to the entire system. This is inaccurate as due to transmission constraints we’ve seen that marginal emission rates can vary significantly across system nodes/regions (see the regional characteristics section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025).

CAPEX modeling which correctly reflects grid development conditions serves as the true description of how an energy project will change the build margin of the grid Recent capacity additions, policy scenarios, and predictive CAPEX modeling seem to approximate CAPEX modeling of the true development conditions reasonably well. However, the average emission rate can be significantly different than the new capacity being displaced. Take for example the average emissions factor in coal heavy US grids such as in the intermountain west (see the regional characteristics section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025) where new capacity being added is in the form of gas and renewables, while the average emissions factor is much higher due to the high legacy coal penetration. In general, as renewables and cleaner new generation technologies come down in price, the average emission rate will become a poor approximation of the new capacity additions which electricity projects displace.

While a company’s ability to perform accurate modeling is outside the scope of our research, we’ve seen characteristics of marginal emission rates tend to remain quite similar within regions (see the regional characteristics section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025) and so creating a set of planning studies which define build margin rates for common project types across regions seems to be a reasonable approach to removing the knowledge and investment burden from entities wishing to perform such accounting on their projects. We additionally note that methods used to calculate marginal emission rates and long run marginal emission rates are project size agnostic, allowing for general calculation approaches to be developed and used across development types.

Long run marginal emission rates have shown promise for combining both the operating margin and build margin impacts of energy projects (Bhandarkar, R et al. “Are EVs Cleaner Than We Think? Evaluating Consequential Greenhouse Gas Emissions from EV Charging” 2025) and may be of interest to investigate as well.

From our simulations we’ve found that nodal granularity is important and leads to higher levels of marginal emission accuracy, and is thus always preferable. However, regarding the minimum level of granularity, from our research we’ve seen that in WECC and ERCOT regions tend to be well connected within themselves and thus tend to share marginal emission rate characteristics, however, when considering interregional transmission we observe more transmission constraints and thus can see significant differences in LMEs between regions. It should be noted there does also exist some intraregional congestion in some cases, particularly regarding wind development areas in the cheyenne-denver corridor and thus nodal LMEs are certainly preferable to larger granularity, however zonal emission rates or even balancing area and regional rates would likely be an overall reasonable approximation if necessary (see the carbon regional characteristics section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025).

In areas with high penetration of VRE resources we see significant hour to hour variance in simulation. In particular, for areas with high amounts of solar development we see marginal emissions trends which are highly correlated to the hour of the day (see the hourly and seasonal characteristics section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025). If data allows, finer grain sub hourly rates would only improve accuracy, however, we recognize that this level of data granularity may be hard to access.

While we have only preliminary results regarding the build margin aspect of consequential accounting, it seems as though the marginal impact on the build margin is best measured through a capacity expansion analysis or a long run marginal emission analysis as we’ve described previously. These approaches should provide information on impacts to both the build and operating margin and thus the respective weights will not need to be guessed but will rather be inherent to the methodology.

LevelTen Energy is the world's largest clean energy marketplace for corporate and institutional buyers. In the last 10 years, LevelTen has facilitated transactions that supported more than 16 GW of new-build renewable capacity across North America and Europe.

LevelTen is not providing detailed responses to this public consultation for Consequential Methods as we believe that corporate buyers interested in pursuing the standard should have the primary voice. However, we are providing feedback on a specific concern that we feel GHGP should consider, which derives from LevelTen’s unique role at the forefront of storage/hybrid contracting.

With increasing amounts of intermittent renewable energy being deployed each year, battery storage will become critical to achieving grid decarbonization. Batteries will be essential to support time-matched strategies, where buyers need to shift renewable generation to match their load profiles. Batteries will also be crucial to support consequential strategies, allowing buyers to direct charging during low-carbon hours and to discharge during high-emissions hours.

To support both use cases, LevelTen is currently developing process workflows (e.g., EAC/GC
registry interface, charge/discharge record tracking) to deliver a seamless solution that is compliant with all relevant standards. LevelTen’s intent is to then make those “storage shift” solutions available at scale to a range of buyers and sellers, including via bilateral contracting mechanisms and traded products.

Our concern is that consequential accounting methodologies could be drafted in a way that
inadvertently eliminates the opportunity to deliver storage shift at scale, which would undercut a critical tool for corporate decarbonization and storage asset finance. Specifically, we are concerned that a strict application of the “counterfactual” principle inherent in consequential methodologies could prevent corporates from claiming GHG emissions reductions associated with executed storage shift contracts.

As an example, imagine a corporate executes a one-year forward storage shift agreement with an operating storage asset that contractually requires the asset to charge during the lowest emissions hours and discharge during the highest emissions hours each day. Because this contract would dictate the battery’s dispatch over the entire year, we believe the buyer should be able to claim the associated emissions reductions under a consequential methodology.
·
Our concern is that a “strict” counterfactual definition might attempt to remove from the emissions calculation certain days when wholesale market prices suggest the battery “might have” charged and discharged during the same hours dictated by the shift contract. LevelTen would argue strongly that this “strict” interpretation would be technically unreasonable and would, in practice, eliminate a critical storage contracting and dispatch strategy that could deliver meaningful global emissions reductions at scale because:

(a) Even if strict counterfactual analysis suggested that emissions-based dispatch coincided with a hypothetical market-based dispatch, the reality is that the storage shift contract locked in the emissions-based strategy by contractually removing the battery’s operational flexibility.

(b) The strict counterfactual analysis would also assume to know which wholesale market signals (e.g., hourly arbitrage, ancillary services, capacity, etc.) the battery would have followed on a given day when, in fact, that could never be known.

In conclusion, the counterfactual should not be based on some model of how the battery might
have dispatched in the absence of a storage shift contract. Instead, it should be based on the fact that, absent the storage shift contract, the battery would have had total flexibility to pursue whatever strategy it wanted, but the contract removed that flexibility to ensure it would be operated exclusively to lower grid emissions.

As a leading battery energy storage developer in the United States, esVolta acknowledges that a consequential accounting method is necessary to accurately characterize the system-level impact of energy storage.
We strongly support the consequential method as a means of incentivizing and rewarding energy storage systems for their role in decarbonizing the electricity grid. Therefore, the consequential method must be incorporated within the GHG Protocol alongside attributional methods.

The proposed formula as currently drafted only accounts for avoided emissions and does not account for induced emissions. At esVolta, we evaluate the avoided emissions of our battery energy storage projects by taking the difference of the induced emissions caused by charging the batteries and the avoided emissions by discharging the batteries. Were we to measure our avoided emissions without subtracting our induced emissions, our inventory would be inaccurate and hugely overstate the avoided emissions of our facilities.

Consequential accounting methods, by their focus on measuring future changes in emissions due to an action undertaken rather than measuring present emissions, can further incentivize emissions-reducing actions and projects. The biggest challenges with the development and use of consequential accounting methods involve verification of projected changes in future emissions and the associated cost of verification, as well as reconciling emissions calculated under attributional accounting for a present time period with what emissions for that same time period were projected to be under consequential accounting, whenever the emissions figures from both these methods differ.

The two formula factors of electricity consumption per transaction/hour and the marginal emission rate per unit of electricity for a given region/time/conditions are appropriately indicative for the formula to quantify effectively the emissions impact of electricity projects.

Secondary effects that should be considered are emissions changes in fuel extraction, refining and transportation, as well as in fugitive and vented emissions and from biofuel consumption. These emissions changes can be quantified using the emissions rates and projected changes in consumption of the fuels involved compared to the baseline scenario.

Reporting the emissions impacts of electricity projects every year, instead of once as a lifetime total, more effectively enables verification that emissions impacts of electricity projects are occurring as projected throughout the lifetime of the project.

For regulatory and timing tests, both are already utilized in multiple other additionality frameworks, indicating widespread recognition of their principles as a useful basis for demonstrating additionality. For common practice tests, it is fair to consider widely implemented types of projects as mainstream, and avoided emissions should not be due to actions that everyone else in a region/sector is also doing. For positive lists, green and net zero technologies contributing to reductions in emissions, which also tend to be newer, less adopted technologies, are a useful basis for demonstrating additionality. But the concern that a positive list can be too broad and end up misused is significant enough that a positive list should only be optional. For performance standard tests, a quantitative benchmark in baseline emissions rate, renewable penetration level, etc. is also a useful basis for demonstrating additionality, but other tests are more useful, hence why a performance standard test should only be optional. For first-of-its-kind tests, the introduction of a new technology, scale or application to a market/region, by its very nature, is different from mainstream practices in that market/region, and on that basis should be considered a useful test of additionality.

Only the contractual/tenor test may not be feasible as a test of additionality, as the financing for a project may have been provided and/or construction started before a long-term contract or commitment with a buyer has been secured. The other eight additionality tests listed in question 28 are all feasible. The regulatory test is feasible as it is simply requires referring to existing laws and regulations and verifying whether the activity is already required under those laws and regulations. The timing test, financial analysis test, barrier test and performance standard test are all feasible using project documentation from the early stages of the project process, where any incentives that were decisive to barriers overcome, expected financial returns, and/or projected outperformances of key benchmarks, as well as to the project going ahead, would be recorded. The common practice test and first-of-its-kind test are both feasible by comparing a project and its technologies/scale/applications used with other projects in the same market/region. The positive list is feasible as project details can be cross-referenced with the list of technologies, project types and/or circumstances that automatically demonstrate additionality.

There are no other additionality tests outside the nine listed in question 28 that should be included in an additionality framework. I instead suggest the inclusion of a requirement that the baseline emissions scenario used for any additionality test for a project be updated on a 2 to 5 year basis, in order to more accurately measure avoided emissions.

The most appropriate methodologies for determining operating margin emission rates for renewable energy projects are the ones that can use empirical or recorded data to quantify emission rates, which is the case for both SCED sensitivity analysis, statistical, and capacity factor based methodologies. In contrast, scenario modeling, heat-rate/LMP, and difference-based approaches all use estimates rather than hard data to quantify operating margin emission rates, and while using estimates can still yield accurate emission rates, it will not be as accurate as emission rates quantified based on hard data.
Recent capacity additions;Policy scenario ;Capacity expansion modeling ;

The recent capacity addition methodology is the only one of the four build margin methodologies to use empirical data in its calculations, and on that basis should be considered appropriate for quantifying build margin emission rates for renewable energy projects. The policy scenario methodology, due to its basis in countries' existing and planned national energy policies as summed up in the Stated Policies Scenario, should also be considered appropriate. The capacity expansion modeling methodology, through its simulations of multiple grid capacity change scenarios, can also be appropriate for quantifying build margin emission rates. Only the average emission factor methodology would not be appropriate, as averaging existing grid generation is a more generalized and less accurate methodology for quantifying build margin emission rates compared to the other methodologies that use hard, specific data or detailed existing and planned national policies.

One significant factor, through which GHG Protocol can assess the applicability of emission rate methodologies towards different types of projects, is project scope. Operating margin emission rates may be more appropriate for projects that only significantly impact the marginal generators in a grid, or whose impact on the grid can be described as a one-time change. Build margin emission rates, on the other hand, may be better suited to larger scope projects that significantly impact the entire grid or whose impact on the grid occurs over multiple phases in time.

Some of the operating margin and build margin emission rates methodologies can also be adapted for use in projects covering ground, marine and air transport, with each vehicle being treated like a marginal unit and an entire vehicle fleet as the equivalent of a power grid for the purposes of measuring emissions impacts.

Grid region was selected as it is the next most granular spatial boundary after the country level, which a majority of the global coverage OMER datasets listed in section 8.1 function at. Setting the maximum appropriate spatial granularity level at grid region creates an impetus for these global OMER datasets to transition to this more granular spatial boundary, improving the detail, quality and applicability of global OMER data for all users. In addition to this, GHG Protocol should also take a proactive role in initiating a transition by all OMER datasets towards a nodal level of spatial granularity in the long-term.

There is already a push towards the use of hourly data in the proposed revision to the GHG Protocol Scope 2 Emissions Standard. Having the maximum appropriate level of temporal granularity for OMER and BMER data be broader than the hourly level will hinder the transition to hourly data that is being pushed for in other emissions standards.

GHG Protocol's own Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Emissions from Grid-Connected Electricity Projects, by its nature of being a complementary tool in GHG Protocol's full slate of standards and other resources, should be considered appropriate for assigning build and operating margin weights to electricity projects. CDM Tool07 is developed by the world's most significant climate change authority in the UNFCCC, whose credibility makes CDM Tool07 appropriate for assigning build and operating margin weights. In addition to these two, intervention lifecycle approaches are an appropriate tool, as whether or not a project is already anticipated in capacity planning, and by extension already part of a large-scale change to the grid, is a useful indicator to determine the extent to apply operating and/or build margin rates to the project.
